articles.title: Germany news: Leftist BSW rules out reducing ties with far-right AfD
articles.summary: A motion had been filed by senior BSW leaders to reject any "de facto" support of a far-right government. Party founder Sahra Wagenknecht has said limited cooperation could provide a "window of…

image.caption: 'We are ready to talk:' The BSW federal party congress met in Dresden on SatrudayImage: Jens Schlüter/AFP

blocks.text: November 28, 2026
Left-wing BSW party votes against measure limiting cooperation with far-right AfD

blocks.caption: BSW founder Sahra Wagenknecht rejected a formal partnership with the far right, but says there is limited scope for cooperation Image: Jens Schlüter/AFP

blocks.text: The left-wing populist party Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW), formerly the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (also BSW) voted against a measure that would have limited cooperation with the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) on the federal level.

During the party conference in the eastern city of Dresden, a majority of the approximately 600 delegates voted against a motion put forth by several founding BSW members calling for a clearer distinction from the far right.

The basis for the vote came after the AfD came out on top in September's state election in the eastern state of Saxony Anhalt with 39 seats. The victory is being seen as a major win for Germany's far right. In October, the AfD's Tobias Rausch in Saxony-Anhalt became Germany's first far-right state parliament speaker since World War II.
With the BSW's five seats, the two parties on the opposite extremes of the political spectrum would combine for a majority of the 83 seats.
BSW Party founder Sahra Wagenknecht and party leader Fabio De Masi have advocated for the-called "Magdeburg Model," named after the capital of Saxony-Anhalt.

This approach rejects a formal coalition with the AfD, offers no support for AfD candidate in the election of a state premiere, and calls for no official tolerance for far-fight platforms. However, the approach envisions joint motions, joint voting, and possibly also written agreements with the AfD.
AfD lawmaker elected speaker in Saxony-Anhalt
Wagenknecht says AfD 'not a long term partner'
On Saturday, Wagenknecht made clear she does not see the AfD as a long-term strategic partner.

"None of us wants to cozy up to the AfD," Wagenknecht said. But the BSW will decide how to proceed if there is "the possibility of reasonable majorities for peace, social improvement, and a reform of public broadcasting."

The AfD and BSW see some overlap in Germany's approach to the Ukraine war, with both taking pro-Russia views critical of military support for Kyiv, while opposing or questioning sanctions on Russia, arguing that they harm the German economy.

BSW executive board members such as Christian Leye, Amid Rabieh and Klaus Ernst had sought to pass the amendment to both rule out coalitions with the AfD, and also "any formal or de facto tolerance, support for an AfD-led government, and long-term agreements on cooperation."
"Since when have we been partners with the AfD?" Leye said after the vote. "This party can only be an opponent."
"In my view, it is a racist party, a nationalist party that also has its issues with democracy. That is why it cannot be a partner," he said.
Germany's Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the domestic intelligence agency, has classified the AfD as right-wing extremist.

articles.title: Police make 33 arrests as part of child sexual abuse inquiry in Southampton
articles.summary:
One man due to be sentenced in January after pleading guilty to sexually assaulting 17-year-old girl

Police investigating claims of widespread sexual abuse of children in Southampton have…

blocks.text: Police investigating claims of widespread sexual abuse of children in Southampton have arrested more than 30 people.
One man is due to be sentenced in January after pleading guilty to sexually assaulting a 17-year-old girl, while another man will stand trial next month charged with raping a 15-year-old.

“We are conducting inquiries into concerns raised about men who were in contact with teenage girls,” a spokesperson for the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said. “As part of these complex investigations, we have arrested 33 people. This has led to us being able to seize more than 80 mobile phones and any other relevant items which may assist in our continuing inquiries.
“While the information on those phones is reviewed, strict bail conditions have been put in place and our local policing teams have been monitoring those conditions.”

Detectives have been looking into the allegations over a lengthy period, with officers saying they have been working to “support and safeguard the girls, and build trust with them, which has allowed for formal reports to be made and statements taken.”

Hampshire police said one man, 22-year-old Sayeed Hashimi, had pleaded guilty to the sexual assault of a teenage girl at an address in Southampton in the early hours of 28 March. It was reported the girl had been “pinned down on a bed” before an attempt was made to forcibly remove her clothes, police said. Hashimi will be sentenced at Southampton crown court.

Aster Simon, 35, has been charged with sexual offences against a 15-year-old girl, including rape, attempted rape, sexual assault and making indecent photographs of a child. The alleged offences took place in the Portsmouth and Southampton areas in April and May, according to Hampshire police. He is due to stand trial at the same court.

Hampshire police said: “We take all reports of the exploitation of children extremely seriously. If you suspect a person of carrying out child criminal or sexual exploitation, or think someone you know has been a victim, please report this to us by calling 101, or by going to our website. If someone is in immediate danger of harm, please call 999.”
Southampton city council’s leader, Sarah Bogle, said the reports were “deeply disturbing”.

She added: “While it is important that we allow the police investigation and justice process to take their course, we want to reassure residents that protecting children and young people is our highest priority. We are working closely with the police to support their investigation in every way we can to help ensure anyone responsible for these appalling crimes is brought to justice.”

articles.title: Woman, 21, killed in car crash in Staffordshire after police pursuit
articles.summary:
Staffordshire police reports itself to police watchdog after Seat Ibiza involved in collision with Vauxhall Astra

A 21-year-old woman has been killed after the car she was travelling in…

blocks.text: A 21-year-old woman has been killed after the car she was travelling in crashed following a police pursuit.

Staffordshire police said it had reported itself to the police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct, after the Seat Ibiza was involved in a collision with a Vauxhall Astra. The woman was a front seat passenger in the Seat.
The force said she had died at the scene in Hednesford in the West Midlands shortly after 11pm on Friday. Both cars were being driven by members of the public.
The Seat had been involved in a police pursuit shortly before the crash on the Rugeley Road, a single-carriageway A-road that runs to the east of Hednesford.
A 23-year-old man from the nearby Walsall area has been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.
The woman’s next-of-kin have been informed. Staffordshire police said the family were being supported by specially trained officers.
West Midlands ambulance service took two people to hospital. Their injuries are not believed to be life-threatening or life-changing.

articles.title: Bojie Dy defends multi-purpose buildings in 2027 budget
articles.summary: House Speaker Faustino "Bojie" Dy III has defended the inclusion of multi-purpose buildings in the House-approved version of the proposed 2027 national budget, saying these structures could serve…

blocks.text: Published November 28, 2026 10:21pm

House Speaker Faustino "Bojie" Dy III has defended the inclusion of multi-purpose buildings in the House-approved version of the proposed 2027 national budget, saying these structures could serve various community needs.
In a report on GMA's 24 Oras on Saturday, Dy said multi-purpose buildings could be used as barangay halls, community centers and other facilities.
Dy said lawmakers, as representatives of their respective districts, were responsible for informing the national government of their constituents' needs.

“Pagka sinabi mo na multi-purpose hall, pwede po ito yung barangay hall or pwede po yung multi-purpose center… Kaya naman po yung atin namang limited sources sa national funding ay ating pong inilalaan sa mga iba’t-ibang pangangailangan ng ating distrito,” Dy said.
(When you say multi-purpose hall, this could be a barangay hall or a multi-purpose center. We allocate our limited national government funding to the various needs of our districts.)

The inclusion of multi-purpose buildings in the proposed budget has drawn scrutiny, particularly over the substantial amounts allocated for their construction and the uneven distribution of projects among local government units (LGUs).
Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson earlier pointed out that most of the proposed multi-purpose buildings were allocated to wealthier LGUs, while poorer localities received fewer projects.— MCG, GMA News
Follow GMA News Online on Facebook for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: AI-generated lawsuits flood German courts
articles.summary: German courts are being overwhelmed by AI-generated lawsuits, many riddled with errors and running to huge lengths. Some state justice ministers want to introduce a fee to stem the flow, but that…

image.caption: Files in Germany's social courts are getting fatterImage: Johannes Eisele/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German courts are reporting a huge rise in lawsuits and complaints, and are blaming the use of artificial intelligence models.

The German media has been filled with reports about the problem, which particularly affects social courts, where citizens can file complaints themselves without legal representation. In most such cases, people appeal against sanctions or cuts to their unemployment benefits, or demands from authorities that benefits be returned, but the complaints can also pertain to other benefits or sudden rises in health insurance contributions.
Marcus Howe, spokesperson for Berlin's state social court, where he is himself a judge, said his court was dealing with 28% more cases this year than in 2025.

"That is of course an enormous increase, which is surely in part because of artificial intelligence," he told DW, though he added that it could also be partly down to the tightening of sanctions on unemployment benefits, introduced by the federal government this year.

Other states have reported similar increases. The Legal Tribune Online news portal reported that the number of urgent proceedings at the eight social courts in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state, rose from around 1,400 in the first quarter of 2025 to 3,600 in the same period of 2026.
How to spot an AI lawsuit
Howe said that in most cases it's still easy for judges to see when a complaint has been generated by AI.

"You can usually tell at first glance," he said. "The font and the layout are different. In the worst cases, they're much too long and bloated, stuffed with content that has very little to do with the case."
What is AI doing to our brains?
Howe has also noticed that the AI-generated lawsuits are more impersonal, which makes his job more difficult.

"You don't really get an impression of what kind of people are behind these cases," he said. "And it becomes difficult to recognize what the actual problem is. The human factor is important because a lot of this computer-generated German can mislead you. It makes arguments that the computer has thought up, but which aren't actually important for the people in question."
This can go to extremes: Friedrich-Johannes Graf von Pfeil, president of the social court in Potsdam, Brandenburg, has received one complaint that stretched to 800 pages.

"You can tell very quickly when one is AI-generated, just because they use specialist legal formulations that no ordinary citizen would use," he told DW. "There's often very little on the facts of the case, and a lot of legal interpretation that no non-specialist could provide. But you still have to respond to all of it."

The problem for judges is that they are obliged to wade through all this material, which often includes references to other legal rulings that either have little bearing on the case — or have been hallucinated by the AI tool.

Nor can the courts simply use their own AI tools to summarize these documents, von Pfeil said. "If we wanted to use AI to assess a legal document, we'd have security and data protection problems, because the AI isn't in-house," he said. "Also, we receive a lot of sensitive medical documents that would end up on a server that doesn't belong to the judiciary. And that's not allowed."
Could courts stem the flow with extra fees?

At a regular conference this month, Germany's state and federal justice ministers agreed to set up a working group to look into the problem, with some conservative ministers calling for a fee to file urgent complaints.

Christian Heinz, Christian Democrat justice minister in the state of Hesse, said that a fee of €15 ($16.40) should be considered. Another proposal was for people to pay court costs for lawsuits that are deemed to have little chance of success or which abuse the system.

blocks.caption: People in Germany have a right to file an appeal when their benefits are cut — unemployment benefits, for exampleImage: Frank Hoermann/Sven Simon/picture alliance

blocks.text: The VdK, a social welfare association that offers legal advice to people dealing with German welfare authorities, is vehemently against those ideas. Holger Lange, head of the VdK's federal legal department, thinks it's vital that people — particularly the most vulnerable — have access to social courts without fearing the costs.

The solution, as far as Lange is concerned, is not to "build walls around the courts," but to streamline their digital access and make it easier to submit clear, concise complaints — in other words, online portals with easy-to-understand questions and word limits on legal documents. "They could steer the procedure a little," he told DW.

Howe is also skeptical of fees, an idea that, he said, has been discussed for decades. But social courts are supposed to have low thresholds to entry, he added: "This isn't a situation that suddenly justifies fees — yet. We want to keep access to justice open."
Judge von Pfeil thinks a fee would be "worth a try," though he acknowledges that a lot of people might apply for legal aid, which means the state would end up with more bureaucracy and costs anyway.
Is this even a real crisis?
Though there has been a recent increase in social court complaints, a broader look at the statistics shows that this is nothing that the social courts haven't seen before.

In the years leading up to the advent of wide availability of AI chatbots, the courts actually saw a big drop in the number of pending cases: from over 445,000 at the end of 2017 to 325,000 at the end of 2024. Analysts suggest that such long-term developments are tied to economic conditions and legal changes in unemployment benefits.
Are humans becoming too attached to AI?

And Lange doesn't think that this new rise in complaints — AI-generated or not — is necessarily a bad sign. "The key thing is enabling people," he said. "We need to ask whether the recent rise isn't also in part the expression of a demand for legal protection that has been hidden so far, because people just haven't dared to claim their rights."
Lange acknowledged that AI-generated complaints can't always be trusted, because of errors and hallucinations. But he stressed that the use of AI doesn't make an appeal invalid.

"It could be a seriously ill person whose pension claim has just been refused," he said. "Or a care-dependent person who desperately needs support. We always need to look at who is behind the complaint."

articles.title: Costa Rica bars UN rapporteur on Palestinian territories from entering the country
articles.summary:
Francesca Albanese, leading critic of Israeli abuses in Gaza and West Bank, barred on ‘national security grounds’

Costa Rica barred entry to the UN special rapporteur on the Israel-occupied…

blocks.text: Costa Rica barred entry to the UN special rapporteur on the Israel-occupied Palestinian territories, Francesca Albanese, earning the ire of the UN human rights chief.

Albanese, an Italian national, went to Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate from the University of Costa Rica. She was stopped at the airport in San José and not allowed to enter the country, and was transferred to a hotel before she travelled to Mexico on Saturday.

The UN human rights office said that Albanese was stopped from entering the country on “national security grounds”. Costa Rica’s migration office said that its decision was made after she was subject of an “alert” over alleged ties to terrorism.

blocks.caption: A protester outside Costa Rica’s embassy demonstrates against the decision to bar Francesca Albanese from entering the country. Photograph: Luis Cortés/Reuters

blocks.text: The UN high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, said that he was “deeply concerned” by the decision to deny Albanese entry. “This is difficult to reconcile with Costa Rica’s longstanding commitment to human rights,” said Türk.

Albanese shared a picture on X of an airport bench and her suitcase, where she was meant to stay the night. “Second night in the airport. Guarded by security at every step. Uncomfortable chairs. Noise. Bright light,” Albanese posted.

Albanese, who acts as an independent expert appointed by the UN human rights council, has been outspoken on Israeli abuses in Gaza and the West Bank. She has drawn ire from Israel and its allies for being one of the first, most prominent officials to accuse Israel of committing genocide in Gaza – a claim Israel denies.

The US placed sanctions and revoked the visa of Albanese for her work on Palestine in the summer of 2025, cutting her off from the global financial system. The sanctions make daily life a struggle for Albanese, who has no access to western banks or credit cards.

Albanese called for an investigation into whether her denial of entry into Costa Rica was connected to the US sanctions, in remarks she made remotely at the ceremony for the acceptance of her honorary doctorate.

Costa Rica’s government, headed by the rightwing president, Laura Fernández, is close to the Trump administration and has cooperated with it on security and immigration issues. The government has also intensified its ties with Israel.
Israel’s envoy to the UN, Danny Danon, praised Costa Rica for its decision, accusing Albanese of using her UN position to spread propaganda against Israel.
On Saturday, Albanese was expected leave Costa Rica for Mexico, with the Italian embassy in Mexico working in advance of her visit to ensure there are no obstacles to her entry into the country.

articles.title: US regulators eye kratom as overdose deaths mount
articles.summary:
Kratom advocates say a ‘critical distinction’ should be made between natural and chemically enhanced versions of drug

The US government is paying more attention to kratom after the apparent…

blocks.text: The US government is paying more attention to kratom after the apparent overdose deaths of young people, but advocates say the synthetic drug hurting people is not the same as the supplement and users should be aware of the difference.

But chemical dependency specialists and law enforcement figures warn that the distinction may not be enough to curb an increasing number of fatalities and treatment center admissions for synthetic and semisynthetic kratom derivatives rather than natural kratom leaf.

Signs of a growing issue around kratom and kratom enhanced with the 7-OH alkaloid are beginning to emerge. Three weeks ago, the US telehealth provider Quick MD released a study showing that the substances now account for more than half of its new addiction treatment patients, a five-time increase from 10% in 2024 to 50%.
“In September, 55% of our new addiction treatment patients sought help for kratom or 7⁠-⁠OH dependence,” said Ryan Lissack, chief executive officer of QuickMD. The company is now advertising on TV.

The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) recently issued two notices recommending that 7-OH, or 7-hydroxymitragynine – one of the major psychoactive ingredients in kratom – should be placed under federal controls while legislation has been introduced to effect stronger controls.

The notice came less than a month after Ole Miss college students Aidan Hamilton, 18, and Robert Strang, 20, were found dead in separate incidents with packages of concentrated kratom-related products discovered at both scenes. Federal prosecutors have said the two students “died of conditions consistent to overdoses”, though toxicology results are still pending.

Promoted as a wellness product that’s often sold in corner stores and gas stations, kratom is a mild opioid derived from the leaves of Mitragyna speciosa (a tropical evergreen tree native to south-east Asia). It’s sold in various forms, including powders, teas, capsules, tablets, extracts, gummies, and raw or crushed leaves.
Enhanced kratom is the latest drug to register as a concern for health authorities and law enforcement.

“Any opioid, synthetic or semi-synthetic, has the potential to be addictive,” says Patrick Trainor, director of the narcotics investigation and drug control unit at the Pennsylvania attorney general’s office. “Any opioid that’s being sold as a wellness drug is of concern.”

A 2023 Tampa Bay Times investigation found that more than 580 people in Florida have died from kratom-related overdoses during the past decade. The paper notes that most of the deaths were caused “by a fatal mixture of kratom and at least one other substance, but 46 people overdosed solely on the herb”.

The National Poison Data System found that between 2015 and 2025 kratom exposure reports surged 1,200%. Estimates of how many people use kratom and 7-OH products in the US vary. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates there around 5 million “lifetime” users. The American Kratom Association puts the number at 11 million to 16 million, with retail sales estimated at $2.2bn in 2024.

Trainor, a former DEA agent who worked on drug interdiction in Philadelphia’s notorious Kensington area, notes a primary concern with kratom is that “it’s being sold from retail locations, there’s a lot of misbranding, or misrepresentation, to what the potency is. People might think they’re taking a legal dose but that may not be the case.”

While kratom is not approved for use in a medical environment, it’s often used to moderate opioid withdrawal symptoms. A development with this use is that the increasing strength of the kratom products containing 7-OH means it can create new chemical dependency issues while trying to solve existing ones.
“For people who are dealing with substance abuse disorder, kratom has potential to get people sick,” Trainor says, using a street term for drug withdrawal symptoms.

This is happening as some harm reduction medications – including the opioid dependency management drug Suboxone – are becoming harder to obtain because of strict distributor caps and dispensary policies.

A study by UC Berkeley found that despite the relaxation of prescribing guidelines, harm reduction drugs such as buprenorphine, one of the ingredients in Suboxone, is only carried by four in 10 US retail pharmacies, and that access is more limited in Black and Latino communities.
The Trump administration has voiced support and showed effort to limit the chemical compounds found in enhanced kratom.
“These are potent opioids being manufactured and sold in consumer products, often under labels that obscure their true risks,” the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, said in August.

The US Food and Drug Administration has said it has observed “a proliferation of products containing 7-OH, and has “serious concerns” about products containing the alkaloid, calling it an “emerging public health threat”. Last December, the agency said that the US Marshals Service seized 73,000 units of 7-OH products – valued at roughly $1m – from three firms in Missouri.

The American Kratom Association has called for a “critical distinction” to be made between natural leaf kratom and chemically enhanced opioid products and welcomed efforts by the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and the Department of Justice to distinguish between them.
after newsletter promotion

“The DEA and the Department of Justice deserve recognition for addressing the critical distinction between dangerous, chemically manipulated opioid products and natural kratom leaf,” said Mac Haddow, senior fellow on public policy for the association, in a statement last month.
The distinction, Haddow added, “is essential to protecting consumers without imposing an unjustified ban on lawful botanical products”.

The Manhattan addiction specialist Dr Andrew Tatarsky said the concerns around kratom maybe misplaced. “We demonize the drug because we don’t want to deal with all the other complexities over why people may be vulnerable to overuse,” he said.

Tatarsky said he and his colleagues in the field were not seeing “significant or rampant problems” with kratom. “But 7-OH is a potentially problematic substance that people should be cautioned and educated about.”

Kratom/7-OH dependency issues have begun showing up in rehabilitation centers. Dr Mohammad Sarhan, medical director of the Caron treatment center at its Florida campus, said the practice treats kratom and 7-OH as different substances.

“Kratom offers a mild opioid stimulant effect whereas 7-OH is a highly potent opioid. Patients using kratom we consider ‘other substance use disorder’, but people who say they’re using 7-OH we consider and treat it as a standard opioid use disorder.”

Kate Appleman, chief clinical officer at Caron’s Pennsylvania campus, said she equated the kratom and 7-OH distinction to the way cannabis had evolved from a drug with a small percentage of THC, its active psychoactive ingredient, to one that might contain up to 90%.

“Cannabis is something natural in nature, but when you start to change the components of it, it’s very different,” she said. “Kratom is very similar. People think it’s natural, it’s legal, but when you start to look at the way it gets manufactured, that’s the part that makes it even more problematic.”

From an addiction standpoint, Appleman pointed out, the brain doesn’t know the difference between fentanyl, heroin and OxyContin, and kratom because it affects the same receptors in the brain. Caron has started stand-alone relapse programs for people who have had recovery from heroin or alcohol but relapsed on kratom.

“We hear stories from patients that kratom is more potent than they had anticipated and they have the same symptoms of addiction as they do for heroin and alcohol. Their life is unmanageable, they have withdrawal symptoms and cravings – everything that is standard with having a substance use disorder.”

Sarhan noted that patients being admitted often express a sense of betrayal and embarrassment at becoming dependent on a product that is sold next to energy drinks. “They say, ‘How dangerous could it possibly be? The packaging said it was botanical, plant-based, all-natural – nothing on the label said it was an opioid.’”

Signs that a new era of opioid dependency is approaching are hard to miss. Los Angeles county officials have linked six fatal overdoses to 7-OH, while the San Francisco department of public health reported the city’s first-known adult fatal overdose involving a semisynthetic kratom-derived opioid in September.

The California department of public health issued warnings stating that 7-OH and kratom-derived products are illegal to manufacture or sell for consumption in the state. Eleven states have made it illegal, while Massachusetts and North Dakota have issued temporary bans.

According Sarhan, it’s a “maybe” on whether Kratom could be considered an epidemic, a characterization typically identified and declared by public health agencies. Since it was not scheduled as an illicit substance, Sarhan said, there were regulatory issues. “If it comes off the shelves, does it become an illicit substance? Are people going to switch to an illicit substance or seek treatment? I don’t know. But whatever it is, we’re still early on.”

articles.title: Black barrister tells of racist abuse after Rupert Lowe viral tweet
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Hard-right MP claimed photo featuring Joseph Ashong was sign of discrimination against white Britons

A newly qualified black barrister who took part in a group photo that went…

blocks.text: A newly qualified black barrister who took part in a group photo that went viral after Rupert Lowe cited the image as evidence of discrimination against white Britons has said he has never before experienced such racism in the UK.

Joseph Ashong, who was in a cohort attending their “call to the bar” ceremony in London, said he was amazed and upset by the reaction to the picture as it was viewed by millions on the afternoon of the ceremony.

Lowe, the leader of Restore Britain, the hard-right rival to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK party, reposted the formal photograph of 80 newly called barristers that was shared by the Middle Temple inn of court on Wednesday.
The Great Yarmouth MP wrote on X: “To those who still say White British men and women face no discrimination in our country, show them this image.”

Lowe’s post has been viewed 2.3m times. It was amplified by the far-right agitator known as Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, and it triggered a wave of racist abuse online. Millions more have since viewed the image and other group photographs shared by Middle Temple this week.

Isabel Oakeshott, the journalist and partner of Richard Tice, the deputy leader of Reform, also posted the photograph. “These are the judges of tomorrow,” she wrote. “One particular demographic appears to be missing. There is something very wrong with our country if we can’t say that there is something not quite right about this.”

According to a survey published in March by the Bar Standards Board, 82.3% of barristers in England and Wales are white. Official government statistics suggest that the proportion of judges from minority ethnic groups is 13% – up from 6% a decade ago. The photograph was just the latest of a series of call to the bar ceremonies held this year at Middle Temple, one of the four institutions entitled to call members to the English Bar as barristers.
Many international students come to the UK because English common law forms the foundation of legal systems in over a third of the world.

Ashong, who is from Ghana but earned a scholarship to pursue a career at the bar in the UK, where he arrived in 2023, was at the front of the image shared by Lowe, which was taken shortly before the ceremony. “If only I had been given a pass for being black,” he said of the tough journey to become a barrister.

blocks.caption: Joseph Ashong. Photograph: Anna Gordon/The Guardian

blocks.text: Ashong, 36, said it amazed him that an MP had triggered the racism. “There may have been unconscious bias in the past but I have not experienced racism to this extent before,” he said.

Ashong said he had chosen to study at City St George’s, University of London, due to the shared English common law heritage between England and Wales and the Commonwealth countries. The Middle Temple has a strong tradition of taking on members from the Commonwealth.

“A friend reached out to me to say there’s a picture on Twitter which is making the rounds and they’ve seen my face in there,” Ashong said. “So I go to Twitter and I find that the MP is making a statement about discrimination. We know what is being insinuated: people who are supposed to look British, so to speak, now don’t and the bar is a mixed bag of people from all over the place, mostly black and brown people. It is ignorant.”

He added: “In my case, I was awarded the Harmsworth scholarship from Middle Temple. That means going through an intense application, going through interviews before you are finally merited the award.”
The Harmsworth scholarship was established by the great-grandfather of the current proprietor of the Daily Mail.

Ashong said he would apply for a pupillage – the final part of training to become a barrister – in the UK but that he was considering returning to Ghana to build a practice. “It’s a bit sickening because what’s going on out there is pure ignorance,” he said. “An MP of all people should know that there’s no design for immigrants to take over the bar.”
after newsletter promotion
Yi Vonne, 23, who had been studying law at Cardiff University since 2024, was in a later group photograph that was also highlighted on social media as apparently showing bias against white people.

blocks.caption: Yi Vonne. Photograph: Sam Frost/The Guardian

blocks.text: She said she would return to Malaysia in December to start her pupillage but had opted for that day’s call to the bar, which was relatively late in the year, to allow for her mother to organise time off from work and join her on a “special day”. She said: “I’ve never been treated like this before here.”
Vonne said Middle Temple had offered for other groups to opt out of the photograph “because of all this racial abuse that’s going on”. “But of course, who wants to do that?” she said.

On Thursday, the Liberal Democrat MP Al Pinkerton raised the row in the Commons, saying that a “wonderful celebratory photograph of young barristers called to the bar at Middle Temple has become the subject of the most appalling racialised abuse, including, I am very sorry to say, by certain members of this house”.

Alan Campbell, the leader of the House of Commons, responded that it was “beyond inappropriate and entirely unacceptable for anyone to follow up online and make the sorts of comments that he talks about”.

Middle Temple has informed its members that the posts were “considered carefully at the most senior level” but that the “conclusion was that there is nothing to be gained from adding to the comments by Al Pinkerton MP in parliament”.
A Restore Britain spokesperson said: “Rupert’s post speaks for itself on the point he was making.”
Additional reporting by Lyndon Li

articles.title: Jess Wilson’s rapid rise is hard to believe - but Victorian Labor’s collapse has been years in the making
articles.summary:
Labor faces possibility of relegation to crossbench as Coalition claims majority government and Greens celebrate ‘wild’ success

  • Full report:

blocks.text: It is difficult to overstate how far the Victorian Coalition has come.

In the days after Christmas 2024, Brad Battin toppled John Pesutto as Liberal leader after a court found the Hawthorn MP defamed his colleague. A million-dollar loan by the party to Pesutto to help cover his legal costs also ended up in court. Battin lasted less than a year before his leadership also came undone and he was replaced by Jess Wilson in November 2025.

A year on, Wilson has become the first woman to be popularly elected as Victoria’s premier and at 36, the state’s youngest leader since federation. As at 10pm, the Coalition had won 53 seats – well above the 45 needed to form a majority government and her Labor opponents have been wiped out – from 56 seats in 2022 to just six declared seats, according to Guardian Australia’s analysis, with a little more than a quarter of the vote counted.

Labor leader Ben Carroll has secured two unwanted places in Australian political history: becoming the first premier to lose their seat at a Victorian election and the state’s shortest-serving modern premier, in the job for just 123 days.
While the final seat tally won’t be known for a few days, the Coalition has won seats in parts of the state it hasn’t ever held.

The state that had come to regard Labor as its natural party of government has consigned it to the electoral wilderness. At the current count, more people voted for One Nation across the state than Labor, with the party recording a 21% primary vote, though this did not translate into seats.

Ironically, this was in part due to them overtaking Labor, on 17.6%. Another irony – the Coalition’s landslide win is off the back of a 34.78% primary vote, only a small increase from the 29.6% it recorded in its 2022 loss. Such has the political climate changed.
There is a real possibility the Greens, who have won eight seats, will end up being the official opposition, with Labor consigned to the crossbench.
“It is wild the number of seats we’re in hunt for,” Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, said on Saturday night.
It’s difficult to see how Labor will be able to rebuild into anything remotely electable in four years.

It’s hard to believe Wilson only entered parliament at the last election after the former member for Kew, did not run again after a drink-driving incident in which he crashed his car into a child’s bedroom.
Immediately promoted to shadow cabinet, then to shadow treasurer and now also leader, she’s taken a party that was deeply divided and turned it into an election-winning, unified outfit.

Wilson is relatable, approachable and a small-l Liberal in a state that remains broadly progressive – if you consider the almost 20% of Victorians who voted for either the Greens or the Victorian Socialists. Much of her success can be attributed to her ability to reach beyond the Coalition’s traditional base.

Her rise has also helped attract a new calibre of candidate. She persuaded several female contenders to contest winnable seats, including Samantha Byrne, who has won Niddrie off Carroll. The party has also made a concerted effort to recruit more diverse candidates and build relationships with multicultural communities Labor has taken for granted.
In her victory speech, Wilson acknowledged it was the first time many Victorians had voted Liberals.
“I realise that you have lent us your vote. We don’t own it. And we will work every single day to demonstrate that you were right to place your trust in us,” she said.
Wilson knows winning an election is one thing but governing is another.
Her first challenge will be translating an election victory into a mandate to govern. Many Victorians voted for change but may not know what that involves.

After all, many voters got their first meaningful taste just 48 hours before polling day, when the Coalition’s costings revealed plans to privatise or sell off around $13bn state government assets, including the state’s sewerage infrastructure.

Then, Wilson will have to manage the competing ambitions within her own ranks. She currently holds the shadow treasurer portfolio, a position several colleagues would dearly like to claim in government. She insists she intends to keep it.

The Coalition has a relatively shallow pool of experience on which to draw after 12 years in the wilderness. Bringing someone like Pesutto on to the frontbench would make sense but enrage others in the party room. It’s no wonder Wilson was tight lipped about the prospect when interviewed last month.
She described the election as a referendum on Labor. Now, she has to deliver for all those who gave her a party a chance.
Recriminations

Meanwhile, in Labor, recriminations have already started. In reality, they had weeks ago. Most of the criticism is the same – Carroll’s campaign focused too much on crime and his inability to acknowledge the 12 years of Labor that came before him – epitomised by the moment he avoided uttering Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan’s names in the debate.
But a result like this was years in the making.

After the 2022 election, Andrews vowed to do more for the communities that swung hard against Labor in the wake of the pandemic. Now, it doesn’t have one. Seats like Kororoit, Kalkallo, Tarneit and Melton in the north and west, Narre Warren North and Narre Warren South in the southeast, which have never been held by a party other than Labor have turned blue.
On Saturday night, the deputy leader, Gabrielle Williams, said while the party increased seats in 2022, it ignored the main message voters were sending.
“There were certainly warning signs from the 2022 result that we should have responded to and perhaps didn’t take the opportunity,” she said.
“It should have been an inflection on point that caused us to stop and see what is happening to our base and what they weren’t getting from us.”
Labor missed another opportunity to reset when Allan became premier in 2023.
“She just tried to carry on as if she was the new Daniel Andrews, it was continuation of the old government,” a campaign source said.

That government, according to a campaign source, was bogged down by debt, alleged corruption on government construction sites, waste, crime and potholes – which became daily reminders of a government that many Victorians felt was no longer delivering.
“Is there no better symbol that shows we failed to get the basics rights?” they said.

items: Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondent

articles.title: Azerbaijan's opposition leader Ali Karimli: A year behind bars
articles.summary: Azerbaijani opposition leader Ali Karimli has been in prison since November 2025. Authorities accuse him of attempting to seize power by force, but human rights groups say his prosecution is…

image.caption: The detention of Ali Karimli (center, seen here at a protest in 2016) has drawn criticism from international organizations and European lawmakersImage: Resul Rehimov/Anadolu Agency/picture alliance

blocks.text: A year after his arrest, Azerbaijani opposition leader Ali Karimli remains in prison.

Karimli has denied charges of attempting to seize power by force, calling them politically motivated. He is the chairman of the Azerbaijani Popular Front Party (APFP), one of the country's main opposition parties.

Karimli is on trial alongside Mammad Ibrahim, his longtime political adviser and a senior party official. Ibrahim has previously served time in prison. In 2016, he was sentenced to three years on hooliganism charges that Human Rights Watch described as spurious. He was detained on November 29, 2025, alongside Karimli.
Amnesty: Government aims to 'crush all political opposition'

Azerbaijan's State Security Service has charged Karimli and Ibrahim under Article 278.1 of the Criminal Code, which covers actions aimed at forcibly seizing power or changing the country's constitutional order. A conviction could carry a prison sentence of 12 to 20 years, or life imprisonment.

In a statement issued on February 12, the State Security Service alleged that Karimli had conspired with the former head of Azerbaijan's Presidential Administration, Ramiz Mehdiyev, and his allies to seize state power. The agency also linked the alleged conspiracy to interference by foreign intelligence services in Azerbaijan's political affairs.

According to investigators, Karimli planned to exploit a mass rally in Baku in July 2020, originally held in support of the Azerbaijani army, to provoke unrest and seize the parliament and state television buildings. In a 15-page copy of a court motion obtained by DW from the APFP leadership, Karimli said he did not attend the rally and that his party was not involved in organizing it.

Nazim Musayev, a lawyer representing Mammad Ibrahim, told DW that both defendants considered the prosecution politically motivated. Shortly after the arrest, Amnesty International demanded that Azerbaijani authorities release Karimli "unless they can demonstrate reasonable evidence of an alleged criminal offence."

"Karimli's detention is the latest outrage in the ongoing consolidation of authoritarian practices in Azerbaijan," said Denis Krivosheev, Amnesty's deputy director for Eastern Europe and Central Asia, in a statement on December 1, 2025. "There appear to be no limits to the government's campaign to crush all political opposition and suppress all dissent in the country."
Trial behind closed doors

In the court motion obtained by DW, submitted at a preliminary hearing on November 3, Karimli made no secret of his desire for political change in Azerbaijan. However, he insisted he has always opposed using violence to achieve it.
"I accept only one way of coming to power — through democratic elections," Karimli wrote. The court rejected his call for charges to be dropped, but added the motion to his case file.

Karimli also disputed the prosecution's claims about the National Council of Democratic Forces, an opposition coalition formed in 2013. He said the group was established openly to support a joint opposition candidate in the presidential election rather than to organize a coup.

Karimli has also denied any cooperation with Mehdiyev, the ex-head of the presidential administration, saying the two have never met or communicated and that they represented opposing political positions for decades. Mehdiyev's lawyer told DW that his client also denies any connection to Karimli.

The trial against Karimli and Ibrahim is held behind closed doors, with foreign diplomats also being denied entry. Lawyer Nazim Musayev said the closed proceedings were justified on the grounds that the case involved state secrets.
In his motion, Karimli expressed little confidence in the fairness of the proceedings, argued that the case is intended to remove him from political life.
Silenced abroad: When censors cross borders
Rights groups raise alarm over Karimli's detention conditions

Karimli's son Turkel, who lives in the United States, told DW that he last spoke to his father in late April or early May. He said his mother had also been denied phone calls and face-to-face visits since June.

Turkel said his father's detention conditions had deteriorated sharply over the summer. Citing information received from lawyers, he said the authorities had temporarily stopped accepting food parcels from the family and restricted the amount of additional drinking water, which had been limited to 5 liters (1.3 gallons) a week. According to Amnesty International, Karimli reportedly fainted from severe dehydration during an August 6 court hearing.

Food deliveries were later permitted again, and lawyers were told earlier this month that the water allowance would be increased to 10 liters a week. Karimli's legal team said he has lost considerable weight during his time in prison.
Karimli has also complained of persistent noise disrupting his sleep, restrictions on family contact and physical exercise, worsening back pain and poor ventilation in his cell.

Rights groups have raised concerns about Karimli's detention conditions, with Amnesty International warning that the reported lack of access to clean drinking water and ventilation could amount to torture or other ill treatment.
Ibrahim's family reports health concerns

Ibrahim's family is concerned that he is not receiving adequate medical treatment in the detention facility. His son Turan Ibrahim, who lives abroad, told DW that his father suffers from kidney problems and insomnia.
According to Turan, doctors appointed by the authorities have examined his father several times. The family has also consulted outside doctors and is trying to arrange medication for him.

Turan said communication and family visits were sometimes difficult for his father. Ibrahim's wife delivers food and supplies to the detention facility once a week, and is allowed to see him through a glass partition twice a month.
Turan said his mother, who is unemployed and lives in rented accommodation, has also faced financial difficulties since her husband's arrest.
APFP opposition members also under scrutiny
Karimli has led the APFP since 2000. The party has continued operating during his detention.

Rahim Hajiyev, a founding member of the party who now lives in France, told DW that the APFP had long relied on collective decision-making and that Karimli's arrest had not brought its organizational activities to a halt.

However, he said party members, particularly those active on social media, continued to face short-term administrative detention. Hajiyev described Karimli's arrest as part of a broader campaign against political opposition.

blocks.caption: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul (left) met his Azerbaijani counterpart Ceyhun Bayramov during his visit to Baku on November 18Image: DW

blocks.text: EU calls for Karimli's immediate release
Karimli's detention has also drawn criticism from international organizations and European lawmakers.

On October 8, the European Parliament adopted a resolution calling for the immediate and unconditional release of Karimli and other political prisoners in Azerbaijan. Lawmakers also urged the authorities to ensure adequate medical care, access to lawyers and contact with family members. Earlier this month, Karimli was awarded the 2026 Magnitsky Human Rights Award.

Karimli's case was also raised at a joint press conference in Baku on November 18, attended by Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov and his German counterpart, Johann Wadephul. Asked about Karimli's arrest, Bayramov said that belonging to the opposition did not exempt anyone from legal responsibility.
Bayramov maintained that the case was being handled in accordance with Azerbaijani law and said the court would make the final decision.

articles.title: Ukraine's expertise comes in handy for international drone alliances
articles.summary: Ukrainian expertise merged with Europe's financial and industrial clout: Germany and other countries are expanding drone partnerships with Ukraine and reshaping Europe's defense industry in the…

image.caption: Drone parts made with a 3D printer: A British soldier makes components for a Ukrainian droneImage: Artur Widak/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany and Ukraine want to further boost their defense cooperation. Following a meeting in Berlin with his Ukrainian counterpart, Yevhenii Khmara, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced that drones for Ukraine will be manufactured in Germany in the future.

The project involves the Ukrainian reconnaissance drone known as the "Babka" ("Dragonfly"). Germany is investing around €34 million in the project, according to Pistorius. German company Wingcopter and Ukrainian manufacturer Shadow Flytech have established a joint venture specifically for this purpose.
A European 'Drone Alliance'

This is far from the first cooperation agreement of its kind that Kyiv has launched with its European partners. The initiatives include numerous joint ventures between Ukrainian companies and defense contractors across Europe.

In July 2026, the EU and Ukraine launched a joint "Drone Alliance." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reached an agreement to establish the initiative. The alliance focuses on joint development, industrial production, supply chains and counter-drone defense. One of its key goals is to combine Ukrainian technologies proven in combat with Europe's industrial production capabilities. The agreement on the Babka drones is also part of this alliance.
New bilateral agreements

As part of its Drone Deal strategy, Ukraine has sealed long-term bilateral agreements with several countries. These include the Netherlands, Norway, Finland and the Baltic states, as well as Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Kyiv is also in negotiations with around a dozen other countries.

blocks.caption: Smoke rises near Dubai Airport following an Iranian drone attack. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has offered Gulf states assistance in developing their own drone defense systemsImage: AFP

blocks.text: The cooperation covers four main areas: joint drone production; the exchange of intelligence and battlefield experience; cooperation in intelligence gathering, electronic warfare and cyber defense; and the training and advising of military personnel.

Although Germany has not yet formally joined the long-term Drone Deal framework, negotiations are afoot. German companies are already deeply involved in Ukraine's drone industry via several cooperation agreements.

This week, Ukraine and the United Kingdom also agreed on a new deal under which the UK will manufacture Ukrainian medium and long-range drones. In March, the two countries agreed to produce Ukraine's "Octopus" interceptor drone under license in the UK.
How AI Is Reshaping Warfare in Ukraine
Rapid rise of the drone industry

Since the start of the war against Russia in the Donbas in 2014, Ukraine has developed a small but highly innovative drone industry. Up until 2022, however, the country only made a limited number of military drones.

With the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, development and production expanded dramatically. Before the full-scale war, only seven drone models had received state approval. By 2023, that number had risen to 67. By early 2024, around 200 companies were operating in Ukraine's drone sector.

"Perhaps some people underestimated the fact that Ukraine is not just an industrial country, but also a country of engineers, with a strong science and technology education system and a well-developed software industry," German security expert Nico Lange, director of the Berlin-based Institute for Risk Analysis and International Security (IRIS), told DW.

blocks.caption: Partners in a drone alliance: Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Ursula von der LeyenImage: Paul Faith/AFP

blocks.text: Ukraine has since massively expanded its domestic production capacity. According to Ukraine's Ministry of Defense, as of June 2026, 95% of the drones procured for its armed forces are now manufactured domestically.
The key question is whether Ukraine has sufficient funding, components and secure production facilities to meet demand over the long term.
Complicated supply chains, new projects

Drones are used at many levels of military operations. They come in various forms, including attack, interceptor and reconnaissance drones, and operate both in the air and at sea. They are significantly less expensive than many other weapons systems and, because of their small size and the sheer numbers in which they are deployed, can be difficult to defend against.
However, drones are mass-produced, and many of them, particularly small attack drones, are often destroyed after just a single mission or neutralized by electronic jamming.

In July 2026, Zelenskyy said Ukraine could manufacture around 10 million drones domestically each year. The goal, however, was to increase production to 20 million annually with support from European partners.
For a long time, supply chains remained a major challenge for Ukraine. As recently as early 2024, around 90% of all drone components — including motors, control chips and cameras — came from China.

"Traditionally, Chinese components have played an important role in the drone industry because of their lower cost," Nico Lange explains. "There are efforts to manufacture these components domestically, but that cannot happen overnight."
Through its defense cooperation agreements, Kyiv has managed to reduce the share of components imported directly from China to around 28% in the first eight months of 2026.
Zelenskyy strengthens defense ties with Canada
'Partnership between equals'

For Ukraine, access to Western supply chains for urgently needed components is a major benefit of the defense cooperation with Europe. Another advantage is that relocating production facilities abroad helps protect them from Russian attacks. Many of the agreements also provide for Ukraine to contribute the technology and battlefield experience, while its European partner supplies most of the funding and industrial capacity.

In the long run, however, Ukraine's most important reason for pursuing these partnerships is likely its ambition to establish itself as a lasting member of Europe's defense community and integrate its military into the European security architecture.

"What began as donations of weapons, ammunition and other equipment in the early stages of the war has evolved into a strategic partnership that offers significant benefits to both sides," says defense expert Lange. "It has rightly been described as a partnership between equals."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Channel 4 defends controversial Huw Edwards documentary
articles.summary:
Film following disgraced former BBC presenter for almost a year faces fierce backlash ahead of airing on 1 December

Channel 4 has defended its controversial Huw Edwards documentary, with the…

blocks.text: Channel 4 has defended its controversial Huw Edwards documentary, with the broadcaster saying the film does not diminish the “seriousness” of his actions nor “entitle him to sympathy, redemption or rehabilitation”.
The film, Huw Edwards – Guilty, which has followed the disgraced former BBC presenter for almost a year, has faced a fierce backlash ahead of airing on 1 December.

Edwards pleaded guilty to three charges of making indecent images of children after he was sent 41 illegal images by a convicted paedophile, Alex Williams. He was sentenced to six months in prison in 2024, suspended for two years.

A Downing Street spokesperson said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, had “no interest in hearing what” Edwards had to say, adding: “Broadcasters are expected to act responsibly and have appropriate regard to their audiences when making decisions.”

A government minister, Emma Hardy, said the planned documentary made her “feel sick”, telling LBC that Channel 4 was proving a platform to “someone who is on the sex offenders’ register”, while another, Anna Turley, told the radio station it made her “deeply uncomfortable”. The shadow culture secretary, Rebecca Paul, said: “This man shouldn’t get a minute of airtime”

On Saturday, Louisa Compton, Channel 4’s director of news, digital and audience trust, responded to the brewing controversy, saying it was in the broadcaster’s remit to “stimulate debate” and that “interviewing someone is not an endorsement of them”.

She said: “Edwards was one of the most prominent and trusted broadcasters in Britain. He pleaded guilty to serious offences involving indecent images of children and has never publicly faced detailed questioning about his criminal behaviour or the complete collapse of his career and reputation.
“There is a clear public interest in confronting him with those questions rather than allowing them to remain unanswered.
“We are also acutely conscious that behind offences involving indecent images are real children and real victims – including those as young as seven – who have been abused.

“Nothing about making this film diminishes the seriousness of that harm, nor does Edwards’ participation entitle him to sympathy, redemption or rehabilitation. His account is there to be tested, not accepted.”

Compton also said that Edwards was not paid for participating in the film nor did he have any control over its content. “We should be capable of examining difficult issues rather than looking away because we don’t like what we see. We understand that some people will profoundly disagree with our decision to make this film.
“But discomfort is not, in itself, a reason for journalism not to ask difficult questions. We believe those questions are in the public interest,” she said.

The film will follow Edwards at home in rural Wales, where he has been since his career ended after his criminal conviction. In a short trailer, the 65-year-old says he had “lost the plot” at the time of his crimes

The film-makers said that after attempts to “ingratiate himself back into public life”, Edwards was shown being forced to “confront his loss of fame, declining health, fractured relationships and his crimes”.
The fall of Edwards, a veteran newsreader who announced the queen’s death on the BBC in 2022, has already been depicted on television in Channel 5’s drama Power: The Downfall of Huw Edwards.

The former presenter later said the programme was a “one-sided account” and has made a complaint to the media regulator Ofcom. It is investigating the programme under its “fairness and privacy” rules.
The drama became Channel 5’s highest-rated show of the year after its broadcast in March, attracting 3.8 million viewers in four weeks.
The two-part series focused on an earlier allegation against Edwards made by the Sun in July 2023 that claimed a “top BBC star” paid a teenager more than £35,000 for sexual pictures.
A Channel 5 spokesperson said: “We stand by the programme and will be robustly defending this complaint.”

items: Huw Edwards – Guilty airs on Channel 4 on Tuesday at 9pm.

articles.title: Argentina's bid to stop Falkland Islands oil drilling rejected
articles.summary: A joint venture between UK-Israeli companies is set to start exploring for oil and gas, but Argentina sought to block it as part of its claim to sovereignty.

blocks.text: Argentina's bid to block an oil exploration project near the Falkland Islands has been rejected by a UN-backed international tribunal.

The Argentinian government had called for the venture to be blocked as it claimed there was an ongoing dispute over the sovereignty of the Falklands, a British overseas territory. The UK has repeatedly rejected Argentina's claim.
In a decision on Saturday, the court's president said there did not appear to be any basis for believing it had jurisdiction as the tribunal is unable to rule on questions of sovereignty.
In a vote 18 to 3, judges from the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea rejected Argentina's challenge.
The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.

Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting from the oilfield within two years, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.
But the Argentinian government claimed the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law.
In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.
Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them.
The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

articles.title: Two Médecins Sans Frontières staff killed in Israeli strike in Gaza, charity says
articles.summary:
MSF and head of WHO denounce attack on Gaza City clinic as Israel claims security guards were members of Hamas

Israeli forces have bombed a clinic run by Médecins Sans Frontières in Gaza…

blocks.text: Israeli forces have bombed a clinic run by Médecins Sans Frontières in Gaza City, killing two of its staff members, the organisation has said.

MSF said Israel directly struck the clinic, despite the fact that its location was known to the Israeli military and that it was well marked with MSF logos. The organisation denounced the attack and said that with the deaths of the two security guards on Saturday, Israel had killed 17 of its staff members during the war in Gaza.
The head of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, condemned the bombing, saying: “Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked.”
“Attacks on health facilities, health workers and humanitarian personnel in Gaza are outrageous and unacceptable … These attacks MUST STOP,” Ghebreyesus said in a post on X.

The Israeli military claimed that the two men whom they killed, Ahmad Abou Hassira and Moaz Alitsbach, were members of Hamas’s military wing. It also added that the strike was “not directed at a hospital” and caused no damage to the facility.

The Israeli military has often accused Hamas of embedding itself within civilian infrastructure, including hospitals. However, in 2024 the head of the international criminal court’s Palestine investigation said claims about the presence of Hamas fighters in Gaza’s hospitals had been “grossly exaggerated”.

Israel has killed Palestinian medical workers en masse since the start of the war in Gaza. According to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, at least 1,700 have been killed by Israeli attacks. Rights groups say the Israeli military has engaged in systematic destruction of civilian infrastructure, including medical infrastructure.
The UN has repeatedly called on Israel to stop its restrictions on the entry of supplies to allow Palestinians to prepare for the winter and begin to rebuild the destroyed strip.
The result is a healthcare system “experiencing systemic collapse, severely undermining its capacity to meet the basic health needs of the civilian population”, according to a UN report in August.
The humanitarian situation is also deteriorating, as heavy rains exacerbate crowded and unsanitary living conditions, leading to the spread of infectious diseases.

Israel has continued to bomb Gaza on a near-daily basis despite a ceasefire signed in October 2025, killing at least 1,705 people since then. Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of violating the understandings of the ceasefire.
The war began after a Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 that killed about 1,200 people.

More than 74,000 people have been killed and more than 175,000 injured in Israel’s war in Gaza. A UN independent international commission of inquiry found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court for war crimes. Israel denies these claims.

articles.title: Argentina fails to block UK-led oil drilling off Falkland Islands
articles.summary:
International tribunal rules there does not appear to be basis for believing Buenos Aires has jurisdiction on islands

Argentina’s attempt to block oil drilling off the Falkland Islands has…

blocks.text: Argentina’s attempt to block oil drilling off the Falkland Islands has been rejected by an international tribunal.
Buenos Aires had called for the international tribunal for the law of the sea (ITLOS) to order a halt to the Sea Lion project, as part of its claim to sovereignty over the Falklands.

But in a decision read out by ITLOS president, Maurice Kamga, on Saturday, the court rejected Argentina’s arguments, saying there did not appear to be any basis for believing it had jurisdiction as the tribunal is unable to rule on questions of sovereignty.
Kamga said 18 judges had voted to reject Argentina’s claims, while three had voted to uphold them.

At a hearing earlier this month, Argentina said drilling should not be allowed until the issue of sovereignty had been resolved and asked ITLOS to issue a temporary injunction until a full arbitration hearing could be held.

But the UK attorney general, Ellie Reeves, said such an order would have “devastating consequences” for the Falkland Islanders and prevent them from developing their natural resources “as they are entitled to do so, pursuant to their fundamental right to self-determination”.
The Sea Lion development is a joint venture in the South Atlantic Ocean between British and Israeli companies, and contains an estimated 1.7bn barrels of oil.
The Argentinian president, Javier Milei, previously described the companies’ activities as unlawful and launched economic sanctions on people and firms involved in oil exploration around the islands.

articles.title: AI data centers in space: Millions of satellites and so many unknowns
articles.summary: SpaceX is seeking approval to launch a million satellites into orbit to build AI data centers in space. Experts are skeptical, citing many unanswered questions. At the top of the list: Who owns the…

image.caption: By 2040, SpaceX's Starship rockets are expected to have deployed 1 million satellites into space. With today's technology, that is impossibleImage: Chandan Khanna/AFP

blocks.text: Elon Musk's space company SpaceX has got the green light from the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to build a network of 1 million satellites designed to host AI data centers in space. The project is called "Starmind."

Official approval comes with an ambitious timeline: SpaceX must have 10%, or 100,000, of the authorized satellites in orbit by 2035. By 2038, that figure must reach 50%. Within 15 years, a total of 1 million satellites are expected to orbit Earth, helping meet the rapidly growing demand for artificial intelligence computing power.
Why is space a potential location for AI data centers?
1. Ample sunshine and no clouds

"Putting data centers onto satellites and into space is somewhat attractive due to the higher availability of solar energy," Ulrich Speidel of the University of Auckland's School of Computer Science in New Zealand told the Science Media Center.
Depending on a satellite's orbit, it would be exposed to sunlight for more than half the day, Speidel said. And, of course, there are no clouds in space.
SpaceX makes a similar argument, saying its satellites would take advantage of space's plentiful energy and cooling possibilities, reducing the burden on Earth.

Electricity consumption by AI data centers is indeed rising worldwide. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), their consumption could more than double to 945 terawatt-hours per year by 2030.
Will Elon Musk's plan to have data centers in orbit take off?
2. No water consumption for cooling

In addition to electricity, data centers on Earth consume large amounts of water to cool their servers. According to a recent study, global water consumption for this purpose ranges from 313 billion to 764 billion liters (82.7 billion to 201.8 billion gallons). Around a quarter of all data centers are also located in regions that regularly experience water shortages, the study's authors said.

Cooling in space, however, is difficult, Ulrich Speidel said. "The only way to remove heat from a satellite in a vacuum is to radiate it away, rather than dissipate it as we can do here on Earth using water or air cooling."
Richard Easther, a physicist at the University of Auckland, also sees cooling as a challenge, "but there are plausible solutions that are entirely consistent with basic physics."

However, Easther told the Science Media Center that the "Starmind" project is "at the very edge of technical feasibility." He also pointed out that Elon Musk's Starlink project would have sounded far-fetched 15 years ago.
Data centers in space: Solution or disaster?
What are the arguments against space as a location for AI data centers?
Easther said he sees the FCC timeline as unrealistic, joining others who doubt that SpaceX can meet its commitments to the agency.

"That would mean launching about eight satellites per hour from now until their deadline to complete the authorized constellation of Nov. 25, 2040," Laura Revell, a professor of atmospheric chemistry at the University of Canterbury in Christchurch, New Zealand, told the Science Media Center.
1. Rockets and satellites damaging the ozone layer

"I am extremely concerned about the levels of pollution that would accumulate in the atmosphere. We already know that emissions from rocket launches can cause depletion of the protective ozone layer," Revell said.
So far, this has not been a major problem because of the relatively small number of rocket launches. But this project could undo "decades of efforts to protect the ozone layer," she said.

The satellites themselves also pose an environmental risk, Revell said. Satellites are typically decommissioned after five years. When they reenter the atmosphere, they burn up, which "fundamentally turns the atmosphere into a crematorium for satellites," she said.
Overall, the long-term effects of vaporized metals on the atmosphere's climate and the ozone layer are entirely unknown.
Could space debris endanger the ozone layer again?
2. Space debris on the rise

Space debris is already a problem. The Starmind project would increase the number of active satellites in orbit by more than 50-fold, Michael Brown, an astronomer at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, told the Science Media Center.
"This greatly increases the risk of collisions with space junk, which could lead to the Kessler syndrome — a cascade of collisions that would make low Earth orbit unusable."
3. Light pollution in the night sky
Earth's increasingly crowded orbit is not the only factor that could make space research more difficult for astronomers in the future.

The Starmind satellites will come equipped with enormous solar panels. These will be larger and heavier than other satellites because of the cooling systems they need. This could have "devastating effects on numerous astronomical observations," physicist Richard Easther said. Even for people who are not astronomers, the view of the night sky could change dramatically.
The FCC made a decision with global implications on its own, dismissing environmental concerns as being "outside its purview," Laura Revell said.
"The question is, who has the authority to protect the upper atmosphere from rocket and satellite pollution for the common good?"
One thing is certain: Protecting the atmosphere should not be left to a company focused on maximizing profits.
This article was originally written in German.
