articles.title: High-security prisoner used soap to escape despite being handcuffed and chained to officer
articles.summary:
Exclusive: inmate from HMP Manchester now back in custody after 13 hours on the run

A prisoner from one of England and Wales’s most dysfunctional high-security jails is believed to have used…

blocks.text: A prisoner from one of England and Wales’s most dysfunctional high-security jails is believed to have used soap to help escape from officers while visiting a hospital for treatment.

The 36-year-old detained at HMP Manchester managed to slip away despite being cuffed and chained to an officer, sources told the Guardian. He is believed to have lathered his metal cuff with liquid soap and slipped his hand out while being given privacy to use a bathroom.
After 13 hours of freedom and a short pursuit on foot, the offender was detained and arrested by Greater Manchester police officers.
The incident has sparked a formal inquiry by the Ministry of Justice, and comes amid an increase in escapes from jails in England and Wales.
This is the second time this year that a prisoner has escaped after attending a Manchester hospital.

Marwan Jumaa, a 20-year-old Sudanese national deemed to be a risk to himself and others, was serving an indefinite secure hospital sentence for attacking two women. He escaped after being transferred from his secure hospital facility to North Manchester hospital for medical treatment in July.
Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the prison officers’ union, the POA, demanded that more officers should escort offenders from category A and B prisons to hospitals.

“This incident highlights the risks that officers face when escorting prisoners to and from hospitals. There should be a minimum of three officers on every hospital appointment instead of two under current rules,” he said.

The number of prisoners escaping from custody has steadily increased over the past three years. In 2025-26, 14 people escaped from custody across England and Wales, compared with 12 the year before, and nine in 2023-24.
HMP Manchester, once known as Strangeways and which houses category A and B prisoners, has been said to have some of the worst conditions across the England and Wales estate.
The category B prisoner escaped on the evening of 20 November after two prison officers accompanied him to a local hospital.
According to prison escort regulations, category B prisoners must wear “double handcuffs” – where both wrists are restrained close to each other and a prisoner is cuffed to a member of staff.

Subject to risk assessment, the double cuff can be adjusted to a single cuff and a ratchet chain when privacy and hand movements are required, such as when using the toilet or shower. This allows the prison officers to give an offender privacy in a room or cubicle while still being attached to an officer via a chain, which can be more than a metre long.

Sources said that the prisoner had been placed in a single cuff and chain but had escaped from his cuff while using a bathroom. Police were alerted at 8.30pm and searched for the man overnight. He was located at 9.30am on Saturday, and was detained and arrested after attempting to flee on foot.
The internal MoJ investigation will focus on whether safety procedures were carried out at all times and if the man was handcuffed properly.
A spokesperson for Greater Manchester police said: “We received a call shortly before 8.30pm on Friday 20 November that a 36-year-old man had absconded from lawful custody whilst at hospital.

“Officers deployed and utilising specialist resources conducted a full search over the course of the evening and into the morning. The man was safely detained at around 9.30am on Saturday 21 November following a short foot chase and further arrested on suspicion of escaping lawful custody. He has been transported back to custody.”
Prison sources said the escape of a prisoner held in a high-security prison was still relatively rare.

In September 2023, Daniel Khalife, 23, sparked a high-profile search when he broke out of HMP Wandsworth by clinging to the underside of a food delivery truck. At the time he was being held on remand for spying charges.
Last year, an escaped prisoner tried to flee armed police by ramming them with his getaway car. Jay Bennett, 33, was serving a nine-year sentence when he absconded from HMP Sudbury in Derbyshire.

An official report into HMP Manchester conducted earlier this year by the prisons watchdog found large quantities of drugs flown in by drones, an obvious rat infestation and violence against prisoners and staff.

The report by Charlie Taylor, HM chief inspector of prisons, said the jail was “in a precarious state”. In 2024, he invoked an urgent notification, which automatically triggers ministers to intervene in the jail’s management.

A Prison Service spokesperson said: “This individual is now back in custody. We have launched an investigation into this incident and any prisoner who is unlawfully at large faces extra time in prison.”

articles.title: Deal with Epstein lawyer and accountant could block victims’ other claims, experts warn
articles.summary:
Concern that settlement to resolve suit against pair may stymie legal claims that involve child sexual abuse material

As the clock ticks toward final settlement for a sex-trafficking-related…

blocks.text: As the clock ticks toward final settlement for a sex-trafficking-related lawsuit against Jeffrey Epstein’s accountant and attorney, some experts are expressing concern that the agreement might stymie survivors’ search for justice in other litigation involving child sexual abuse images.

The suit involves Darren Indyke and Richard D Kahn, who for decades worked as Epstein’s personal lawyer and accountant respectively. Both men also serve as executors of Epstein’s estate. Indyke and Kahn have insisted they knew nothing about Epstein’s crimes and have rejected allegations of wrongdoing.

In the soon-to-be-settled 2024 Manhattan federal court civil complaint against them, survivors’ attorneys allege that Indyke and Kahn “were personally essential to the Epstein enterprise’s success – among other things, they helped structure Epstein’s bank accounts and cash withdrawals to give Epstein and his associates access to large amounts of cash in furtherance of sex trafficking”.

A final settlement hearing in this trafficking-related case is scheduled for 2 December, during which a judge might sign off on the agreement brokered between survivors’ attorneys at Boies Schiller & Flexner LLP, and Indyke and Kahn. This agreement would establish a $35m settlement pool for survivors who qualify for compensation with these claims, according to court papers.

Epstein, a high-powered financier who counted numerous wealthy and prominent men as his associates, was arrested in July 2019 and charged with sex-trafficking minors following years of allegations against him. The Manhattan US attorney’s office said that his victims were as young as age 14 when he abused them. He killed himself in jail while awaiting trial.

Jennifer Freeman of Marsh Law, who helms other litigation against Epstein, has voiced concerns about the proposed settlement, namely that this deal might set up roadblocks to legal claims against his estate that involve child sex abuse material, or CSAM.

Survivors and law enforcement have said that Epstein possessed, transported, produced and distributed CSAM over decades. Freeman said she fears that Epstein’s estate could try arguing that the proposed Kahn/Indyke settlement protects his estate from any possible litigation brought by CSAM survivors.

“We objected to the settlement on the grounds that CSAM has its own separate claim with its own statutory remedies and this was not, in our view, considered in putting together this settlement,” Freeman told the Guardian.
Freeman represents two women in a 15 September lawsuit involving CSAM claims, as well as several class members of the trafficking-related litigation.

“We fully support the existence of a settlement for survivors, and we want that to go forward, and we very much hope it does,” Freeman said. “However, we believe that the release of [Epstein’s] estate doesn’t make sense here, since the case was not against the estate – it was against two individuals, the lawyer and the accountant.”

Freeman also said she had concerns that survivors might not be aware of the proposed settlement and what she believes might be potential implications on CSAM claims against Epstein’s estate. Freeman wants any Epstein survivor who endured CSAM abuse – including those who participate in the trafficking settlement – to have an opportunity to pursue claims related directly to CSAM.

While the judge on 16 September extended the deadline for survivors to submit or opt out of trafficking-related claims, Freeman said that “we’ve heard from many, particularly those who are outside the United States, [who] had no idea anything was going on”.
“They don’t have class actions typically in their countries, so this would not be a familiar process for them to look out for or understand … that it might apply to them.”

CSAM claims “should not be included in the settlement at all. That should be explicit,” Freeman said of her hopes for the final agreement. “The release of the estate should be at least limited and, in my view, eliminated.”
Asked for comment, attorneys for Indyke and Kahn deferred to prior statements on allegations against them.

In a recent lawsuit against them brought by New Mexico’s attorney general, Raúl Torrez, one of their lawyers said they “emphatically rejected” claims “they were complicit in or in any way knowingly facilitated Mr Epstein’s sexual abuse or trafficking – conduct that by all accounts occurred behind closed doors, in secluded locations, and at times when neither Mr Indyke nor Mr Kahn was present.

“Not a single woman has ever accused Mr Indyke or Mr Kahn of committing sexual abuse or witnessing sexual abuse, nor claimed at any time that she or anyone else reported to them any allegation of Mr Epstein’s abuse,” the statement also said.

Attorneys for Indyke and Kahn do not agree with concerns that the trafficking-related settlement is over-broad. Daniel Ruzumna, who represents Indyke, said: “As the parties pointed out at the hearing and the court appeared to recognize, the putative class only includes women who were sexually abused and/or trafficked by Epstein.”

“That would include any woman who also may also have a CSAM-related claim, in which case that woman may be entitled to a larger recovery from the settlement fund,” Ruzumna said. “But if a woman only had CSAM-related claims, she would not be part of the class … at the September 16 2026 hearing, the parties made clear that women with CSAM-only claims (ie who were not abused or trafficked themselves) are not part of the class and therefore would not release claims.”

Epstein’s apparent possession of CSAM has been detailed by law enforcement officials, as well as materials released under the Epstein Files Transparency Act. An FBI memo, for example, said files included “a large volume of images of Epstein, images and videos of victims who are either minors or appear to be minors, and over ten thousand downloaded videos and images of illegal child sex abuse material and other pornography.”

Maria Farmer, whose sister Annie was abused by Epstein and his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell at age 16, told authorities in 1996 that he possessed nude images of her siblings. “Complainant [Maria Farmer] stated that she is a professional artist and took pictures of her sisters 12 and 16 yrs for her own [personal] Art Work,” the law enforcement report stated.
“Epstein Stole the photos and Negatives and is believed to have sold the pictures to potential buyers,” the authorities’ report on Maria’s allegations also said.
Maria also reported “pictures of young girls at swimming pools” and recounted that Epstein said “if she tells anyone about the photos he will burn her house down”.

articles.title: US oligarchs enriched by ‘transactional’ Trump face fierce scrutiny in new Congress
articles.summary:
Democrats pledge aggressive investigations into Trump-allied billionaires and how president’s policies have boosted their bottom lines

For an elite circle of Donald Trump billionaire allies…

blocks.text: For an elite circle of Donald Trump billionaire allies who lavished tens of millions of dollars on his campaign, vanity projects and crypto ventures, his second administration has boosted their bottom lines through lax oversight, tax breaks, federal contracts and other perks.

But with Democrats winning control of Congress in the midterms, House and Senate investigations are being planned for 2027 into several Maga oligarchs in hi-tech and crypto industries, examining how their firms and the president benefited from his “transactional” governing style, according to Democratic lawmakers and scholars.

Trump allies expected to face scrutiny by congressional panels looking, in part, at how Trump’s pay-to-play modus operandi has financially and politically benefited them include Space X mogul Elon Musk, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, and crypto titans such as Binance founder Changpeng Zhao.

blocks.caption: Elon Musk at the ‘New Golden Age’ summit in Washington last month. Photograph: Evan Vucci/Reuters

blocks.text: Trump’s own wealth soared by $2.7bn since he won the presidency again in 2024 – due in good measure to “crypto ventures and overseas deals”, according to a Forbes report in September.

Additionally, Trump’s sons, Eric and Donald Jr, have notched sizable financial gains in tech, crypto and other areas since Trump won again, and are expected to face Capitol Hill inquiries into ways their Oval Office ties may have benefited them.

White House and justice department lawyers in November sent threatening letters to key congressional Democrats, warning they could face scrutiny, and perhaps criminal charges, if they investigated some of Trump’s big-money patrons and their federal contracts.

Scholars and legal experts who have tracked some of Trump’s financial moves, boosting his personal fortune and increasing the wealth of his big patrons, see ample evidence that the ties between Trump and some of his leading donors and business allies have hurt American democracy.

“The personal wealth of Trump, his family, and those in his inner circle, as well as Trump’s vanity projects, are being funded by the very tech titans whose own wealth and power has been boosted by this administration’s policies and actions,” Cornell economist Eswar Prasad said in an email.

blocks.caption: Jensen Huang, the Nvidia CEO. Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters

blocks.text: Prasad earlier this year raised red flags about Trump’s dealings with “crypto tycoons”, telling the Guardian: “Trump and his family have hardly been shy about cozying up to crypto tycoons, and have been quite brazen in their pay-for-play approach to this sector.”
While the Hill investigations are in planning stages, tech leaders led by Elon Musk have clearly been big winners in the second Trump administration.

Trump and Republicans forged especially close ties with Musk, the world’s richest man, who spent almost $300m in 2024 to help Trump win, and then about $450m in the midterms in mostly failed efforts to help GOP candidates.

According to an in-depth report this fall from the nonpartisan Democracy Defenders Fund, Musk firms secured $6bn in government contracts while he was leading Trump’s “Doge” drive to cut federal spending, and another $10bn in contracts since he left his post last year.
Moreover, the study found 25 federal agencies or departments have “taken actions benefiting or potentially benefiting his businesses”.

blocks.caption: Trump with his sons at the Republican national convention in Milwaukee in July 2024. Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty Images

blocks.text: The DDF report – Trump and Musk, 17 Months Later – also found that Musk’s net worth “more than doubled since he left Doge in May 2025, growing from approximately $419bn to between $900bn and $1tn”.

“The central finding is that the current government ethics framework allows the world’s richest person – a major political donor and former government official – to earn billions from federal contracts while his companies receive favorable treatment across government,” the report concluded.

Before the elections, Musk on X vowed to hit back against those who go after him, writing: “Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them.”

Separately, Huang, who resigned as Nvidia CEO after reports of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy spurred fears of China gaining significant access to Nvidia’s valuable microchips, looks to have benefited from the president’s pay-to-play governing style.

In a stunning twist, 11 days after Huang quit, and facing clear pressure from Trump and others in his administration, Nvidia announced Huang would return as CEO, a move which fueled bipartisan concerns and calls for hearings next month.
Huang in 2025 was among the biggest known donors to Trump’s prized ballroom, reportedly giving $25m to finance the venture, according to Public Citizen, a liberal watchdog.

Moreover, Trump’s financial disclosures in 2026 revealed Nvidia stock trading over 100 times since he returned to office with a combined transaction value between 27m and 97m, according to Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (Crew).

Trump has said all his stocks are managed solely by independent outside advisers and he has no role in stock trading. Trump has also repeatedly denied any conflicts of interest or quid pro quos as president.

Trump and his billionaire commerce secretary Howard Lutnick reportedly ignored national security intelligence warnings and allowed Nvidia to sell its advanced chips to the Singapore-based datacenter firm Megaspeed, which was until August 2025 run by Alice Huang, the alleged spy who had an affair with Jensen Huang.

According to press reports, Alice Huang was in touch with China’s spy agency for months when her firm sold some of Nvidia’s advanced chips to other datacenters in south-east Asia with China ties, and some of which were suspected of being smuggled to China, fueling bipartisan criticism and some internal administration dissent.

Separately, several major crypto companies have profited from the administration’s lax crypto regulatory oversight, including Binance, the world’s biggest crypto trading platform. Last year, in a complex deal, Binance helped the Trump family’s crypto venture World Liberty Financial, which only launched in the fall of 2024, secure a $2bn infusion from an Abu Dhabi-backed state investment fund.
Trump reported earning over $1.4bn from World Liberty and other crypto ventures in 2025, or about two-thirds of the $2.2bn in earnings his 2025 financial disclosures showed.
Responding to media questions about his stunning earnings last year, Trump told reporters: “You know why I’m profiting? Because the stock market’s going up. Everybody’s profiting.”

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty in 2023 to anti money-laundering and sanctions violations, and Binance agreed to pay $4.3bn in fines and restitution to the government. Zhao, who reportedly owns 90% of Binance stock, served a four-month sentence and was pardoned late last year by Trump in a controversial move.

Since he won a second term, Trump has issued executive orders boosting the crypto industry by easing regulations and oversight by the Securities and Exchange Commission, a huge shift from under Joe Biden, which Trump promised in a talk in mid-2024 at a major bitcoin conference.

Crypto moguls and allied groups poured tens of millions into the midterms, largely trying to defeat Democrats. Legal experts and economists now see ample reason to investigate the close ties between Trump and his crypto and hi-tech oligarch allies.

Former Federal Election Commission general counsel Larry Noble said: “Despite the efforts of Musk and other tech and crypto oligarchs, they are now going to be facing members of Congress questioning their past actions and future plans, and demanding answers about their transactional and mutually beneficial dealings with Trump, not meaningless photo ops and compliments.
“They just learned that democracy is not some computer game or theoretical idea. It’s voters exercising their power in real time, and the voters were not happy.”
Prasad raised similar concerns.

He said: “Trump and his acolytes have openly peddled their influence and twisted the policy apparatus they now control in order to favor tech moguls, who have been equally open about their direct and indirect paybacks to Trump, his family and associates, and his political and other causes.”
A few incoming chairs of House and Senate panels have signaled investigations that in part will look at leading billionaires, including Musk.

Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, who will lead the permanent subcommittee on investigations, and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who will head the banking committee, are likely to continue to examine some of the tech and crypto moguls who have benefited from their close Trump ties.

New scrutiny of some Trump-allied oligarchs is also expected in the House from Robert Garcia of California, who will lead the House oversight committee and Jamie Raskin of Maryland, who is poised to run the House judiciary committee.
Raskin in an email pinpointed some specific concerns Congress will investigate, including foreign investors in World Liberty Financial and Zhao’s pardon by Trump.

“Four days before Trump took office [in 2025], a firm backed by the UAE’s national security adviser reportedly agreed to pay $500m for a 49% stake in World Liberty, the Trump family’s crypto venture,” Raskin said.

“By May, the Trump administration had announced a deal giving the UAE access to advanced American AI chips. Congress will look into whether doing business with the president’s family helped Zhao get his pardon or the UAE get access to those chips.”
Raskin also indicated that the hundreds of billions in ballroom funding by super-rich donors will be investigated.

“Some of the tech executives who sat behind Trump at his inauguration run companies now helping to pay for his billionaire ballroom. What business did those companies have before the administration when they lined up to fund his vanity project? When Democrats take the gavel, we’ll investigate the rampant conflicts in the Administration and write legislation to crack down on this pervasive self-dealing.”

In pre-emptive responses to a few Senate and House Democrats, administration lawyers in November sent strongly worded letters warning that they could face stiff scrutiny and perhaps face criminal charges if they mount aggressive probes of top Trump allies.

Attorney general Todd Blanche, a hardcore Trump loyalist, said on CNN in early November that Democrats had “done nothing but threaten everything that’s happening in this administration” and suggested that members of Congress might be criminally investigated.

Just a day later, White House counsel Will Scharf launched an extraordinary assault on Congress’s constitutional authority in a letter to Garcia claiming that oversight investigations “may cross the line into blatant criminality”. He charged Garcia with displaying intent to “transgress” congressional power.

Garcia has forcefully rebuked these legal warnings. “What Todd Blanche is doing right now is a threat,” Garcia said on CNN. “He is threatening our committee. He’s trying to stop us from doing real oversight.”

And on 11 November, Garcia released a tough rebuttal to Scharf. “It appears Donald Trump has something to hide. Let’s be clear: Congress’s authority comes from article I of the constitution, not from the permission of the White House.”
Raskin, likewise, pushed back on administration attacks.

He said: “The president’s lawyers can spare us the crackpot heckling about congressional revenge. That’s their MO, not ours. We in Congress will do our job regardless of all the heckling and tirades. In truth, they’d be better off using this time to get their records in order.”
Scholars and ex-prosecutors call the legal threats from Trump’s lawyers intimidation tactics that will not affect planned investigations and will not stand up in court.
“The Trump administration has developed a symbiotic relationship with the tech billionaires,” said former federal prosecutor Barbara McQuade, who now teaches law at the University of Michigan.

“The tech bros make campaign contributions and donations to Trump’s vanity projects, and the Trump administration protects them from accountability or regulation. Both groups fear investigations that could cut off the unchecked flow of money. These threats of criminal prosecution strike me as part of the old strategy that the best defense is a good offense.”

articles.title: Whose lane is it anyway? Why the Alberta UCP is wading into municipal issues
articles.summary: Protecting provincial jurisdiction is part of current Premier Danielle Smith’s mantra. Yet, that same government has overruled local decision makers on a growing list of issues in the last two years…

image.caption: Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas and Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack are not happy. They say the provincial government is repeatedly stepping on the toes of cities. (CBC News)

blocks.text: Edmonton·Analysis

Protecting provincial jurisdiction is part of current Premier Danielle Smith’s mantra. Yet, that same government has overruled local decision makers on a growing list of issues in the last two years including bike lanes, photo radar and zoning rules.
Edmonton, Calgary mayors accuse province of overreach
Alberta’s premiers have long complained about Ottawa sticking its nose in provincial affairs.
Whether it's calling for fewer restrictions on resource development or pushing back on federal gun control, protecting provincial jurisdiction is part of Premier Danielle Smith’s mantra.

Yet, that same government has waded into a growing list of municipal issues in the last two years including bike lanes, photo radar and zoning rules. And Alberta’s big city mayors are not happy about it.
“We've seen significant overreach, overreach in a way that I've never experienced in my 13 years serving,” Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack told CBC’s West of Centre.

“I think it is time to have a real conversation about what we expect from municipalities, making sure they have the authority to address those things without this fear that you're going to have backseat drivers.”
Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas, while talking with reporters last month, said the government needs to stay in its own lane.
“Overreach is bad when Justin Trudeau does it,” he said. “It’s bad when Danielle Smith does it.”
LISTEN | From bike lanes to photo radar. Alberta and its cities collide:
But tensions between cities and the province in Alberta are nothing new. The UCP jumped into local government issues multiple times since Smith won a majority mandate in 2023. Including:

items: Banning electronic tabulators in municipal elections.
Bringing in municipal political parties and allowing corporate and union donations in local elections.
Banning photo radar, a major source of revenue for municipalities.
Controlling how local taxes and development fees work, including disallowing communities like Canmore from charging a higher tax rate on some vacation properties.
Repealing all local council codes of conduct, and imposing a universal code councils must abide by.
Requiring public libraries to restrict youth access to books with sexually graphic images.
Wading into a Calgary noise bylaw, with Smith calling council the“fun police."
Legislating a provincial ability to remove municipal councillors and repeal bylaws it doesn’t like.
Stopping municipalities from using diversity, equity and inclusion in hiring decisions or mandatory training.
Preventing municipalities from accepting federal deals without provincial approval.
Requiring provincial approval on future LRT transit plans.
Granting the province the ability to remove existing city bike lanes.
Repealing Edmonton’s zoning bylaw and freezing zoning rules in Calgary.

blocks.text: Creatures of the province

The Canadian Constitution only recognizes the federal and provincial governments. The Alberta government delegates authority to cities, towns and other municipalities in the Municipal Government Act. That authority can be taken back or changed at any time.
Municipal Affairs Minister Dan Williams has said it’s his responsibility to set the ground rules for how municipalities operate.
But that doesn’t mean the province is following political norms.

“We absolutely are creatures of the province, but we are also a duly elected level of government,” Krista Gardner, a spokesperson for Alberta Municipalities and mayor of Calmar, a town south of Edmonton, said in an interview.

Gardner said if people are unhappy with decisions being made at local councils, they can vote differently. And if the province is dissatisfied, she’d rather see it work with councils instead of unilaterally rolling back bylaws.
At an announcement to repeal Edmonton’s zoning bylaw in October, Smith said she wants to leave municipalities to make their own decisions, but she felt compelled to act in this instance.
“When municipalities have taken actions that are undermining people’s property value, when you see the kind of reaction that we’ve seen from residents, then we have to step in,” Smith said.
But Calgary’s mayor doesn’t agree.
“It’s about power, it’s not about zoning,” Farkas told CBC last month.
Nothing to lose, columnist says
Some experts say it's not surprising the UCP is taking this approach, noting heated local issues are something the party could capitalize on.
Brendan Boyd, an associate professor of political science at MacEwan University told CBC’s Edmonton AM that it could give the party an edge among certain urban voters.

“The province is stepping in because they're going to get the support of the people who are opposed to bike lanes in the cities,” Boyd said. “And maybe that's a bit of a strategy for how they're going to set things up for the next election.”

items: Edmonton and Calgary rejected her referendum. Does Danielle Smith have a city problem?
Province to install ‘City of Champions’ signs on highways into Edmonton

blocks.text: Edmonton Journal columnist Keith Gerein told West of Centre that’s especially true in the capital, where the UCP has only won a single seat in the last three provincial elections.
“It's basically been an NDP fortress,” Gerein said.
“If they can walk in and be the saviour, … maybe they can swing — or they believe they can swing — a few ridings their way. It's worth a shot, right? They've got nothing to lose.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Emily is a reporter and producer with CBC's West of Centre podcast. Previously, she covered Edmonton city hall. She can be reached at emily.williams@cbc.ca.

articles.title: OpenAI counter-sues Apple over alleged theft of trade secrets
articles.summary: The ChatGPT-maker alleges that tech giant Apple stole trade secrets through a former employee.

blocks.text: ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has counter-sued Apple, alleging that the iPhone maker stole trade secrets through a former employee.

In a federal lawsuit filed in July, Apple sued the artificial intelligence (AI) company and two of its employees who previously worked for Apple, claiming it had engaged in a "pattern of theft" of proprietary information.

A countersuit, filed in California on Friday, alleged that Apple gained confidential information through the hiring of a former OpenAI employee and accuses it of discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices.
Apple denied the counterclaims, describing them as "a transparent attempt to distract from the substance" of its own case.
OpenAI is developing AI-enabled personal devices, which it claims in the countersuit could threaten to "outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf".
The filing alleged Apple had gained confidential information by rehiring a former employee who had worked at OpenAI for six months.

OpenAI accused the employee, who it said gained access to information on a new device and the company's roadmap for future physical products, of sending "dozens of OpenAI documents" to his personal phone numbers. It also said he presented OpenAI's plans to senior Apple staff "at Apple's request".
OpenAI said: "Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place."

The counterclaim also alleged Apple encourages employees to mix work files with their personal iCloud (Apple's cloud storage service) accounts so it could later accuse those who leave to work for competitors of theft.

A spokesperson for Apple said: "This case is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products - not about inadvertent retention of Apple information."

In its own lawsuit, the tech giant alleged that at least two long-time Apple workers who left the company to join OpenAI took part in a "pattern of theft" by emailing themselves internal Apple information.
Apple also accused the AI firm of undertaking a "strategy to extract Apple's confidential information".
A spokesperson for OpenAI previously denied the claims, telling the BBC: "We have no interest in other companies' trade secrets."

Along with OpenAI, and two former Apple employees, Apple is also suing io Products, the design startup founded by Sir Jony Ive, a long-time Apple executive who designed the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad.
OpenAI acquired the company last year in a $6.5bn (£4.7bn) deal.

articles.title: As Spain votes, what could change for Europe?
articles.summary: Spain votes on Sunday. A loss for Pedro Sanchez and a shift to the right in Madrid could affect how one of the EU's largest countries approaches migration, defense and the war in Gaza.

image.caption: Recent polls have predicted a tight race, putting the conservative People's Party (PP) and the Socialists led by Pedro Sanchez (above) neck and neckImage: Francisco Seco/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Walking through the halls of the European institutions in Brussels these days, it feels as if people are whispering about the end of an era. What happens when one of the most vocal leaders of Europe's center left is no longer at the table?

Pedro Sanchez is one of the few social democratic prime ministers left in the European Union, and Spain is the largest member state still led by one. That's why this election raises questions that go beyond who governs in Madrid.

After more than eight years in office Sanchez called a snap election at the beginning of October, three days after parliament rejected two emergency decrees aimed at tackling Spain's housing crisis. Anger over soaring housing costs has brought protesters onto the streets nationwide this year.

blocks.caption: On November 11, protesters took part in nationwide general strike over the country's housing crisisImage: Thomas Coex/AFP

blocks.text: Sanchez's minority government was already under pressure over its handling of the summer migration crisis in Ceuta and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which both he and his wife have denied.
Polls on Monday predicted a tight race, putting the conservative People's Party (PP) at around 32% and the Socialists led by Sanchez at 31%.

With the right-wing populist Vox party in third place at around 17%, the polling projected an absolute majority for the PP and Vox combined. The two parties would still have to decide whether they want to govern together.

blocks.caption: Alberto Nunez Feijoo leads the opposition People's Party, and could be Spain's next prime ministerImage: Juan Medina/REUTERS

blocks.text: Important center-left voice may be 'silenced'

A change of government in Madrid would cost Europe's center left one of its most influential voices, Javier Carbonell, a policy analyst at the European Policy Centre in Brussels, told DW. "This voice might now be silenced."

Carbonell said three positions have set Sanchez apart: his willingness to challenge US President Donald Trump, his support for Palestinian statehood and his defense of immigration into Europe. Sanchez has been one of the few EU leaders who have continued to argue that migrant workers help fill labor shortages, support an aging Spanish and European population and sustain growth.
Could Spain's train disaster upend Sanchez's election campaign?

Earlier this year, his government opened a program to grant legal status to eligible migrants already living in Spain. It received more than 1 million applications. Spain's economy grew by 2.6% last year, nearly double the eurozone average, and the government expects GDP to grow by 2.6% this year and 2.2% in 2027.
Will Spain take a tougher line on migration?

The conservative PP has campaigned for tighter immigration controls while keeping routes open for workers in sectors facing shortages. Vox wants sharper cuts to immigration, more deportations and an end to regularization for new arrivals. It also wants Spanish citizens to get priority for subsidized housing and other social benefits.

This stance is nothing new at the European level. "With a PP-Vox government, Spain would join the general European trend towards an anti-immigration policy," said Carbonell, adding that he could see Madrid moving closer to countries pushing for tougher return policies. Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands are already in talks with Rwanda about setting up a hub for people whose asylum claims have been rejected.

Camino Mortera-Martinez, an associate fellow at the Centre for European Reform, agrees that a shift in Madrid would reinforce a trend already underway in Europe. "This anti-migration tendency doesn't come from European leaders, but from voters," she told DW.
How the far right hardened Europe's migration stance
PP, Vox back higher defense spending

Another domain where Spain could potentially change course and influence its European neighbors concerns its defense policies. Spain raised defense spending from 1.24% of GDP in 2024 to 2% in 2025, reaching NATO's previous benchmark.

Nevertheless, Sanchez has pushed back against the alliance's new annual target of 5% of GDP by 2035, which includes both military spending and broader security investments. He has argued that Spain could meet its NATO capability commitments by spending around 2.1% of GDP.

Both the PP and Vox favor higher defense investment but leave the exact figure open in their election programs. "They have a voting base that has no problem to increase defense spending, contrary to Sanchez," said Mortera-Martinez.
A shift on Israel and Palestinian statehood?
Mortera-Martinez also expects a change in Spain's approach to the Middle East, should Sanchez lose the election.
"The current government has been at the forefront of defending the last bastions of international and public law," she said.

Spain formally recognized a Palestinian state in May 2024. Sanchez has accused European leaders of applying double standards by rallying behind Ukraine against Russia's invasion, while failing to defend international law with the same resolve in the Middle East. In April, he pushed to suspend the EU's agreement with Israel, which makes respect for human rights an essential part of the relationship.

Carbonell, too, believes a new conservative government would be less vocal in its support for the Palestinians. "Sanchez was able to influence people on the subject matter, moving the consensus a bit more towards pro-Palestine," he said.

If Sanchez comes up short on Sunday, Europe's social democrats would lose their strongest foothold among the EU's largest countries. But, said Carbonell, a defeat in Spain could reignite a debate across the European center left about how to win back voters and stay politically relevant elsewhere.

articles.summary: A breach of over 5,000 petabytes is roughly equivalent to 5 million terabytes of data. This is how much 5G mobile data is being used as of the first nine months of 2026. Smart advances AI-powered…

blocks.text: A breach of over 5,000 petabytes is roughly equivalent to 5 million terabytes of data. This is how much 5G mobile data is being used as of the first nine months of 2026.
Smart advances AI-powered mobile experiences with 5G

Mobile services provider Smart Communications, Inc. (Smart), the wireless arm of PLDT Inc., is accelerating its 5G network expansion and advancing network-based innovations to meet growing mobile data demand and deliver better digital experiences to subscribers. As of September 2026, Smart had deployed 6,100 5G base stations nationwide, up from 5,400 in 2025. The number of individual 5G devices on its network reached 12.9 million, compared with 10.5 million a year earlier, reflecting the continued adoption of 5G-capable devices among subscribers.Smart’s 5G network covers 99% of the population across Metro Manila and Rizal, while its combined 5G and 4G network reaches 97% of the Philippine population. Mobile data traffic also continued to rise, reaching 5,029 petabytes in the first nine months of 2026, up from 4,393 petabytes during the same period in 2025. The growth underscores the increasing role of mobile connectivity in everyday activities, from video streaming and gaming to online learning, remote work, and the use of AI-powered applications.
Turning network investments into better digital experiences

Smart’s accelerated 5G expansion is complemented by efforts to improve network performance and develop services that help subscribers make more of their connectivity. In the first half of 2026, Smart earned Ookla’s Best Mobile Video Experience award in the Philippines for the second consecutive year, recognizing its performance in delivering mobile video experiences.In October, Smart introduced AI.Smart, a one-stop platform that brings together multiple AI tools, including AWS Nova, ChatGPT, Claude, Google Gemini, and Thinking Machines, in a user-friendly interface. The platform gives users access to AI-powered capabilities for writing, research, presentations, image generation, and data analysis.

In early November, Smart began rolling out PureVoice, Asia-Pacific’s first commercially launched native AI voice enhancement service built on the telecommunications core network. Designed to improve call clarity by filtering background noise at the network level, PureVoice does not require users to upgrade their devices or download a separate application. The service has already earned international recognition, winning Best 5G-A Service Innovation at the Global Core Summit Awards in Bangkok, Thailand.
Making the most of Smart 5G

Smart also offers subscribers ways to maximize its 5G network through its Unli 5G promos. For just P90, Smart Prepaid users can enjoy three days of unlimited 5G data plus non-stop 4G data, helping them stay connected as they stream, create content, browse, and pursue their interests. Smart will also bring its S-Tier 5G experience closer to subscribers through an on-ground activation at the Market! Market! Activity Center on December 19 to 20, 2026. The event will feature lifestyle and hobby partners, giving visitors opportunities to explore their interests and discover new experiences powered by Smart.

articles.title: Ten students killed and over 100 injured in explosion in Afghanistan, official says
articles.summary: A spokesman for Afghanistan's interior ministry says the blast was caused by carelessness at an explosives depot nearby.

blocks.text: At least 10 students have been killed and 110 others have been injured following an explosion near a school in Afghanistan, a spokesperson has told the BBC.
The incident happened on Saturday morning in the Anderseir area of Asadabad, the capital of Kunar province, the spokesperson for the Taliban government's interior ministry said.
Posting on X, Abdul Mateen Qani said that according to initial investigations, the blast was caused by "negligence and carelessness" at an explosives depot belonging to nearby mining companies.
An investigation into the incident was ongoing, he added.
Footage shared on social media showed several wounded children being taken out of cars and carried into the emergency department at a hospital in Asadabad as a large crowd watched on.
Photos from inside the hospital also show children lying next to each other in hospital beds with bandages strapped around their heads.
Mining is a major industry in Afghanistan but safety standards are often poor, leading to accidents.

articles.title: Spain to vote in election that could put far right in power for first time since Franco
articles.summary:
Socialist PM Pedro Sánchez’s high-stakes gamble could end in defeat to a coalition including the far-right Vox

Spaniards head to the polls on Sunday to vote in a high-stakes snap general…

blocks.text: Spaniards head to the polls on Sunday to vote in a high-stakes snap general election that could put a far-right party in government for the first time since the country’s return to democracy after the death of Gen Francisco Franco in 1975.

Although the next election was not due until summer next year, Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, called the vote in October after three rightwing and far-right parties voted down the emergency legislation that his government had proposed to address the country’s housing crisis.

Huge public anger over soaring rents exploded in September after the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was removed from her home in Madrid because she could not afford the 230% rent increase demanded by the investment fund that had bought her apartment.

blocks.caption: A protester holds a sign with the slogan ‘Fair rents now’ during a protest at Puerta del Sol in Madrid in October. Photograph: Alejandro Martinez Velez/Reuters

blocks.text: Faced with nationwide protests, Sánchez’s coalition minority government put together a package of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.

Sánchez opted for one of his characteristic gambles and announced the early election after the proposals were torpedoed by the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox and the rightwing Catalan separatist Junts.

The prime minister – an inveterate risk-taker whose penchant for unpredictable moves has fuelled his political survival – calculated that his opponents’ decision to block the housing overhauls could work in his electoral favour.
On Friday morning, Sánchez said he was confident of victory. “I can’t conceive of us losing,” he told Cadena Ser radio, adding: “When progressive Spain gets going, it’s unstoppable.”

But while his Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE) has managed to narrow the distance between it and the PP, which is leading the polls, to fewer than three percentage points, the right looks likely to form the next government in coalition with the far right.

Survey after survey predicts the PP will finish first but fall short of a majority, leaving it dependent on a deal with Vox. Between them, the two parties are forecast to secure a joint majority well above the 176 required seats in Spain’s 350-seat congress of deputies. Even if the PSOE enjoys a last-minute surge and comes first, the parliamentary arithmetic suggests it would struggle to cobble together another coalition administration with the support of its allies in the leftwing Broad Front alliance and with that of regional nationalist parties.

Choosing housing as a key battleground allowed Sánchez to attempt to shift the focus away from the corruption allegations facing his inner circle. It also offered him the chance to move on from his government’s much-criticised handling of the crisis in Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta, which was sparked when about 80,000 people crossed into the territory from neighbouring Morocco in the space of 48 hours.

blocks.caption: Sanchez’s government was criticised after tens of thousands of people crossed into the Spanish city of Ceuta in north Africa from Morocco in July.  Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: But some of the energy of the government’s resurgent campaign was sapped at the end of October when 69 people were killed in Spain’s second deadly rail crash in just nine months.

The PP and Vox have used the two crashes to accuse the government of failing in its basic duty to keep Spaniards safe. More broadly, the PP and Vox are using the poll as a referendum on what they disdainfully refer to as “sanchismo”. They argue that the style of government favoured by the prime minister and his allies is cynical, corrupt, opportunistic and self-serving.

blocks.caption: Cranes lift one of the wrecked carriages after a train crash in Toledo last month. Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “Spain deserves a decent prime minister and [Sánchez] isn’t one,” the PP leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, told viewers during a head-to-head debate between the two men last week.

Sánchez, however, insisted that while he had made errors, Spain was in a better state than it was when he came to office in 2018. “My government hasn’t been perfect; I’ve made mistakes,” he said. “But I’m also fully aware that we have always governed in the right direction.”
The prime minister has also sought to depict the snap election as a stark choice between progressive forces and reactionary ones – as typified by the PP’s putative alliance with Vox.

“You must decide whether you want our country to move backwards or continue moving forwards, and whether you prefer a government that works for the interests of the majority of society,” he told Spaniards as he announced the vote.

Over recent days, the government has tried to underline its commitment to social justice and equality by proposing a new tax on fortunes of more than €100m (£84m) that would help fund childcare, housing and public services.

blocks.caption: (From left): Vox’s Santiago Abascal, the PSOE’s Pedro Sánchez, the PP’s Alberto Núñez Feijóo and the leftwing Frente Amplio’s Ada Colau before a TV debate. Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The PP, meanwhile, is promising to lower taxes, build 1m homes, and “restore the country’s ambition and self-esteem”. Vox’s manifesto, which includes plans to have Sánchez and his government prosecuted “for treason and crimes against the security of the state” over the Ceuta mass crossing, focuses on deregulation, “remigration” and giving Spanish-born people priority over those born abroad for housing and public services.

Although the PP’s previous leader, Pablo Casado, famously repudiated Vox and its ideology, accusing the party of practising a politics based on “fear, anger, resentment and revenge”, the PP has repeatedly entered into regional coalition governments with Vox and now runs four of Spain’s autonomous regions with the party.

In recent days, the PP and Vox have attempted to call into question the fairness and transparency of the election, making baseless claims that the government may seek to rig postal votes. Vox’s leader, Santiago Abascal, has also suggested, without providing evidence, that Sánchez is working to undermine democracy and change the country’s demographic makeup.

An explosion at a school in the eastern Afghan province of Kunar killed seven people and wounded more than 90 on Saturday, the province’s culture and information director said, adding that the blast appeared to have originated in a neighbouring depot for explosives.

Sami ul Haq Bayan said initial information indicated the blast at the school on the outskirts of the provincial capital, Asadabad, occurred due to negligence at the depot storing explosives belonging to mining companies. An investigation into the incident was underway, he said.
Up to 15 of the wounded remained in hospital, while the rest were discharged after treatment, he added.

articles.title: Afghanistan: Several killed in blast near middle school
articles.summary: Officials have said improperly stored explosives at a mining site ignited, damaging nearby buildings including a school. An investigation is ongoing.

image.caption: Children were brought to to Asadabad Provincial Hospital after the blastImage: Shakirullah Safi

blocks.text: An explosion near a middle school on Saturday in Afghanistan's eastern Kunar province killed at least seven students and injured nearly 100 others, according to the Interior Ministry.

Early reports cited by the ministry's spokesperson indicate the blast was caused by negligent storage of explosives at a depot near the school belonging to a mining company in the Andir Sir area of the provincial capital, Asadabad.
No further details were provided on what caused the explosives to ignite.
Earlier, Kunar Provincial Police Headquarters spokesperson Farid Dehqan said the explosion occurred at around 10 a.m.
Unverified video footage posted on social media showed injured children being taken to the provincial hospital.

Samiulhaq Haqbayan, provincial director for information, told Germany's DPA news agency that the explosives were intended for use in mining operations and for clearing hazardous rocks from mountain slopes along the nearby Kunar-Nuristan highway.
Third blast near a school this week
The ministry said an investigation into the incident is ongoing and further details will be announced once it is completed.
Saturday's incident is the third explosion near educational facilities in Afghanistan in the past week.

Two separate blasts near religious schools in Kapisa and Farah provinces killed a total of five students, with local officials attributing both incidents to unexploded ordinances left behind from previous conflicts.

articles.title: EXPLAINER | Duterte at ICC: Inside the Prosecution's trial brief -- Who died, when, and where?
articles.summary: In the continuation of this Explainer series, GMA News Online examines the trial briefs of the different parties in the crimes against humanity case confronting former president Rodrigo Duterte…

blocks.text: SECOND OF A SERIES
Published November 28, 2026 6:10pm

THE HAGUE – In the continuation of this Explainer series, GMA News Online examines the trial briefs of the different parties in the crimes against humanity case confronting former president Rodrigo Duterte before the International Criminal Court (ICC). The second part of the series takes a closer look at the Prosecution's charges against Duterte, particularly the 56 charged incidents during the former president's drug war that will be scrutinized by the ICC judges.

The Office of the Prosecutor’s (OTP) updated trial brief presents 56 charged incidents to illustrate a “widespread and systematic attack” against civilians, tracing how the “Davao Model” of “neutralizing” alleged drug users became a nationwide policy after Duterte took office in June 2016.

Prosecutors allege that the Davao Model was implemented within “formal structures” in the Philippine National Police (PNP) and through appointing key people within Duterte’s circles to strategic leadership posts.

On July 1, 2016 – Duterte’s first day as president – senator and then-newly appointed PNP Chief Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa issued Command Memorandum Circular (CMC) 16-2016, formally launching “Project Double Barrel” nationwide. It established two operational tracks:

items: Project Tokhang: House-to-house visits driven by barangay and police station watchlists, requiring local units to conduct neighborhood clearance raids.
Project High-Value Target (HVT): Directed at upper-tier figures, manufacturers, and public officials listed on the “PRRD List.”

blocks.text: Prosecution witnesses, along with police records cited by lawyers, attempt to establish that operational directives calling for the “neutralization” of targets were widely understood within police ranks as orders to kill. An alleged covert cash reward system further incentivized lethal force, paying bounties for fatalities, which increased depending on the “level of target.”
Why 56 incidents?
The final roster of 56 charged incidents came after heated litigation among the Prosecution, the Defense, and the victims’ representatives in mid-2026.

items: April 23: Pre-Trial Chamber I confirms the charges against Duterte based on 49 representative incidents, noting that the “actual scale” of deaths was significantly greater during the charged period.
August 31: Nearly four months later, the Prosecution notifies the Defense of eight additional incidents, upping the total to 57 incidents supported by over 62,000 items of disclosed evidence.

August 31: On the same day, Duterte’s Defense counsel, Peter Haynes KC, immediately challenges the filings under Rule 134(1) and files a motion requesting a judicial determination. The Defense argues that adding new incidents without Pre-Trial Chamber authorization violates Duterte’s right to fair notice and forces them to face a “virtually unlimited” landscape of crimes.

October 9: Trial Chamber III decides that seven additional incidents – Incidents 50 to 56 – fall within the confirmed scope of the charges, but strikes out Incident 57 for exceeding Count 2’s temporal boundary.

October 16: Six days later, the Prosecution submits its Updated Trial Brief, officially reflecting the deletion of Incident 57 and locking the trial roster at 56 charged incidents across three counts: Count 1 (During Duterte’s mayorship in Davao City, 2013 – June 2016): Covers at least 19 murder victims executed by the Davao Death Squad (DDS) across nine incidents (Incidents 1-9) in Davao City, including three children. Count 2 (High-value targets killed during Duterte’s presidency, July 2016 – August 2017): Covers at least 16 murder victims killed across six incidents (Incidents 10-14 and Incident 56). High-profile killings include a Chinese known as “Mico Tan” (Incident 12), Albuera Mayor Rolando Espinosa, who was shot inside his jail cell in Leyte (Incident 13), and Ozamiz City Mayor Reynaldo Parojinog Sr., who was killed in a residence raid (Incident 14). Count 3 (Barangay tokhang sweeps during Duterte’s presidency, July 2016 – September 2018): Covers at least 52 victims (50 murders, 2 attempted murders) killed during local police station clearance operations across 41 incidents (Incidents 15-55). The heaviest concentrations were recorded in the National Capital Region (22 incidents, including 15 in the City of Manila) and Bulacan Province in Region 3 (18 incidents).

blocks.text: How did Trial Chamber III rule on the contested 56 incidents, and what impact did it have on victims?

On October 9, the ICC Trial Chamber III issued a ruling that resolved the core dispute over the scope of the charges: It confirmed Incidents 50-56, but struck out Incident 57 for exceeding Count 2’s temporal boundary (“between July 2016 and July 2017”). This decision clarified the Prosecution’s legal parameters, but immediately raised concerns among participating victim families.

October 29: The ICC Registry (through the Victims Participation and Reparations Section) reported that applying the Chamber’s tightened temporal cutoff threatens to exclude at least 16 previously authorized victims (across 13 applications out of 539) whose relatives were killed on dates just outside the strictly interpreted window for the counts. It asks the Chamber for urgent guidance on whether their participation status should be revoked.

November 12: The Common Legal Representatives of Victims (CLRV) forcefully oppose the Registry’s proposed exclusions, warning that stripping procedural status from families recognized months earlier causes “profound sadness and anxiety.” The CLRV argue that procedural decisions limiting Prosecution evidence must not artificially narrow victim participation rights, urging Trial Chamber III to affirm that indirect victims retain their right to participate even if specific incident dates fall outside tightened prosecutorial count windows.
As of November 27, Trial Chamber III has yet to release a decision on the CLRV request for clarification.
What else does the Prosecution’s trial brief show about Duterte’s drug war?
The Prosecution’s updated trial brief links presidential speeches directly to surges in fatal police operations.

On August 15–16, 2017, police conducted a simultaneous “One Time Big Time” (OTBT) raid across Bulacan, killing 32 people within 24 hours. Speaking on August 16, Duterte publicly praised the body count:
“They said that 32 died in Bulacan in a massive raid. That’s good. If we could kill another 32 every day, then maybe we can reduce what ails this country.”

On that same night, 17-year-old student Kian Loyd delos Santos was killed in Barangay 160, Caloocan City (Incident 30). While police claimed Delos Santos opened fire, security camera footage and eyewitnesses proved he was unarmed, dragged into an alley, and executed while kneeling.
How did accountability measures fare?
The deaths during anti-drug operations across the country between 2016 and 2019 prompted public outcry, but the Prosecution notes that internal accountability mechanisms failed.

It cites a 2025 congressional panel report stating that 99.17% of administrative complaints filed before the PNP Internal Affairs Service (IAS) resulted in the exoneration of PNP personnel involved, and that only 30 of 32,803 police officers charged during the Duterte administration were dismissed.
The evidence the Prosecution establishes in its brief forms the legal backbone of the charges now pending before ICC Trial Chamber III. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Buklod: Songs of an unfinished struggle
articles.summary: Forty years after the EDSA Revolution, the music of folk group Buklod remains a haunting reminder of a promise left unfulfilled — and a fight that is far from over

blocks.text: Forty years after the EDSA Revolution, the music of folk group Buklod remains a haunting reminder of a promise left unfulfilled — and a fight that is far from over

items: Post-EDSA protest musicians faced challenges in a society eager to celebrate democracy, yet they continued to perform and advocate for social issues.
The folk group Buklod, consisting of Noel Cabangon, Romeo Dongeto, and Rene Boncocan, emerged from a tradition of protest artists and gained recognition for their politically charged songs.
Despite the disbandment of Buklod, their music remains relevant, resonating with current social issues and serving as a reminder of the unfinished fight for justice and equality in the Philippines.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

To be an activist in the years immediately after the 1986 EDSA Revolution meant sailing against the optimistic tide that swept the nation following the ouster of the Marcos dictatorship. Democracy had been restored, Cory Aquino was president, and the mood was blazing yellow. Everyone, it seemed, wanted to move on and celebrate.

And to be a protest musician at a time when vacuous pop, delivered by singers and bands with gelled hair and shoulder pads, ruled the airwaves meant strumming an acoustic guitar in the middle of Euphoria: nobody could hear you, and those who did wished you weren’t there.
They played on anyway.

Protest musicians of the post-EDSA years did not come out of nowhere. They followed a tradition of protest artists from the ’70s and early ’80s whose songs were in the form and vernacular of folk and folk-rock: Jess Santiago, Paul Galang, Susan Fernandez, Pancho Lara, Gary Granada; folk groups like Pahayagan and Sinaglahi. Asin and Heber Bartolome’s Banyuhay carried it into the mainstream, proving that a song about the environment, or the daily struggles of working people could sell records.
The folk group Buklod was that period’s best-kept secret.

Noel Cabangon, Romeo Dongeto, and Rene Boncocan sang at political gatherings long before anyone thought of them as recording artists. Their first album, Bukid at Buhay, came out in 1988 as a trio; Boncocan left the following year, and Cabangon and Dongeto carried on as a duo in “Tatsulok” (1991) and “Sa Kandungan ng Kalikasan” (1992).

Buklod’s songs found a home in mainstream compilation albums such as Karapatang Pantao and Dear Cory, masterminded by maverick producer Ed Formoso, known for the psychedelic-folk group Dinosaur, a trio with Boy Camara and Jett Montelibano, and for birthing the supergroup Lokal Brown.
It wasn’t until “Kanlungan” was used in a burger commercial, and “Tatsulok” was covered by Bamboo many years later, that the secret was out.

“Kanlungan” became the song everyone requested from Cabangon, by then an established solo recording artist. It didn’t matter, of course, that a song about longing and the passing of time performed by activists became a jingle for an American fast food chain. Or that “Tatsulok,” an indictment of oppressive class structures, became a rock anthem for a generation largely spared from a policeman’s truncheon. By then, Buklod had long disbanded.

Buklod would jam occasionally, but there was never a full reunion or a new album. Not until 2018, 30 years after their first record, when the three went back to the studio for 3 Dekada: Ang Muling Pag-awit.

The comeback, the urge to make their voices, now older, heard again, was triggered by the brazen extra-judicial killings and rights violations under the then two-year old regime of now detained former president Rodrigo Duterte. Three decades on, the old songs still resonated and it was the trio’s way of joining the outrage.

A few nights ago, they reunited again, this time for a fund-raiser for ailing painter Federico “Boy” Dominguez, known in activist and art circles as BoyD. In the crowd were battle-hardened activists, finding comfort in familiar songs.

Forty years after EDSA, Buklod’s songs still carry the same weight as the day they were first sung. The promise of the EDSA Revolution has since soured: old and new elites, despots who use the rhetoric of democracy to undermine its values, disenchantment with its failure to lift people from chronic hunger and poverty, activists who dared to protest treated with the same iron fist as Marcos the father. And Marcos the son is back in Malacañang.

Buklod and the other post-EDSA protest artists were right all along: The revolution left too much undone. In the face of public indifference, they still said it and sang about it, even if it meant preaching to the converted, dodging bullets at rallies, raising families on a folk singer’s income, or enduring years of separation over ideological and political disagreements.

In the end, it is the songs that outlast the quarrels. Songs that bring old friends and comrades together and remind them, and the rest of us, that the fight they sang about was never finished. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Remulla dismisses rumors Romualdez set to post bail
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Saturday quashed rumors that former House speaker Martin Romualdez would be able to post bail soon in relation to the detained leader's P7.4-billion plunder case.

blocks.text: Published November 28, 2026 5:53pm
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Saturday quashed rumors that former House speaker Martin Romualdez would be able to post bail soon in relation to the detained leader's P7.4-billion plunder case.
Speaking on his radio program, Remulla said he was aware of such rumors circulating in legal and judicial circles.

"Ngayon, mayroong may matinding kumakalat, ito dididretsuhin ko na: baka raw makakuha ng piyansa 'yung isang suspek natin na nakakakulong ngayon, na malaki, the biggest, in other words that's Martin Romualdez. Pinapakalat nila 'yan. Propaganda. Parang gusto nilang kondisyunin na 'wag kayo magugulat kung makakuha ng [piyansa]. Pero kami we're vigorously opposing that," Remulla said.

(Now, there is something intense going around, I'll get straight to the point. There's talk that one of our incarcerated suspects, a big one, the biggest, in other words, that's Martin Romualdez, has a chance of posting bail. They are spreading that. Propaganda. They want to condition us to not be surprised if he is granted [bail]. But we're vigorously opposing that.)
Remulla said they will not be swayed by propaganda, saying it has been attempted before but the Ombudsman's strategy will not be ruined.
New witness

The Ombudsman said the Sandiganbayan has already allowed Samchan Foreign Exchange Corp. President Felicito Guevarra to be removed as a co-accused in Romualdez's case. The Sandiganbayan Third Division has approved the amended charge sheet dropping Guevarra, who surrendered to authorities earlier in November.

Guevarra was previously declared as an Ombudsman witness after he returned the money he allegedly processed for Romualdez. He supposedly got some P373 million, which is 1% for every transaction he processed.
This meant that he handled around P37 billion, according to Remulla.
Remulla alluded to people attempting to locate the witness, saying there was also a case where they attempted to impersonate Sandiganbayan Judge Karl Miranda, who was handling Romualdez's case.
"May nag-impersonation ng isang justice… Somebody was trying to impersonate Justice Karl Miranda and trying to get the whereabouts of our witness," Remulla said.
(Someone was impersonating a justice… Somebody was trying to impersonate Justice Karl Miranda and trying to get the whereabouts of our witness.)
Remulla even posited that former National Bureau of Investigation officials were being used to locate the witness.
GMA News has reached out to Romualdez's office and will update the story once they respond. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Will Sara Duterte finally attend her impeachment trial?
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte says she had repeatedly told her defense lawyer, Michael Poa, 'Allow me to lawyer for myself and stand there as a lawyer'

blocks.text: YEAREND PRESSCON. Vice President Sara Duterte answers questions from the media during the Office of the Vice President's thanksgiving event in Mandaluyong City on November 27, 2026.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
Vice President Sara Duterte says she had repeatedly told her defense lawyer, Michael Poa, 'Allow me to lawyer for myself and stand there as a lawyer'
Will Vice President Sara Duterte ever show up at her impeachment trial?
That question has persisted since Day 1 of the trial on July 6, amid mounting calls for the Vice President to appear in court and personally respond to the allegations against her.

Duterte has visited the Senate on at least two occasions outside her trial. The first was on July 7, when she met with her defense team and delivered a one-sentence statement to the media, “In this bloodbath and bludgeoning, I will be bloodied but unbowed.”
She left the Senate before the trial could resume.
On November 26, Duterte returned to the chamber while the trial was suspended to attend plenary deliberations on her office’s proposed P785.2 million budget for 2027.

She exchanged pleasantries with some of the senators serving as judges in her trial. But when the media asked questions, including whether she will attend her trial, she only responded with “Merry Christmas.”
Duterte’s defense team has repeatedly said her attendance would depend on how the trial unfolds, stressing that her physical appearance is not required because she is fully represented by counsel.
Duterte herself said in August that the participation of her lawyers was “sufficient” and tantamount to her attending the impeachment proceedings.

But in a rare, nearly hour-long press conference at the Office of the Vice President central office in Mandaluyong City on Friday, November 27, Duterte claimed that she had long wanted to attend her trial. It could be recalled that the Vice President herself had repeatedly questioned the impeachment proceeding itself, describing it as “political theater” in the guise of accountability.
On Friday, Duterte said that her defense lawyer and former spokesperson, Michael Poa, ignored her whenever she raised the possibility of her appearance at her trial.

“Ilang beses na ako nagsabi sa kanya: ‘Michael Poa, allow me to enter my appearance for myself. Allow me to lawyer for myself and stand there as a lawyer.’ Hindi niya talaga ako pinapansin at all. Somehow, nililihis niya ‘yung usapan,” Duterte said at her latest press conference.

(I’ve told him several times, “Michael Poa, allow me to enter my appearance for myself. Allow me to represent myself and stand there as a lawyer.” He really didn’t pay attention to me at all. Somehow, he keeps steering the conversation away from the subject.)
Poa, defense spokesperson, has yet to respond to requests for comment.

Asked whether she could still be presented as a witness at this point, with the defense nearing the end of its presentation, Duterte said she had yet to discuss the matter with her lawyers. “We are not there yet but sabi kasi nila tapos na sila this week e. So hindi pa namin napag-uusapan kung a-attend ako as witness o hindi,” Duterte said.
(We are not there yet but they said they will be done this week. So we have not discussed yet if I will attend as a witness or not.)

The defense team is set to present two witnesses when the trial resumes next week. Both are expected to testify in relation to Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company at the center of allegations of unexplained wealth against Duterte.

Will Duterte at least be present when the impeachment court hands down its decision? The court targets a ruling by December 18. The Vice President indicated that this event, which her political fate hinges on, is not a priority.
“If I’m in Davao, then no. Because we have a series of activities for Davao thanksgiving for December,” she said in response.

Duterte also said her office is “preparing for the worst” and that she would accept the court’s decision. However, she cautioned that removing an elected vice president would have “consequences,” pointing to possible negative public reaction.

blocks.caption: Will Sara Duterte finally attend her impeachment trial?

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the Vice President said she would not fly to The Hague for the trial of former president Rodrigo Duterte for a crimes against humanity case before the International Criminal Court beginning November 30. She said it would be a “waste of money” as visits to her father would not be allowed during the trial.

She shared that she owed friends at least P5 million which helped cover for her trip to The Hague last year, as well as legal expenses for her impeachment trial and her father’s case. She said she planned to sell properties to repay her debt.

Duterte is facing one remaining allegation in her impeachment case: unexplained wealth. The House prosecution panel dropped the three other articles of impeachment, which involved grave threats, misuse of confidential funds, and bribery. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Did that tip seem steep? The math might have included the tax
