blocks.text: Cost of Living

You've heard of "tipflation" and "tip creep." But what may not be clear when you're prompted to tip your barista, hairdresser or even your mechanic is that you're often tipping on the total — tax included.
Consumer advocates, researchers say consumers find it harder to ascertain how tips are calculated these days
LISTEN | Doing the math when you leave a tip:
Cost of Living3:57Why you should do the math why you leave a tip
You've heard of "tipflation" and "tip creep."
But what may not be clear when you're prompted to tip your barista, hairdresser or even your mechanic is that you could be tipping on the total — tax included.
Back when leaving a tip meant having to do some mental or back-of-the-napkin math, the custom was to look at the subtotal before taxes and calculate from there.
But with point-of-sale terminals spitting out numbers lickety-split, it's hard to get a handle on how tipping equations are being run.

"In effect, a consumer has to take out their calculator to check if it was calculated before or after the tip, so it gets more difficult," said Sara Eve Levac, a lawyer for the Quebec-based non-profit Option Consommateurs, a consumer watchdog.

Sara Eve Levac of the Quebec-based non-profit consumer watchdog Option Consommateurs says the organization held discussion groups about tipping with consumers across Canada, and the findings were that 'people felt like it wasn't clear' if they included tax. (Maude Desbois Photographie)
In response to consumer feedback about the issue, Levac said their organization tested some restaurants and found cases where the tip was indeed calculated after the taxes.

Bonnie Simpson, a professor of consumer behaviour at Western University in London, Ont., said that in many places where we're being asked to tip these days, we often don't get itemized receipts with a clear delineation between total and subtotal.
"We get a tiny screen and it does not show us a breakdown," said Simpson, who has researched consumer attitudes toward tipping.
Sure, most sit-down restaurants still hand you a paper breakdown of everything you ordered, said Simpson, but it's straight to the point-of-sale terminal in a lot of other tipping contexts.
Even when there is a receipt that delineates the total before and after tax, it's often not obvious which is used to calculate the tip.
Levac said Option Consommateurs held discussion groups about tipping with consumers across Canada, and the findings were that "people felt like it wasn't clear."
In Quebec, new rules brought in with Bill 72 last year mean it's now against the rules for any establishment to prompt customers to tip on the tax-in total.

items: Quebec has new rules on pricing and tip calculations. Here's a breakdown

blocks.text: The Quebec government's consumer protection office told CBC in an email it has received 988 complaints and issued 389 notices since these provisions came into effect on May 7, 2025, and that the majority were for restaurants, bars and other food-related services.
It's the only province with clear rules on how tips are presented on pay machines.
Quebec moves to clamp down on growing ‘tip inflation’ at restaurants

Industry association Restaurants Canada said in a statement to CBC that it advises restaurants to "ensure automated tip suggestions on payment terminals are calculated on the pre-tax amount and presented in a clear, neutral way to ensure customers feel confident in making the best choice that reflects their experience."
Is the tech to blame?
Levac said she's read media reports in which merchants said it's difficult to change their payment terminal to calculate the tip before taxes.

But when the research team at Option Consommateurs looked at 12 common payment systems, Levac said they found it was "actually pretty easy for someone with minimal technical knowledge to be able to change the settings."

items: Tip-flation has some restaurants asking for up to 30% in tips

blocks.text: Moneris and Square are among the most used payment processors in Canada. They rent and sell the payment machines that are used by a lot of Canadian businesses.
In emails to CBC, both said their machines can be customized and it's up to businesses to decide how their tips are calculated and whether to include the tax or not.
Time for a new model?
In Edmonton, Sarah Burns said she feels privileged to be able to go out for coffees and the occasional dinner given the high cost of just about everything these days.
"But I do not like tipping on GST on my bill," she told Cost of Living.
"I would really prefer a European model where I believe servers are paid a living wage."

Western University Prof. Bonnie Simpson says tipping is a social contract we engage in as consumers and that it would take a lot of consumer pressure — and eventually legislation — to arrive at a new system. (Submitted by Bonnie Simpson)

Western University's Bonnie Simpson said tipping is a social contract we engage in as consumers and that it would take a lot of consumer pressure — and eventually legislation — to arrive at a new system.

"Somebody would need to study and propose an alternative that still allowed the hospitality industry success and still allowed the people working in it to make great wages. But it would be a huge change."
Produced by Danielle Nerman

articles.title: Would you use LinkedIn to find love?
articles.summary: LinkedIn is primarily used for professional networking and career development, but some people have discovered that it might also be a useful dating app.

image.caption: Some users on LinkedIn say they use the site to vet potential dates and even to meet romantic partners. (Dado Ruvic/Reuters)

blocks.text: Business·New
LinkedIn is primarily used for professional networking and career development, but some people have discovered that it might also be a useful dating app.
Survey says 1 in 8 have used it to meet a romantic partner
Savannah Giedroyc and Robert DeMichele had mutual friends when they started dating, but their love story didn't begin the way you'd expect.
Instead of approaching DeMichele through their social circle, the Toronto-based accountant decided to take matters into her own hands — and shoot her shot on LinkedIn.

"I decided to send him an invite and then he accepted. It's so cheesy, because he ended up viewing my profile," said Giedroyc. "So then I viewed his back so that he would get the alert that, like, I was also looking at his profile. Then about a month later, he actually messaged me back on Instagram, because we were mutual."
"He says if I didn't add him [on LinkedIn] and I didn't … clue into his profile, he would have never put two and two together."
Savannah Giedroyc and Robert DeMichele on their wedding day in Toronto in August 2026. (Submitted by Savannah Giedroyc)

LinkedIn is primarily used for professional networking and career development, and allows people in the job market to post their resumés and browse listings and gives employers an opportunity to potentially find hires. Many people also publish their thoughts on business trends on the site, although users have noticed an increased number of AI-generated posts.
Recently, it’s made headlines for misleading job postings that funnelled applicants to a multi-level marketing company that asked for money.
But amid a sea of job postings (both real and fake) and AI slop, could LinkedIn actually be an underrated dating app?
Could you find your soulmate on LinkedIn?
A way to find, research potential partners

A poll by Zety — a professional development site that provides resumé and cover letter building services — surveyed more than 1,000 U.S. employees and found one in eight people said they formed a romantic relationship that started on LinkedIn. Twenty-two per cent said they reached out to, or responded to, someone on LinkedIn with romantic intent.
Some say the app also shines in another way: one in five respondents admitted to using LinkedIn to research a potential romantic partner.
"You see, like, where they went to school, their job — it kind of answers some questions. If you have certain boxes that you want to tick, it's all listed there for you," said Giedroyc.

"I would be lying if I said I haven't done it," said Emily Durham, a Toronto-based recruiter and content creator. "Dating is such a personal experience. I've always just been interested to see what [potential partners are] interested in."

More people are moving away from traditional dating apps such as Tinder, Bumble and Hinge. The Harris Poll, a global market research firm, surveyed 2,177 Americans and found 56 per cent of respondents agree the app meetups are "cringe" and 72 per cent said these apps have made dating feel more "transactional" than "romantic."
Almost half of those surveyed said they find information on LinkedIn to be more trustworthy than on traditional dating apps. (Mauro Pimentel/AFP/Getty Images)
Meanwhile, 48 per cent of respondents to the Zety survey find information on LinkedIn to be more trustworthy compared to actual dating apps.
Advances must 'feel safe'
Durham cautions that these types of advances must be reciprocal, with respect and consent at the centre of it all.

"For many women, when we show up online to advance our careers, what we also get is an onslaught of romantic advancement and sexual harassment," said Durham. "I think it's really about understanding how to make [those approaches] happen in a way that they'll feel safe … in a situation where there is reciprocity and it's mutual."
Not everyone is up for LinkedIn becoming more personal. Sixty five per cent of respondents to the Zety survey said they believe using the site for dating could harm their reputation.
But proponents say LinkedIn could help you judge whether a potential love interest is a go-getter.
"I think career and ambition says a lot about someone," said Giedroyc. "It’s one of the most important factors of someone's life — you know, what they do in the day-to-day."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sidra Al Jammal is a producer at CBC News Network, based in Toronto. You can reach her at sidra.al.jammal@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Melania Trump says she helped another group of children return to Ukraine. The reality is more complicated
articles.summary: Nine children and a 29-year-old woman with disabilites returned to Ukraine on Friday via Belarus, part of a reunification mission to unite families separated by Russia's war with Ukraine.

image.caption: Alina Sydorenko sees her son, Artem, 8, for the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. He arrived in Ukraine with eight other children from Belarus on Friday. (Briar Stewart/CBC)

blocks.text: When Alina Sydorenko woke up last week and discovered that drones and missiles had dealt a devastating blow to Russia's prized Kerch Bridge — causing a central section to collapse — it was the first time she felt annoyed by a Ukrainian win in the war against Russia.

Her mother was planning to cross the bridge from occupied Crimea into Russia to escort Sydorenko's eight-year-old son, Artem, out of their home in the southeastern port city of Berdyansk, which Russian troops seized during the early days of the war against Ukraine.
Sydorenko was in northern Ukraine when the full-scale invasion began in February 2022 and said she was separated from her only child for years.

items: There can be no peace with Russia until Ukrainian children come home, says advocate

blocks.text: While Ukraine says it has confirmed more than 20,000 cases of children being deported or forcibly transferred to Russia, thousands of others remain separated by the war — either trapped in occupied territory or in Russia because the relatives they were with at the start of the invasion fled there.
"The negotiations took a very long time," Sydorenko said in an interview with CBC News on Friday at a Ukrainian checkpoint a few kilometres from the border with Belarus.
"I can't even say how much stress and effort we went through to bring the child back here. It's terrifying to worry every single day about whether they are alive."

Artem and his grandmother ended up waiting a few days before taking a train to Russia. From there, they joined a larger group and travelled through Belarus as part of a humanitarian reunification mission secured in part with the help of U.S. first lady Melania Trump.

Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who met with Melania in Washington, D.C. after she was credited with securing a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied community of Oleshky, even went so far as to say she is now their chief mediator when it comes to the return of children.
Families separated by war reunite at Ukraine-Belarus border
Politics, public pressure play role in return

Before starting the long journey to reunite with their children, families face a mountain of paperwork and permissions. However, politics and public pressure are also factoring into how and when some of those who have been separated or forcibly deported to Russia are brought back to Ukraine.
The group that arrived on Friday included nine children and 29-year-old Anastasia (Nastia) Mamotiuk, who lives with a disability and has been in institutional group care since she was a young child.

items: 'We need strong support': Ukraine fighting to bring children back from Russia

blocks.text: She was one of more than 80 children and vulnerable young adults taken to Russia from the Oleshky Children’s Boarding School in southern Ukraine in the fall of 2022.

In recent months, the Emile Foundation, a humanitarian organization with offices in the Netherlands and Ukraine, has been able to track down more than 40 of the school's former residents. Bringing them back to Ukraine has been challenging due to medical needs, legal hurdles and the difficulty of locating individuals in the first place — especially as some have been shuffled between different care facilities.
Anastasia (Nastia) Mamotiuk, 29, arrives by ambulance at the Ukraine-Belarus border checkpoint on Friday. She had been placed at a facility in Russia. (Nicolas Hameon/CBC)
The foundation made contact with Mamotiuk in the spring and kept in touch on WhatsApp through messages and video calls.

"We were in touch with her all the time," said Mariam Lambert, co-founder and CEO of the Emile Foundation, who spoke to CBC News via Zoom. "There were good moments, there were really bad moments, there were moments where she was scared."

items: Ukrainian children abducted by Russia appeal for help from Canadian MPs

blocks.text: Mamotiuk was placed in a facility in Penza, Russia, a city about 500 kilometres southeast of Moscow. The home was managed by Sofia Lvova-Belova, the sister of Russia's children's commissioner, Maria Lvova-Belova, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court and accused of unlawfully deporting Ukrainian children to Russia.
Lambert said it was during their regular communication with Mamotiuk in May that she began expressing concern about being given more medication than she typically took.
A boy looks out from a bus transporting children from Belarus back to Ukraine on Friday. The children have been living away from home because of war with Russia. (Briar Stewart/CBC)

Then in the fall, she suddenly stopped communicating with those in Ukraine for several days. That prompted Lambert to go public with Mamotiuk’s case, speaking to the media and appealing to Melania Trump to intervene.
"We understand the political side of it, and this is why we made an appeal," Lambert said. "We were asking, of course, the international community to put pressure on Russia in order to return her."

items: Melania Trump hosted officials from Russia and Ukraine. Just what's behind her peace push?

blocks.text: A few days later, Mamotiuk was back in touch and was told arrangements were being made to get her a passport so she could travel.
CBC News reached out to the office of Russia’s children’s commissioner but has not received a response.
'Is it becoming a political game?'

While Lambert praised the International Committee of the Red Cross for helping arrange Mamotiuk's travel, she was dismayed by how much of her return to Ukraine unfolded. She said they first heard about the reunification from Melania, who posted about it on social media on Nov. 25.
In a press release, the White House stated that the latest agreement meant 43 children had now been "reunited through her humanitarian efforts."

The statement made it seem as though the children were already back with relatives, when in reality they were still in transit and had not yet reached Belarus — which they needed to pass through in order to cross into northern Ukraine.

Olha, right, who didn't want her last name published because of the high profile and sensitivity of the humanitarian mission in the midst of war, reunited with her nephew, Sasha. He had been living in occupied Kherson with his mother. When she died four months ago, he asked if he could leave and relocate to Kyiv to live with his aunt. (Briar Stewart/CBC)
After the announcement, the first lady reposted U.S. coverage of the reunification interspersed with posts promoting a new docuseries about her that's streaming on Amazon Prime.
Lambert only found out that Mamotiuk was arriving on Friday when the young woman got in touch herself.
"Is it really a humanitarian action, or is it becoming a political game?" she said.
Alevtyna Abibulaieva, left, kisses her niece, Valeriia Levchenko, 11, who crossed the border into Ukraine from Belarus by bus on Friday. (Evgeniy Maloletka/The Associated Press)
Bus arrives to waiting family, officials, media
Because they are not directly related, no one from the Emile Foundation was invited to the border checkpoint to welcome Mamotiuk — and neither was her closest contact, Viacheslav Shchyrskyi.

The 61-year-old had been in touch with Mamotiuk for more than a decade. He previously ran a small group home in Ukraine's Kherson region and was making arrangements to take her in before the war. But all of the legal paperwork was shelved after Russia's full-scale invasion began.

items: Russia is accused of deporting thousands of Ukrainian children. 17 returned home this week

blocks.text: Shchyrskyi told CBC News that he spoke to Mamotiuk at the border as she was leaving Belarus.

"Finally, she's got what she wanted. She's been brought to Ukraine, but she's confused," he said in a phone interview with CBC News from Romania, where he currently lives. "Even though she's 29 years old, deep down she's still a child — a little girl who has been moved from one place to another, and then moved again."
The Emile Foundation's Maria Lebedieva, seen on a cellphone screen, speaks with Mamotiuk near the border checkpoint between Ukraine and Belarus on Friday. (Briar Stewart/CBC)

As the bus carrying the children arrived at the checkpoint on Friday afternoon, relatives, Ukrainian officials and a crush of cameras rushed toward the opening doors. Off to the side, an ambulance pulled up carrying Mamotiuk.
When CBC News entered the vehicle to greet her, she lay on a stretcher staring at the ceiling. She appeared quiet and unsure.

items: 'They wanted children': Ukrainian doctors say they lied to keep kids safe from Russian troops

blocks.text: When we asked if she wanted to say hello to Maria Lebedieva, director of the Emile Foundation's Ukraine branch, who was waiting on the other side of the secured checkpoint, Mamotiuk's mood lifted.
Seeing a friendly face on a video call, a smile spread across her face. She said she hoped to see Lebedieva soon and wanted to know when she could see Shchyrskyi.
Sydorenko tightly hugs her son Artem after being reunited at a checkpoint about five kilometres from the Ukraine-Belarus border on Friday. (Briar Stewart/CBC)
Outside of the ambulance, some children got back on the bus with their relatives, while others, like Artem, got into vehicles to make the onward journey.
"I am even happier than I thought I would be," Sydorenko said as she prepared to leave with her son and head back to Kyiv.
As for Mamotiuk, a Ukrainian flag was placed over her legs like a blanket just before the ambulance carrying her pulled away toward a medical facility south of the capital.
9 children returned to Ukraine in Melania Trump-brokered deal with Russia

articles.title: They gave birth in the south. Now, they're helping Inuit deliver closer to home
articles.summary: Margaret Tukkiapik and Kayla Annanack-Lauzon study through the Puvirnituq Inuulitsivik Health Centre's midwifery program to provide prenatal, labour and post-natal care for Inuit who would otherwise…

image.caption: Midwife trainee Kayla Annanack-Lauzon, left, and Margaret Tukkiapik, right, study through the Puvirnituq Inuulitsivik Health Centre's midwifery program to provide prenatal, labour and post-natal care for Inuit who would otherwise travel outside of their region, culture and language. (Josianne Letour

blocks.text: Margaret Tukkiapik's hands are peppered with some of the accomplishments of her work.
Small circular tattoos line each one of her fingers — representing every umbilical cord she's cut in her time assisting labouring mothers.
"I'm missing a few dots," said Tukkiapik, holding up her hands proudly.
The midwife at the Ungava Tulattavik Health Centre's maternity ward, who has attended 95 births, jokes that the stick-and-poke tattoos can be quite painful.

In Inuit traditions, cutting the cord of a baby is an honour and a responsibility — marking the start of a special relationship with the child, who is referred to as the cord-cutter's arnaliaq, if the baby is a girl, or angusiaq, for a boy.
Tukkiapik has 10 of each.

Margaret Tukkiapik was a self-taught doula before starting to study as a midwife five years ago. She gets a marking on her fingers every time she cuts a baby's umbilical cord. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)
"As they're cutting the cord, they will install values in the child," she said.
As they grow, the children present their accomplishments — their first sewing project, fish or caribou — back to the person who cut their cord, says Tukkiapik.
Tukkiapik's arnaliaqs and angusiaqs are part of what pushed her into midwifery in her home community of Kuujjuaq, Que.

items: 746 births over 36 years: Inuk midwife long served her remote community

blocks.text: She was a self-taught doula for years before she started studying through Puvirnituq's Inuulitsivik Health Centre midwifery program — now celebrating its 40th year in operation.
This month, Tukkiapik passed her exam after training for five years.

She joins the ranks of other Inuit midwives who have stepped up to provide safe options for pregnant Inuit who would otherwise have to fly south to deliver outside of their region, culture and language.
Inside the northern maternity unit helping pregnant Inuit deliver close to home
A 'night and day' difference
For Kayla Annanack-Lauzon, a midwife in training, this mission is personal.

She's edging closer to her due date with her second baby, and plans to deliver in Kuujjuaq. But she can't help but compare this pregnancy to her first — when she had most of her prenatal follow-ups and delivery in Montreal.
"There's really been a difference, like between night and day," she said.
"I'm able to be served in my language at home and not going into … a big crazy hospital that I'm not familiar with."
Kayla Annanack-Lauzon, left, will deliver her second child in December, in the same maternity ward where she currently works as a midwife. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)

After studying nursing, Annanack-Lauzon began training with the Inuulitsivik midwifery program in May, and has attended four births. She says patients "always have something good to say about their experience when they compare it to the South."
But up north, there's no continuous monitoring, epidural or inductions, notes Tukkiapik. In cases of emergency, the doctors on staff in the hospital step in and transfer the patient to trauma rooms.
Some women have to be sent out of the community if it's medically necessary.
It's what happened to Tukkiapik during her first pregnancy.
Margaret Tukkiapik hopes each of the six other communities on the Ungava coast can have their own midwifery services. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)
"I did not like that at all," she said.
"It's not how I was treated. It was just being away from home for so long, and then not knowing what to expect."
When she became pregnant with her daughter, in 2013, she said she took better care of herself — adamant that she wanted to stay home to deliver.
Doing things differently
Tukkiapik gave birth just down the hall from the current maternity ward, years before the unit created its own wing in the hospital.

Her daughter's birth was the first month Marilyn Mesher was on shift as a student, says Tukkiapik. Mesher later became the first Inuk from the Ungava coast to graduate from a midwifery program. She's now Tukkiapik's colleague.
"We're very proud," said Elena Mesher, Marilyn's sister.
Elena sat in a patient room in the maternity centre, holding her two-year-old son, Vincent — who was born at home, thanks to the help of the midwifery team, who also do house calls.
Elena Mesher delivered her son, Vincent, at home with the help of the midwives working in Kuujjuaq. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)
"It's very important to have local midwives there with you because they understand what's going on," she said. "You can speak to them in your own language."
That's a sticking point for Tukkiapik.

Walking down the maternity ward's hallway, lined with parenting and newborn pamphlets, she pointed into some of the birthing rooms — whose doors have a notice posted on the outside: "Thank you for speaking Inuktitut or English in this room."

items: Changing childbirth in Nunavut: Arviat Cultural Safety Project plots a new path for midwifery in the territory

blocks.text: "Everyone's most comfortable in their first language," she said.
"If they don't understand, they will not ask you … But when you talk to them in their own language, they understand more and [are] able to ask for better care."
When appointments are done in Inuktitut, she says patients also have a better understanding of the level of care they should be receiving.
Piles of pamphlets are available at the maternity clinic, which is connected to Kuujjuaq's hospital centre. (Rachel Watts/CBC)
It's part of why both Tukkiapik and Annanack-Lauzon want to see their small ward expand.
Kuujjuaq's maternity centre began developing in the '80s. Decades later, they're still doing things differently.
In one of its two delivery rooms is a double bed — much bigger than a standard hospital bed, and made for women who want family members or partners close to them while they labour.
"We don't ask them to just be laying on their back as they're delivering. They can deliver in whatever position they're comfortable," said Tukkiapik.
Just to the right of the room is the centre's bulletin board, lined with babies' footprints, names and birth details — posted as a reminder of every child born in the ward in the calendar year.
"When it's a new year, we'll put them in a binder and start our new footprint collection," she said.
Talks of expansion

For over 40 years, the fertility rate in Nunavik has remained nearly twice as high as the Quebec average, according to a 2021 health profile of the region by the Nunavik Board of Health and Social Services.

In Kuujjuaq's maternity centre, deliveries over the past 10 to 15 years have also increased, and now the centre — consisting of the two birthing rooms and a few consultation rooms on the hospital's first floor — sees an average of 100 births every year, says Larry Watt, the executive director of the health centre.
"Our space … is very limited," said Watt.
Larry Watt, the executive director of the Ungava Tulattavik Health Centre, says there are plans to expand the midwifery building. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)

But he says there's a plan to get a bigger facility in the next few years to offer more services, in part because the ward also takes on births, prenatal and postpartum care from neighbouring villages along the Ungava Coast.
Just next door to the maternity wing is the Maison de Transit, a temporary housing facility for the patients and family members from isolated communities who are flown in for care.
But for Tukkiapik, she dreams of a time when each of the 6 other communities on the Ungava coast have their own midwifery services.
"'Cause it makes a big difference," she said. "Each community must fight to have their own."
Annanack-Lauzon agreed, encouraging more Inuit to join.
"That's what we want," she said, cradling her baby bump. "It's really, really, awesome that we get to have this care."

articles.title: Legal wording once intimidated me. Now, it's becoming a language I can explain
articles.summary: Adu Asare remembers what it felt like to sign a legal document without fully understanding what it meant. Now he's studying to be a paralegal, hoping to help those in his Ghanaian community make…

image.caption: Adu Asare is a paralegal court and tribunal agent student at Centennial College in the Greater Toronto Area. (Submitted by Adu Asare)

blocks.text: Canada·First Person

Adu Asare remembers what it felt like to sign a legal document without fully understanding what it meant. Now he's studying to be a paralegal, hoping to help those in his Ghanaian community make sense of legal and government documents.
As I study to be a paralegal, I’m gaining knowledge and confidence to help others navigate the law
This First Person article is the experience of Adu Asare, who lives in Scarborough, Ont. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.
Two years after I arrived in Canada, I found myself holding a piece of paper containing legal jargon I did not understand.
Of course, I had questions. But I felt uncomfortable asking them.
So after the lawyer meant to help me with my Workplace Safety and Insurance Board Benefits asked me, I signed the document — without fully knowing its financial implications.
The document mentioned a contingency fee, which dictated my lawyer would retain a percentage of any settlement.

Now, I’m a paralegal student; at school, I’ve learned about contingency fees and the rest of what I was being asked to sign. But the experience in May 2023 taught me something else: that I want to help others make sense of the law.
A struggle for answers
My challenges with legal language began in my home country of Ghana.

Asare grew up in Ghana and immigrated to Canada in 2021. He had to navigate the legal paperwork of an asylum claim, seeking protection from threats, discrimination and the risk of harm if he returned to his home country. (Submitted by Adu Asare)

There, in 2019, I hired a lawyer to help with my divorce. I asked them questions, such as: What documents do I need to file? What are the legal grounds for divorce? How long will the process take? What are my rights and financial responsibilities?
The answers were often very technical, and I struggled to understand the practical implications and what I needed to do.

I faced that same sense of uncertainty when I immigrated to Canada in 2021 and had to navigate the legal paperwork of an asylum claim. I sought protection from threats to my safety, discrimination and the risk of harm if I returned to my home country.
I relied on an immigration consultant for help with my documents who, at times, did not offer the clarity I needed. That confusion made the process even more overwhelming.
How these experiences shaped me

These instances showed me that having access to a legal professional does not mean that a client feels comfortable asking questions or can make decisions with confidence — and that it can be even harder to know your legal rights when, like with my workplace accident, you are already going through a difficult time. I decided to learn about the law so that I can help others navigate legal challenges and make legal information easier to understand.

In January 2025, I enrolled in Centennial College’s Paralegal Court and Tribunal Agent program in Toronto. Learning the terminology did not change what happened in 2023, but it helped give me the confidence to ask questions.
It’s where I began to see that knowing legal terminology and explaining it clearly are two different skills. Plain language can help close that gap.
Asare is shown here in class at Centennial College. (Submitted by Adu Asare)

I put what I am learning into practice in my Ghanaian community. On one occasion, I helped someone understand an Ontario Works letter explaining that their assistance had stopped after they failed to tell their caseworker they had started a job. I have also helped people understand lawyers’ retainer agreements, sometimes explaining information in Twi, a dialect of our Akan language spoken in Ghana.

These conversations have shown me how everyday language can be used to help someone understand what a document says, and I always let them know that they can ask me any questions. Right now, I see my role as helping people understand the paperwork in front of them and to help them recognize when they need further assistance. (I am a student, not a licensed paralegal, and I know that explaining information in plain language is not a substitute for qualified legal advice.)
And I hope that by writing about legal issues, like in this essay, I can make the law and legal documents more accessible.

I am still learning how to communicate legal information accurately and responsibly. What I do know is that making the law easier to understand does not mean promising outcomes or pretending every issue has a simple answer. When I think about the person who signed that agreement in 2023, I do not see someone who lacked intelligence, I see someone trying to navigate an unfamiliar process without feeling equipped to ask the right questions.
Asare wants people to know they do not have to pretend to understand a document simply because they are afraid to ask questions. (Submitted by Adu Asare)

Looking back, I wish I had asked how the lawyer's fees would be calculated, what percentage would be deducted from any settlement and what services the agreement covered. I also wish I had asked whether the agreement could be explained to me in plain language before I signed it
I cannot change what I did not understand then. But I can use what I am learning now to help make the next person’s experience less confusing.

I want people to know they do not have to pretend to understand a document simply because they are afraid to ask. Sometimes, the first step toward making an informed decision is being able to say, “Can you explain that to me?” — and waiting for the thoughtful answer you deserve.
Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to us.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Adu Asare is a paralegal court and tribunal agent student at Centennial College. His interests include legal research and public legal education, with a focus on making legal information easier to understand and advancing access to justice.

articles.title: X Files creator Chris Carter on Mulder-Scully reunion rumours, a Millennium reboot — and his new movie
articles.summary: Chris Carter spoke to CBC News about the future, and the past, of The X Files and his new, self-financed feature film.

image.caption: TV producer and director Chris Carter is seen at the ACE Eddie Awards in Beverly Hills, Calif., on Jan. 29, 2016. (Emma McIntyre/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Chris Carter has a complicated relationship with nostalgia.

Not that looking back has been a bad strategy for the American director, who is currently shopping around a new film, Queens for a Day. Given that he's the creator and showrunner of the incredibly successful and now resurgent sci-fi series The X Files, people’s tendency to look back has mostly worked out for him. Even if it keeps him coming back to something he finished nearly 30 years ago.

"It's funny, I'm a nostalgic person by nature. I look back at time past and while I can't avoid recognizing the bad things, the good things are always what stand out," said Carter, who shared that he's actually considering making a documentary about nostalgia, rooted in his up-and-down life and experiences.
"Really, if I were to visit the places that were formative for me and meant something to me, I'm gonna have to acknowledge the good with the bad."

Lately, it seems mostly good. There’s the upcoming Ryan Coogler reboot of The X Files with two new stars, which Disney subsidiary Hulu picked up for a series order in October. For an added boost of nostalgia, Coogler credited Carter as executive producer — despite the fact he's not creatively involved.

From left, actor Gillian Anderson, director Chris Carter, producer Frank Spotnitz and actor David Duchovny attend the world premiere of The X Files: I Want To Believe in Hollywood on July 23, 2008. (Stephen Shugerman/Getty Images)
Meanwhile, the Sinners director went to the wistful lengths of filming the show's pilot in dreary, moody Vancouver, returning the series to the place where Carter created it.

But according to Hans Dayal, production manager caucus representative for the Directors Guild of Canada's BC branch, the rest of the series will be filmed in Chicago in the spring. Star Himesh Patel said Coogler was still writing the show as of mid-November, while representatives for Disney did not respond to a query by CBC.

"I don't know about that decision," Carter said about the reboot's potential move away from Vancouver, before revealing he hasn't so much as read the scripts. "I decided not to read it, because I didn't want to have the experience spoiled: of sitting down with ... a bowl of popcorn and watching it like everyone else."

What's behind the sustained popularity of the original show? Carter doesn't deny that younger audiences' appetite could be fuelled by X Files' themes around questioning authority — and, more literally, the government.

Looking back at the original production, he describes himself as "a child of Watergate." He believed, and believes, there were conspiracies born of it. And from that belief, he says, grew everything from The X Files to Queens for a Day, which he calls a "fist in the air in protest for what's going on in the U.S. right now."

items: The X-Files began filming in Vancouver 30 years ago. It became a cultural touchstone and local point of pride

blocks.text: He says the refocused attention on The X Files stems from other factors, too. There is the obvious appeal of David Duchovny's Mulder and Gillian Anderson's Scully, Carter's "ideal of a man-woman relationship" based in platonic love but without fear of disagreeing with or doubting one another.
"It was an ideal that I chose to write about and has lasted through the decades now," he said. "If it weren't for that relationship, we could really be just another sci-fi show."
Dealing with fan yearning

Fans can't seem to shed their nostalgia for that pair, either. After months of speculation, Anderson suggested she had read Coogler's pilot script before it was shot and Duchovny revealed he had spoken to Coogler about the possibility of appearing in it.

Carter has also felt the fan yearning. Earlier this month, he said in an interview that his own 2016 X Files revival set up the potential for a show or movie bringing Mulder and Scully back together. And when he made a passing comment that he would like to make something like that one day, a raft of headlines followed, hinting it might happen.

He throws cold water on the seriousness with which some have taken the remark. Duchovny and Anderson have gone off to other things and there’s no current studio involvement. And the Coogler reboot has already headed into production.

"I don't want to compete with it. I don't want to overshadow it in any way," Carter said. "Even the fact that I'm talking to you about it now is a little troubling to me, because I want that show to come out and shine."
Duchovny, left, and Anderson appear as Mulder and Scully in an image from the original X Files series. (Fox/Getty Images)
The project he's more invested in revisiting is Millennium, his dark crime-horror series, which was filmed on the same Vancouver soundstages as The X Files, and ran from 1996 to 1999.
"It ended too soon. I actually chose to pull the plug too soon on the show. The show had lots more life in it," he said.

Carter says it was his ill-advised focus on launching the one-and-done series Harsh Realm that convinced the network, Fox, to cancel Millennium. And now, like everyone else, he's banking on the past for his future — working on a reboot pilot that he would also aim to shoot in Vancouver.
New film
And then there's Queens for a Day, which will show at the Whistler Film Festival in December and is currently hitting a smattering of individual theatres elsewhere.

It's a serious departure for the longtime studio-based TV producer. First, he made the entirely self-financed film from an unproduced 30-year-old script written by his wife, author and screenwriter Dori Carter, loosely based on her relationship with her mother.

Second is the genre. He describes it as a politically charged, nightmare reinterpretation of Dickens's A Christmas Carol. A right-wing newscaster who's forced to live through her mother's youth — including giving birth to herself — quickly realizes that her rose-coloured view of America's past doesn't necessarily square with reality.
A still from Chris Carter's new film, Queens for a Day. (Chris Carter)
On paper, the personal touches are still there, such as the dark hints at the supernatural. Carter insists on calling the film a "comedy nightmare" or "horror fable" rather than true horror.
"Horror scares people; there are people who won't go to see a horror movie."
There was also a return to the same Vancouver sound stages for filming.
"I brought this to Canada without hesitation," he said, pointing to Alberta director of photography Craig Wrobleski as the only crew member not from B.C.

items: The X-Files as a TV game changer
X-Files actor, Canadian Peter Donat, dead at 90

blocks.text: But there is also change. There is the comedy at the heart of Queens for a Day. There is the unabashed political celebration, as Carter describes it, which is serendipitously in line with the recent "blue wave" in the U.S. midterms. So in line, and in protest of the recent political climate, that he says it would have been impossible for an American studio to make the film.

It's all a mix of forward and backward in his description. Forward in how he views nostalgia, a "glossy look at the past" that is "always dangerous." It makes him want to try new things like Queens for a Day. After finishing The X Files, genre television or movies were the last things he wanted to do.
But there are more mundane realities, too. Such as being constantly asked about a show he created nearly 40 years ago, while promoting his new film.
Surprisingly, it has never bothered him.

"I'm not hindered by it. [The X Files] certainly provides a knock, and an opening, and a door and a greeting. But that's about all it is for," he said. "It's part of my portfolio, if you will. I still have to produce the goods."

articles.title: Victorian election 2026: Coalition projected to win state poll, ending 12 years of Labor government
articles.summary: Opposition leader Jess Wilson set to become premier as ABC calls election for Liberal and National parties

blocks.text: The ABC has projected the Coalition will win the Victorian election, ending Labor’s 12 year run of government in the state.
The national broadcaster’s election and data analyst, Casey Briggs, called the election for the Liberal and National partners at 7.40pm on Saturday evening. .
While it is unclear whether the party will govern in minority or majority, Briggs said there was no pathway for Labor to win a fourth term.

It means the Liberal leader, Jess Wilson, will become premier. At 36, she will be Victoria’s youngest leader since federation and the first woman to be popularly elected as the state’s premier – a feat neither Jacinta Allan nor Joan Kirner achieved.
The deputy Labor leader, Gabrielle Williams, said she was “deeply saddened” by the result but there was a responsibility for the party to learn from it.
“Clearly we have to be deeply humbled by the results and take the lessons from them,” Williams said.

“We need clearly to take the lessons from the result tonight. But I would go further and say we actually need to go back and have a look at the lessons from 2022 and where those warnings really began to emerge.”
The Labor leader, Ben Carroll, is also facing a swing away from him in seat of Niddrie, in Melbourne’s northwest, which the party has held for its entire 50-year history.

articles.title: Lacson urges Marcos: 'Referee' Senate, House during bicam for 2027 budget
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo "Ping" Lacson on Saturday urged President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. to mediate between the House of Representatives and the Senate as the 2027 budget process reaches the…

blocks.text: Published November 28, 2026 4:40pm

Senator Panfilo "Ping" Lacson on Saturday urged President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. to mediate between the House of Representatives and the Senate as the 2027 budget process reaches the bicameral conference.

Lacson's statement came hours after the Senate announced early morning Saturday that it had finished marathon deliberations for the proposed P7.2-billion national budget at 1:25 a.m. The House of Representatives' version of the budget bill, also amounting to P7.2 trillion, was passed back in October.

"Ako'y nananawagan sa kanya, makialam kayo dito. Langit at lupa ang diprensya, ang agwat ng House at Senate version. Marami siyang kaalyado sa Senate and House, siya ang pwede maging referee para mapatino ang 2027 budget," Lacson said in a radio interview.

(I am calling on the President to mediate. The difference between the House and Senate versions of the budget bill is like heaven and Earth. The President has allies in both Houses of Congress. He can act as referee to make sure the 2027 budget is clean.)

After the House of Representatives was flagged by budget watchdogs for allegedly making insertions into the 2027 budget, the Senate trimmed several items in its own version. Among the Senate's reductions is P97 billion from the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) due to noncompliance of several projects.
Lacson had flagged several questionable items in the budget, including alleged misplaced budget priorities such as P247 billion in "ayuda" or government aid.
The House's questionable allocations could make it appear that Marcos has lost control of the budget, Lacson said.
Lacson said priorities should not be realigned, especially with the current economic difficulties that the Philippines was facing.
Items such as the Financial Assistance to Local Government Units (FALGU), which have been previously tagged as presidential pork due to being a lump-sum, could be realigned to more pressing needs.
"Kaya malaki ang dapat na role ng Pangulo. Pagkasunduin muna at this point, hindi after, ang House and Senate at economic managers. Mag-usap-usap kami. We will talk," Lacson said.
(The President has a big role to play. He has to mediate and have economic managers meet with the Senate finance committee and House appropriations committee at this time, not after the bicam.)
GMA News has reached out to Malacañang regarding Lacson's call, but it has yet to respond as of posting time. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: What are AI chips, and what’s so special about Nvidia’s?
articles.summary: How Nvidia’s GPUs evolved from powering video games to becoming the backbone of the global AI race

blocks.text: The commotion around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and reinstatement, the central role of Nvidia in the U.S.-China AI competition, and the U.S. economy’s reliance on the AI boom might leave you asking: What’s so special about Nvidia’s chips?
The answer comes down to graphics processing units, or GPUs, and how far they’ve come from their humble beginnings as sidekicks to computers’ main chips: central processing units, or CPUs.
GPUs now power the most visible advances in generative artificial intelligence, but they began as modestly priced add-on cards for video games and video rendering.

As a researcher of high-performance computing and computer processors, I see three factors that explain how GPUs have become so important to the modern economy and how Nvidia became their dominant supplier: software that made GPUs useful beyond graphics, a research breakthrough that showed what they could do for AI, and a global commercial and political race to build ever-larger AI models.

The CPU is built to handle a wide variety of complicated tasks quickly, a few at a time. In contrast, a GPU typically operates on simpler mathematical tasks, such as multiplying two sets of numbers, but it can perform many of these simpler operations in parallel.

A GPU’s design turns out to be ideal for AI. Training a neural network, the kind of AI model behind today’s chatbots and image generators, comes down mostly to multiplying enormous grids of numbers, over and over. Today’s top AI GPUs can perform more than a quadrillion, or thousand trillion, of these operations every second.

Early GPUs could only draw graphics. Programmers controlled them with small programs called shaders, which calculate things such as the color of each pixel and which can be repeated across millions of pixels in parallel. Nvidia dominated the market for graphics chips in the late 1990s and 2000s.

In the early 2000s, Stanford University researchers built software tools that let programmers use this hardware for other kinds of calculations. That work provided the basis for Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, which was released in 2007. CUDA allowed scientists and engineers to run scientific and more general purpose programs using the GPU’s parallel execution model.

The second major shift occurred when AlexNet, a neural network model developed and trained on GPUs, won the 2012 ImageNet challenge, an annual competition to see which software could most accurately identify objects in a set of photographs. AlexNet was trained on two Nvidia GPUs, and it made far fewer mistakes than any competitor. The result showed that GPUs made it practical to train neural networks big enough to beat the older techniques, and AI researchers quickly adopted them for their work.

Because Nvidia had spent years building CUDA and the software around it, it was positioned to benefit more than anyone. Competitors, including AMD, which also makes GPUs, and Google, which designs its own AI chips, called tensor processing units, have since built strong alternatives.

Nvidia and other chipmakers then began redesigning GPUs for AI with specific features. These include adding hardware specialized for the matrix multiplication math that neural networks rely on, using reduced precision numbers to improve the speed of neural network training and adding larger amounts of fast memory to keep these chips supplied with data for AI workloads.

In 2017, Google researchers introduced the transformer, a neural network design originally built to translate between languages. Transformers turned out to perform remarkably well in terms of accuracy as the model and dataset size grew, and this design became the foundation of today’s chatbots and many other generative AI systems.

The growth of these new transformer models has also led to the current boom of generative AI companies, including U.S.-based companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google and xAI, as well as Chinese companies such as DeepSeek, Alibaba and Baidu. Each of these companies is actively focused on building large data centers composed of high-end GPUs to train next-generation foundation models.

These foundation models, exemplified by Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude Fable and OpenAI’s GPT Astra, are very large neural networks that can reason, write software code and analyze information in response to plain language instructions. The companies working on foundation model training are betting that the best models will automate much of the world’s information work and generate enormous economic returns.
Nvidia’s GPUs dominate the AI market, but rival companies developing other chips are trying to knock Nvidia off its throne.

Nvidia trains some AI models of its own, but most of its profit comes from selling the chips and software that other companies use to build theirs. This AI boom has led to record profits for Nvidia, but it has also drawn attention from the U.S. government, which has debated how far to restrict sales of advanced chips to China. The Trump administration tightened its export controls for advanced GPUs in the immediate aftermath of the scandal involving Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Demand for AI chips looks likely to keep growing as the leading AI companies compete to build more capable models, but the boom faces real limits. AI data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, raising questions about the power costs and environmental impacts to local communities.

The most advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s, are fabricated largely by one company, Taiwanese chip giant Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., known as TSMC. Demand for AI hardware has also strained supplies of memory chips, creating shortages that reach gaming graphics cards and smartphones.

Nvidia also faces direct competition from AMD, cloud companies designing their own chips, and startups, all promising to run AI more cheaply and with less power. Whether Nvidia’s software and hardware advantages can hold off these challengers is one of the biggest open questions in the industry. – Rappler.com
This article first appeared on The Conversation.
Jeffrey Young, Principal Research Scientist, Partnership for an Advanced Computing Environment, Georgia Institute of Technology

articles.title: Marawi court issues arrest order vs. Levito Baligod, others for cyber libel
articles.summary: A Marawi Regional Trial Court (RTC) issued an arrest warrant against lawyer Levito Baligod and 18 others in connection to a cyber libel case, with a bail set at P30,000 each.

blocks.text: Published November 28, 2026 4:00pm
A Marawi Regional Trial Court (RTC) issued an arrest warrant against lawyer Levito Baligod and 18 others in connection to a cyber libel case, with a bail set at P30,000 each.
Baligod and other respondents were ordered to appear before presiding judge Samina Sampaco Macabando-Usman of Marawi RTC-Branch 8 over the charges lodged against them.
"The bail for the release of the accused in this case is fixed at P30,000.00 each for CYBER LIBEL," the warrant read.
The warrant was signed on November 26 at Marawi City, Lanao del Sur.

Baligod is the counsel for the 18 men who introduced themselves as bodyguards of former congressman and alleged flood control scam mastermind Zaldy Co. They had claimed to have delivered suitcases full of cash to several politicians and personalities upon Co's instructions.
Several of the respondents in the Marawi arrest warrant have also been named in previous news reports as the ex-bodyguards.

No individual was named as the complainant, as "The People of the Philippines" was indicated as the plaintiff. However, Lanao del Sur 1st District Representative Zia Alonto Adiong later issued a statement saying that he had filed a case against Baligod and the others.

"Napakadali po para sa iilan ang gumawa ng istorya online, ito po ang nag-udyok sa akin upang magsampa ng kasong cyber libel. Hindi po tama na basta-basta na lamang magparatang ng kasinungalingan laban sa kapuwa, lalo na kung ang layunin ay manira at magdulot ng kaguluhan sa isip ng publiko," Adiong said.

(It is so easy to fabricate a story online. This is what prompted me to file a cyber libel case. It is not right that they will just make accusations and lies against others, especially if the purpose is to smear the reputation of others and cause chaos in the mind of the public.)

Adiong said he supports free speech, but said there is a difference if the purpose is to besmirch someone. Libel and are is not part of legitimate forms of expression, Adiong asserted, as it is already outside of the law.
Several of the bodyguards have already recanted their statements.
GMA News Online has reached out to Baligod regarding the charges, but he has yet to respond as of posting time. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Hackers breach US Air Force flagship Cloud One computing platform
articles.summary: The breach of Cloud One, a one-stop shop for the US Air Force's IT needs, raises concerns over sensitive military data security and operational disruptions

blocks.text: Hacker code is seen in this illustration taken October 30, 2026.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
The breach of Cloud One, a one-stop shop for the US Air Force's IT needs, raises concerns over sensitive military data security and operational disruptions

WASHINGTON DC, US – Hackers have breached the US Air Force’s flagship cloud computing platform, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters, in a development that could jeopardize a vast swathe of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data.

The intrusion at Cloud One was discovered within the past month or so during work to upgrade the system, two of the people said, adding that the discovery has led to disruption across the platform. Reuters could not establish the identity of the hackers, the full scope of the intrusion or whether any data had been stolen.

In a statement to Reuters, the Air Force said it “does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the Air Force) information, systems and mission capabilities.”

Initiated in 2017, Cloud One was meant to serve as a one-stop shop for the Air Force’s IT needs, combining the resources of four operators — Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet — to power scores of applications including ones that manage personnel data and pay or logistics and maintenance.

Among them are the Air Force’s Cloud-Based Command and Control, which collates air defense radar and other data feeds from across North America, and the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System, which tracks bombs and missiles across more than 200 US Air Force locations around the world.
SAIC was the prime contractor for Cloud One until 2026, when Leidos took over. SAIC did not respond to a request seeking comment. Leidos referred questions to the Air Force.
Cloud One is among the US military’s biggest cloud platforms, according to two of the sources.
“A breach here is a big deal,” one of the sources said.
Investigators have called in Cyber Command, the US military’s cyber force, to assess the damage, one of the sources said.
Cyber Command did not respond to requests for comment.

The discovery of the hack led to a range of disruption. Two of the sources, along with a fourth person familiar with the matter, said that efforts to migrate back-office applications to Cloud One, a longstanding military priority, have been paused.

Updates to applications already running on Cloud One were blocked, leaving Air Force personnel unable to apply fixes just as a new batch of serious software vulnerabilities has been disclosed across the technology industry. A fifth source said that some users had their administrator rights revoked.
All five sources spoke on condition of anonymity.

One source said that the cyber intruders exploited a software vulnerability to reach the control plane. That person likened the control plane to a universal remote, as intruders in theory could leverage their access to check the operational status of military aircraft or the movement of spare parts, though it was unclear whether the hackers did so in this case.
Reuters could not identify the specific vulnerability exploited by the hackers.

News of the breach comes amid heightened anxiety over AI-powered intrusions, a particularly serious problem for cloud-based networks because of the ability of AI models to swiftly detect weaknesses across wide surface areas.

The US government already has been dealing with the fallout from at least six other recently disclosed cyber incidents, including two at the FBI, a previous hack of Pentagon data, a recent leak of Department of Homeland Security personnel information, a breach affecting at least two spy agencies and a hack at the Treasury Department.
Cloud One has long been in the crosshairs of hackers.

In a 2023 commentary carried by the online publication FedScoop, Cloud One’s leadership touted what they called a “100% success rate” in beating back what they said was a “staggering” number of attempts to penetrate the platform.
“There is no room for error when it comes to security,” Cloud One’s leadership wrote. – Rappler.com

articles.title: In ‘Shux,’ Bicol band Kilyab calls out ‘ayuda’ politics, climate neglect
articles.summary: Drawn from a Gen Z expression of disappointment, the track urges voters in Camarines Sur and across Bicol to look beyond band-aid relief efforts

blocks.text: GRASSROOTS MUSIC. Kilyab performs in the streets and at venues across Naga City and the Bicol region.
Drawn from a Gen Z expression of disappointment, the track urges voters in Camarines Sur and across Bicol to look beyond band-aid relief efforts

items: Bicol pop band Kilyab's new single 'Shux' addresses climate change and systemic neglect in their community, urging citizens to reflect on their voting choices.
The band highlights the exploitation of disasters by politicians for self-promotion and emphasizes the need for socially relevant music to inspire civic engagement.
Kilyab's lyrics criticize the disconnect between local leaders' priorities and community needs, linking environmental issues to political accountability and urging action against corruption.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

ALBAY, Philippines – Bicol pop band Kilyab isn’t just singing about change — they’re marching for it in the streets, too. With their new single, “Shux,” the band pushes back against the idea that climate suffering is unavoidable, blaming decades of systemic neglect for the ongoing struggles in their community.

“Drawing inspiration from Camarines Sur, we saw how even delivering ayuda (relief aid) is being used to mind-condition voters instead of really solving the issues that worsen climate change,” songwriter and lead vocalist Karl Ramirez said.
“If we don’t talk and do something about it, most of our fellow citizens will continue to fall prey to the same system,” he added.

blocks.caption: PROTEST. Kilyab’s lead vocalist Karl Ramirez speaks on the importance of socially relevant songs during a rally against Pax Silica in Naga on November 17, 2026. Photo by Jascyl Jee Hugo Sayson

blocks.text: The band emphasized that voters are often left with almost no real alternatives when choosing their leaders, trapping them in a recurring cycle: enduring calamities while politicians exploit those same disasters for self-promotion.
“These politicians don’t even hide it anymore — they even post videos on their social media accounts showing them handing out money disguised as prizes during their relief operations,” Ramirez said.
For Ramirez, “Shux” reflects the band’s firm belief in using socially relevant music to awaken their fellow citizens — and help end the cycles of neglect in their province and the wider Bicol region.

“Now and any time is the right time to sing songs that reflect the hardship and condition of our nation, and inspire all of us to continue taking a stand against corruption and imperialism,” he noted.
Verna Velasco, Kilyab’s keyboardist and a Bicol Pop mentor who coined the song’s title, said the word comes from a Gen Z expression.
“Shux” is a shortened version of “shucks,” used to convey disdain or disappointment.
“Using the ‘shux’ expression feels like a call for the youth and their communities to be more vigilant, starting with reflecting on why we vote for the people we put into power,” Velasco said.

“Like what the lyrics ask, ‘Ba’t ba kasi sila ang binoto niyo?’ (Why did you vote for them in the first place?), the song explains to us that we also have a shared responsibility for the neglect happening now amid the sufferings and issues we face,” she added.

blocks.caption: CIVIC ADVOCACY. Bicol Pop band Kilyab performs its original hits in Naga City at major gatherings advocating for youth empowerment and anti-corruption accountability.

blocks.text: In a world quick to move past pressing issues, Velasco hopes the song will help people remember — especially when selecting new leaders.
That call for electoral reflection lands in a province long shaped by entrenched political power. Camarines Sur has been dominated by the Villafuerte dynasty for nearly 40 years.

In the 2025 midterm elections, the family maintained its grip on the province as Luis Raymund “LRay” Villafuerte reclaimed the gubernatorial seat, while his sons, Migz and Luigi, also secured seats in Congress. (READ: Iriga City bet decries harassment, vote buying in Camarines Sur).
Ramirez told Rappler that the song’s lyrics were written in one sitting during a songwriting class with Bicol Pop students back in April.
Set against soaring oil prices and looming warnings of a Super El Niño, the track was sparked by growing frustration over the government’s failure to step up.

“Our government can do major things regarding the climate crisis, or at least to ease the suffering of those affected. But instead of helping, we still allow some of our local watersheds — like Mount Isarog in Camarines Sur — to be destroyed,” Ramirez said.

That environmental vulnerability is already playing out on the ground. In 2025, San Jose Mayor Jerold Peña pointed out that rampant quarrying near the Rangas River had accelerated erosion within the Mount Isarog watershed and worsened flooding.

“What we are witnessing is not only the force of nature, but also the consequence of human actions — rampant quarrying and a widespread lack of understanding of the natural dynamics of the Rangas River,” Peña said at the time.

blocks.caption: SOCIAL RELEVANCE. Kilyab recorded its new single, ‘Shux,’ to reflect issues surrounding El Niño and inflation caused by bad governance.

blocks.text: A year later, in preparation for El Niño, the mayor assured residents that the local government had formed a task force to monitor the watershed and secure community water supplies, though he acknowledged that meeting agricultural demands during the dry season would remain a steep challenge.

For Kilyab, the strain on Mount Isarog and Bicol’s watersheds highlights a stark disconnect between what local leaders prioritize and what communities actually need to survive worsening climate impacts.

Rather than treating floods and dry spells as mere acts of nature, the band argues that years of unchecked quarrying, weak environmental enforcement, and band-aid relief operations are the real drivers of the region’s recurring crises — the exact cycle of neglect that “Shux” wants to expose.

Rooted in their environmental protection advocacy, Kilyab cuts straight to the heart of political accountability with the song’s biting line: “Bakit ba kasi sila ang binoto niyo? Oh ayan, naghihirap tayo (Why did you vote for them in the first place? Look now, we’re suffering).” – Rappler.com

articles.title: She killed his sister and her family while driving drunk. Now they're speaking together about forgiveness
articles.summary: In 2016 Catherine McKay killed a family of four in a car collision outside of Saskatoon. A court later heard her blood alcohol was three times the legal limit.

image.caption: Chad Mierau and Catherine McKay on Friday, Nov. 27 in Tisdale, Saskatchewan. McKay killed Mierau's sister and her family in 2016 while she was driving impaired. (Maeve Ellis)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan
In 2016 Catherine McKay killed a family of four in a car collision outside of Saskatoon. A court later heard her blood alcohol was three times the legal limit.
Catherine McKay, Chad Mierau speak about healing, forgiveness ten years after crash that killed family of four
Chad Mierau remembers when he first met with the woman who killed his sister and her family.
"Those conversations were beautiful. They were heartfelt. They were full of tears. The first one it was really hard to make eye contact. We both had a heck of a lot of stuff going on," he said.
In 2016 Catherine McKay killed his sister and her family of four in a car collision outside of Saskatoon. A court later heard her blood alcohol was three times the legal limit.
Now they're speaking publicly together about the power of forgiveness and healing trauma.
"It was important for me to have her know that I forgive her. It was for me. It was something I had to do. It was my healing journey. I had to set some things down. It was so heavy," he said.
Their first two talks in a series of public conversations were on Friday in Tisdale, a town of about 3,000 in central Saskatchewan. They spoke with students and then a group of about 15.

items: Woman who killed Saskatoon family while driving drunk receives statutory release

blocks.text: Chanda Van de Vorst, her husband, Jordan, and their two children, Miguire, 2, and Kamryn, 5, died when McKay drove through an intersection just outside Saskatoon. She later pleaded guilty and received a nine-year sentence.

Jordan Van de Vorst, 34, his wife, Chanda, 33, and their two children, Kamryn, 5, and Miguire, 2, all died after a drunk driving crash at the corner of Highway 11 and Wanuskewin Road north of Saskatoon in January 2016. (Submitted by Chad Mierau)
Mierau remembers the junior RCMP officer who first called couldn't bring himself to say the full impact.

items: How forgiveness brought 2 strangers together after a deadly crash in Saskatchewan

blocks.text: "The hardest part beyond the hospital was the house. They literally just went to Costco the day of the accident. The fridge was full of groceries," he said.
He remembers the initial hours of confusion in the hospital.
"You're trying to figure out what is my new normal? What does my new life look like without four of my favourite people?," he said.
Chad Mierau poses for a photograph with his five-year-old niece, Kamryn Van de Vorst and two-year-old nephew, Miguire, before they were killed in a drunk driving crash. (Submitted by Chad Mierau)
McKay said that when an officer told her she killed someone, she couldn't believe it.

"None of us ever think that we can possibly be that person. I mean anybody, friends or people that knew me well would have told you, six months, a year before that, 'there's no way that would be her,'" she said.

"That's part of the reason I'm here is that it's really important for you to realize that this could easily happen. So easily that you could be literally sitting in a jail cell and go 'I don't understand,'" she said.
Mierau said he reached out to McKay's daughter in a long message when he saw hatred against the family on Facebook.
"I said 'I really want to reach out to your mom and tell her I forgive her,'" he said, as McKay was still detained.
"I have people question me quite often, 'How do you do that? How do you find forgiveness for someone that's taken four family members?' and I don't really know how to put that into words."
Chad Mierau grieves "four of his favourite people" after McKay went through a stop sign and killed his sister, her husband, and their two kids in January 2016. (Chanss Lagaden/CBC)
McKay remembers sleepless nights and years of suicidal thoughts. She eventually found part of her path to recovery in a healing lodge while she was carrying out her sentence.
"Before all of this happened I was basically an atheist. I had no beliefs, I had no spirituality at all, which was part of the reason I was so sick. I didn't feel that there was any hope," she said.
They spoke about the importance of healing trauma to prevent ongoing harm.
McKay said she experienced sexual abuse as a child and only sought help for it as an adult. As a single mother of five, she fell into alcoholism.
"I didn't take care of problems. I didn't take care of the trauma I'd been through. I didn't reach for help. I reached for a bottle," she said.
Son of drunk driver who killed family says he was 'destroyed and heartbroken' by what his mother did

McKay said alcohol is too prevalent and encouraged in Saskatchewan, and she had her first drink when she was 10. She said she's particularly upset about the rising rates of highway fatalities in the province.

"I don't know why I'm here but I do know that because I'm here that there's something that I'm supposed to be doing and I'm supposed to make a difference so this doesn't happen to anybody else," she said. "So there doesn't have to be another family like Chad's that has to pay the ultimate price for someone that didn't take care of their shit."

items: Sask. shifting to immediate penalties instead of criminal charges for some impaired driving

blocks.text: Mierau said his life will never be the same afterwards. Old business ventures like his rental properties are off his mind.
"If Catherine and I can lean on each other as we heal, surely to God, other people can lean on their neighbours," said Mierau.
Mierau said he hopes that them speaking together would make their message more profound.
"It can have a bigger impact if we combine efforts to do this and for me that's the big picture," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Maeve Ellis is a reporter and associate producer with CBC News based in Saskatoon. You can reach her at maeve.ellis@cbc.ca or maeveellis_ on X. She would love to hear from anyone with Sask-related story ideas.

articles.title: Two staff killed in Israeli strike on Gaza medical clinic, MSF says
articles.summary: The Israeli military says it targeted "Hamas terrorists" in the strike which has been condemned by the World Health Organization.

blocks.text: Two workers for the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have been killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza, according to the organisation.
MSF said the strike was a direct hit on one of the charity's clinics, the location of which was known by the Israeli military.

In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the two people were Hamas operatives "acting as security guards at a clinic operated by MSF". The IDF added the strike was "not directed at a hospital" and caused no damage to medical infrastructure.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said that attacks on health facilities and health workers in Gaza were "outrageous and unacceptable".
In a post on X, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote: "Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked."

In its statement, MSF - which is also known as Doctors Without Borders - said that the two workers who were killed were watchmen, and added that the strike brought the number of its colleagues killed in Gaza to 17.

The organisation said it was "devastated and outraged" and added: "​Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military."
In its own post on X, the IDF said that the two men, who they named as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, were "terrorists in Hamas' military wing".
The Israeli military added it was another example of Hamas "embedding itself within international organizations".

It said that "precautionary measures were taken to minimize harm to civilians" before the strike on Gaza City, adding the men had "advanced plans to carry out attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops".

Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under the control of Hamas, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to tens of thousands of shelters for displaced families.

The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,770 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.
