articles.title: Senate concludes marathon debates on P7.2-trillion 2027 budget
articles.summary: The Senate concluded its deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027 early Saturday, November 28, after suspending the impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: November 28, 2026 | 2:40pm
Senators deliberate on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027 during a plenary session at the Senate on Nov. 27, 2026.
Senate of the Philippines via Facebook / Joseph Vidal

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate concluded its deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027 early Saturday, November 28, after suspending the impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte to make way for the debates.
The Office of Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said the Senate finished its deliberations at around 1:25 a.m., GMA News reported.

In a Facebook post, the Senate said it had taken up the proposed allocations of several major government agencies, including the Department of Public Works and Highways, which is seeking P587.9 billion, and the Department of Health, with P378.629 billion.
The Department of National Defense has a proposed allocation of P326.9 billion, while the Department of Agriculture is seeking P175 billion.
The Senate also took up the proposed P84.132-billion budget of the Judiciary and P27.89 billion for the Congress of the Philippines.
Other agencies included in the deliberations were the Commission on Higher Education, with P38.821 billion, and the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW), with P11.894 billion.
Gatchalian also announced the conclusion of the deliberations in a separate Facebook post.
“Tapos na ang pagtalakay ng Senado sa 2027 national budget!” he said.
“Ilang araw natin itong pinagpuyatan para masuri nang mabuti ang panukalang pondo ng bawat ahensya,” he added.
Gatchalian thanked his fellow senators, his staff, Senate employees and the People’s Budget Coalition for helping monitor the proposed allocations.
He said their efforts were aimed at ensuring that the funds would be transparent and beneficial to the public.
The Senate also took up the proposed budgets of offices handling peace and regional development.
The Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity is seeking P9.304 billion, while the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples has a proposed allocation of P1.738 billion.
The Marawi Compensation Board has a proposed budget of P1.247 billion, while the National Amnesty Commission is seeking P266.6 million.

The Commission on Filipinos Overseas has a proposed allocation of P187.8 million, while the Metropolitan Baguio City, La Trinidad, Itogon, Sablan, Tuba, and Tublay Development Authority is seeking P45.4 million.

Other executive offices included in the deliberations were the Department of Information and Communications Technology, with a proposed budget of P8.514 billion; the National Intelligence Coordinating Agency, with P3.086 billion; and the National Security Council, with P1.122 billion.

The Senate also took up the proposed allocations of the Anti-Money Laundering Council, with P335 million; Film Development Council of the Philippines, with P311 million; Philippine Racing Commission, with P202.8 million; Movie and Television Review and Classification Board, with P69.742 million; and Optical Media Board, with P53.462 million.

articles.title: DBM chief urges public to monitor public funds via 'COMPASS' spending tracking platform
articles.summary: Department of Budget and Management (DBM) Secretary Kim Robert De Leon urged the public to use the government's unified budget transparency platform to monitor how public funds are released and…

blocks.text: Published November 28, 2026 2:34pm

Department of Budget and Management (DBM) Secretary Kim Robert De Leon urged the public to use the government's unified budget transparency platform to monitor how public funds are released and spent, and to ensure that the institutions managing them are held accountable.

In a news release on Saturday, the DBM, citing Episode 20 of A.S.K. – Alamin Kay Sec. Kim— said the Budget chief demonstrated how Filipinos can use the Centralized Open Monitoring Platform for Appropriations and Spending Statistics (COMPASS) to view available information regarding government funds, from budget allocation to actual expenditure.

In September, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Executive Order No. 126 on September 28, institutionalizing the Centralized Open Monitoring Platform for Appropriations and Spending Statistics (COMPASS).
The DBM said it aims to consolidate into a single online platform financial information that previously had to be searched for across various government institutions.

Under EO No. 126, concerned national government agencies and instrumentalities, including government-owned or -controlled corporations (GOCCs) and government financial institutions (GFIs), are mandated to submit, publish, and update the information required under the EO.
Local government units (LGUs) are also encouraged to participate.

Through the initiative, public access to information will be broadened, institutional accountability will be strengthened, and citizens will be encouraged to participate in monitoring the use of public resources, according to the DBM.

COMPASS will also be linked to existing digital systems, including the integrated Financial Management Information System, Budget and Treasury Management System, Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System, Digital Information for Monitoring and Evaluation, and the E-Gov PH App.
Meanwhile, the COMPASS Council will oversee the platform.

Malacañang said the council will be chaired by the DBM and co-chaired by the Department of Information and Communications Technology. The Department of Finance and the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) will serve as members. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Sandiganbayan drops Samchan exec as co-accused in Martin Romualdez plunder case
articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan Third Division has removed a businessman as a co-accused in the plunder case against former House speaker Ferdinand Martin Romualdez, clearing the way for the former to testify for…

blocks.text: Published November 28, 2026 2:18pm

The Sandiganbayan Third Division has removed a businessman as a co-accused in the plunder case against former House speaker Ferdinand Martin Romualdez, clearing the way for the former to testify for the prosecution.
In an 11-page resolution, the anti-graft court approved an amended charge sheet dropping Samchan Foreign Exchange Corp. president Felicito Guevarra from the case.
Prosecutors will now present Guevarra as a witness during the bail hearings, replacing former Public Works secretary Manuel Bonoan.

Guevarra surrendered himself to the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) and was granted conditional immunity "because his testimony and records are necessary to establish the truth in this case," according to the Office of the Ombudman.
The Ombudsman said the conditions are as follows:

items: Guevarra will cooperate fully and truthfully turn over all of Samchan's records and devices
he will remain in the Philippines
he will stay under the protection of the Department of Justice (DOJ)

blocks.text: The Sandignbayan ruled that prosecutors correctly followed the rules for removing an accused person before they enter a plea, rather than the stricter process for turning someone into a state witness.
"His (Guevarra) testimony and records will help the prosecution trace the movement of funds alleged in the charge sheet. The charges against the other accused stand as filed," the Ombudsman said.
The Sandiganbayan, meanwhile, noted that it "finds merit in the prosecution's contention thatGuevarra's willingness to testify against his co-accused is a supervening event."
The anti-graft court added that the Resolution issued by the Office of the Ombudsman directing the exclusion of Guevarra was issued only on November 20, 2026.

Due to security risks, the Sandiganbayan also granted the prosecution's request to keep Guevarra in the custody of the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) while his application for the DOJ's Witness Protection Program is being processed. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Palestinian tells of ‘devastating’ struggle after being made redundant by EU in Gaza
articles.summary:
Mohammad Baraka unable to access redundancy pay for almost 20 years’ service as family’s situation becomes ‘increasingly desperate’

A Palestinian man who worked for the EU in Gaza has told…

blocks.text: A Palestinian man who worked for the EU in Gaza has told of a “devastating” struggle to survive after he was made redundant by bosses in Brussels.

He was let go last year after being evacuated to Egypt but his redundancy payment was made to an account to which he has no access. “My family’s situation has become increasingly desperate,” said Mohammad Baraka, a former staffer at the EU border assistance mission (EUBam).
“Both of my daughters have suffered severe psychological distress as a result of the war, displacement and the prolonged uncertainty surrounding our future.”

blocks.caption: Mohammad Baraka’s house was finished just three months before it was bombed. Photograph: Mohammad Baraka

blocks.text: The 220,000 Israeli shekels (£52,000) payment for almost 20 years’ service was made on 5 August last year to the Bank of Palestine but access to the money has been blocked, a risk he was aware of given the relatively large sum being transferred.

He said he wrote on several occasions to the European Commission, asking it not to make the payment into that bank because of a known risk that a large sum of money could be misconstrued as war funds. “I am now in the devastating position of having money in my name that I cannot access, while my family is experiencing severe financial hardship,” said Baraka.
Instead he had asked for the payment to go to a new account in an Abu Dhabi bank, but that never materialised.

Baraka was evacuated in 2023 after his house in Gaza was bombed and family members killed. The EU tried to relocate him to alternative offices in the West Bank but travel for Palestinians in Gaza was severely restricted. After a hasty three-day concession agreed with the Egyptian government, Baraka was able to leave for Cairo.

As the conflict continued, Baraka was initially able to work remotely from Cairo as an EU employee and had the comfort of a salary, private healthcare and access to schools for his two children. But when Brussels decided to close its EUBam office in Rafah, he was let go, leading to what he says have been traumatic consequences for himself and his wife and two daughters.

blocks.caption: The remains of Mohammad Baraka’s house in Gaza after it was bombed. Photograph: Mohammad Baraka

blocks.text: He says the evacuation to Egypt with no plan for onward travel to an EU nation or a diplomatically secured place in another country has rendered him stateless, with no residency rights and no right to healthcare or schooling for his seriously ill wife and two daughters, both of whom he says are suffering from the trauma of war.

One of his daughters has an acute mental health condition and Baraka says he cannot pay for her treatment. “I am not asking for charity or special treatment. I am asking for access to my own money, and for accountability over a decision that could have been avoided,” said Baraka.
“I had specifically asked the [EU] mission to transfer my money to my new bank account in Egypt to avoid precisely this situation,” he said.

“If the EU argues that it fulfilled its obligations simply because it transferred the settlement, I believe the legitimate question is whether an employer can consider its responsibility discharged when it knowingly disregards an employee’s repeated warnings about the destination of such a substantial payment.”

blocks.caption: EU Commission president Ursula von der Leyen. Photograph: Thierry Monasse/Getty Images

blocks.text: Last year he wrote to the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, pleading with her to reverse what he called his “unjust dismissal” and asked her to restore his employment, even temporarily, “until a dignified and legal solution is arranged”.

He also wrote to the European ombudsman to ask them to open an investigation but they replied last week to say they had no scope for an inquiry. “We fully appreciate that you and your family are in an immensely difficult position. The hardship you are experiencing as a result of the war and your displacement are clear from your complaint,” wrote Tina Nilsson, the head of inquiries.

“I realise that this conclusion will be disappointing. I nevertheless hope you can understand why, based on the information available, there are insufficient grounds for the ombudsman to intervene further.”
He is now suing the commission for alleged breach of Belgian employment law but the case could take years to be heard.
Without the “laissez-passer” document that allowed him to be evacuated from Gaza, he cannot leave Egypt, he says, putting him in an impossible position.
A spokesperson for the commission said: “Due to the ongoing related court case, we cannot comment on this further.”

articles.title: House prosecutors ready to cross-examine Sara Duterte if she takes witness stand
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel is prepared to cross-examine Vice President Sara Duterte if she decides to take the witness stand in her Senate impeachment trial.

blocks.text: Published November 28, 2026 1:28pm
The House prosecution panel is prepared to cross-examine Vice President Sara Duterte if she decides to take the witness stand in her Senate impeachment trial.
At a news forum on Saturday, House prosecutor Manila Representative Joel Chua said the prosecution team is expecting a "surprise witness" in the upcoming trial next week.
"Inaasahan ng panel of prosecutors na magdadag sila ng witness dahil apat 'yung trial dates na December 1 to 4 pero 'yung witnesses na kanilang ipi-present ay dadalawa lamang," Chua said.
(The panel of prosecutors is expecting they will add more witnesses because there are four trial dates upcoming from December 1 to 4 but they are about to present only two witnesses.)
Chua added that a "surprise witness" might be "in the person of the respondent, the honorable vice president."

The vice president's team had asked the Senate impeachment court for the issuance of subpoenas to two witnesses, namely Cale88's Lourdes Lebosada, the alleged business partner of Duterte's husband Atty. Manases Carpio; and Agaton Teodoro Uvero, deputy commissioner for the Bureau of Customs' Assessment and Operations Coordinating Group.

"But in any event, handa po kami, handa po ang panel of prosecutors at kung sakali naman po na uupo ang ating bise presidente bilang testigo ng defense ay nakahanda po kami na i-cross [examine]…," Chua said.
(But in any event, we are ready, the panel of prosecutors is ready. And if the vice president testifies for the defense, we are ready to cross examine her.)
This came after Duterte said she had asked her legal team to allow her to lawyer for herself in the impeachment trial, but her defense counsel Michael Poa supposedly ignored this.
"Handa kami na i-cross examine ang ating Bise Presidente. In fact may naka-assign na po na abogado in the event na siya ang umupo sa witness stand," Chua said.
The House prosecutor said that prosecution panel is preparing all possibilities, including Carpio also taking the witness stand.
"Lahat naman 'yan possibility kaya hindi 'yan tinatanggal sa table," Chua said.
The impeachment trial is tackling the sole remaining charge of unexplained wealth against Duterte after the prosecution team dropped all other three articles of impeachment.

The vice president earlier said she and her defense team are always "preparing for the worst" now that the trial is nearing its end and the Senate impeachment court is expected to issue a verdict soon, as she reiterated that she would not be stepping down from office amid her impeachment trial. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: La succession: France’s wealthiest family said to be battling over who will take over LVMH
articles.summary:
Bernard Arnault’s children – described as ‘modern-day French royals’ – are subject of rivalry rumours over who will succeed him

They are France’s richest family, leading the world’s biggest…

blocks.text: They are France’s richest family, leading the world’s biggest luxury goods empire, dressed in matching Dior suits – a clan so powerful they have been described as modern-day French royals.

But in recent months, the family dynasty of Bernard Arnault, 77, the billionaire head of the LVMH group whose brands range from Louis Vuitton handbags to Tiffany jewellery, has become the subject of speculation about internal rivalry over which of his children could take over the company.

This week it emerged that the health-conscious Arnault, who likes to play tennis with the Swiss champion Roger Federer, can continue to lead the family holding company until he is 95, according to a new filing, pushing back any decisions on his succession.
Last year, the age cap of Arnault’s chief executive role at LVMH was raised to 85 to allow him to stay on in the position. The fashion tycoon once joked about still leading the business at 100.

blocks.caption: Bernard Arnault (centre) with his wife, Hélène, in Paris in 2021, with (from left): Frederic Arnault, Delphine Arnault, Antoine Arnault and Alexandre Arnault. Photograph: Chesnot/Getty

blocks.text: The question of which of Arnault’s five adult children could eventually lead the family company is seen as key to the French economy and the political class.
LVMH, which has more than 75 brands including fashion, perfumes and champagne, is a big employer in France.

Arnault, nicknamed the “wolf in cashmere” for his acquisitions of leading brands and whose personal wealth is estimated at more than $100bn, owns almost all of France’s business and economic press as well as the daily newspaper Le Parisien and the celebrity magazine Paris Match.
He attended Donald Trump’s second inauguration, as a personal friend, and is regularly present at official French state dinners with world leaders.

This month, Émilie Lanez published an account of what she called the emotional tensions inside the Arnault family’s unresolved succession challenge, based on what she said were hours of off-record conversations with insiders. “I was really struck by the family’s ethereal, otherworldly nature: they are like deities in a performance, and France is a spectator,” she said.

blocks.caption: Delphine Arnault, the CEO of Dior, receives an honorary doctorate in South Korea in November. Photograph: YONHAP/EPA

blocks.text: The book, Monsieur et les siens, now in discussion over a possible publication in English, traces the family’s story from Arnault’s childhood in Roubaix, in the former industrial heartland of northern France, where he took over his family’s building company before moving into property development and then luxury goods.

Lanez describes Arnault’s wife, the classical pianist Hélène Mercier-Arnault, working out on her treadmill in the early morning watching the HBO series Succession about a family business power-struggle, and then being at pains to publicly deny any rift or friction among the Arnault children.

The book depicts Arnault’s deep personal involvement in his children’s education. Schooling was so important in his own upbringing that when at age 10 he said farewell to his grandfather at his funeral, he put his glowing school report card into his grandfather’s clasped hands in his coffin.

When he had two children with his first wife, Anne Dewavrin, he devised a system to personally teach his daughter Delphine to read at a young age. At 51, she is now the chief executive of Christian Dior Couture, one of the most important roles at LVMH. Her brother Antoine, 49, has an important communications role, running the group’s image and environmental strategy.

blocks.caption: From left: Frederic Arnault, CEO of Loro Piano, Alexandre Arnault, deputy CEO of Moët Hennessy, and Antoine Arnault, head of image and sustainability at LVMH in July. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty

blocks.text: Arnault later married Mercier-Arnault and had three more sons who all work for LVMH brands. Alexandre, 34, is deputy chief executive of the drinks brand Moët Hennessy; Frédéric, 32, runs the luxury fashion brand Loro Piana; and Jean, 28, is watch director at Louis Vuitton.

When the youngest three were teenagers and preparing for higher education, Lanez writes that Arnault personally hired and interviewed tutors. The boys would come home from their day’s classes, then study with a tutor from 8pm to 11pm then go to their father’s room so he could ask them about the equations they had been tackling.

“They are likened to royals because of the power and influence they have in France,” said Lanez. “And also because they have a kind of court, courtesans and counsellors. It’s a dynasty, and the children, particularly the three youngest, have been raised to perpetuate the empire.”
after newsletter promotion

Just as Arnault as a child would be shown round his father’s family building business, he regularly took his own children, and then grandchildren, on his favourite weekend activity: inspecting his luxury shops.

Arnault is aware that any family divisions can make a company vulnerable. This year, when Mercier-Arnault was promoting her latest classical music record, she did a high-profile round of media interviews in France, seeking to reassure that there were no rifts between the five children.

blocks.caption: From left: Alexandre Arnault, Bernard Arnault, Hélène Mercier-Arnault, Jean Arnault, Frédéric Arnault and Antoine Arnault attend the reopening of Tiffany’s flagship store in New York in 2023. Photograph: Cindy Ord/Getty for Tiffany & Co

blocks.text: But with the Arnaults’ vast wealth often cited as an example of the growing power of billionaires in France amid widening economic inequality, Mercier-Arnault’s comments were scrutinised.
French media reported that in an edited radio segment she had said that being homeless could be seen as a “lifestyle choice”.

Mercier-Arnault said later on a TV show that there had been a misunderstanding and she had been referring to her experience as the carer of her late sister, a violinist who was bipolar and had died by suicide, and who had begun a relationship with a person who was homeless. She told the newspaper Libération she was “deeply sorry”.

blocks.caption: Delphine Arnault with her husband, Xavier Niel, attend a state dinner near the Palace of Versailles. Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: The cast of characters in the Arnault clan includes another high-profile and influential French billionaire, the telecoms executive Xavier Niel, who is the life-partner of Delphine Arnault. The couple have two children.
“The arrival of Xavier Niel in this family was like a theatrical scenario,” Lanez said, comparing the family saga to a novel.
Asked by the Guardian to comment on the book and speculation of tension or rivalry over the succession, LVMH declined to comment.

In July, Arnault, commenting on a series about him in Le Monde, joked about his family being likened to royals, but added that the comparison was good for sales at Dior. He said there were no divisions in the family or between his children, writing on social media that it was possible for “five strong personalities to work in the same firm without it turning into an Italian opera”.

articles.title: Yuri and I used to play football together. Then I spotted his name among Russia’s war dead
articles.summary:
I had no idea he had gone to fight in Ukraine and without hacked data I would probably never have learned of his death

One evening, after weeks spent counting Russia’s war dead, I began…

blocks.text: One evening, after weeks spent counting Russia’s war dead, I began looking for names I might recognise.

My colleagues and I had been working our way through more than 11m death certificates leaked from Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, and identifying nearly half a million Russian soldiers who had died in the war in Ukraine.
We had sorted the dead by age, region and cause of death, building the most detailed picture yet of Russia’s losses in nearly five years of war.
Now I typed in the names of the places where I had grown up.

My childhood was spent in Rublevka, a stretch of pine forest west of Moscow that has been home to the Russian elite since Soviet times. With the collapse of communism and Russia’s chaotic embrace of capitalism, the dachas of party officials gave way to the sprawling estates of oligarchs.

Vladimir Putin and Dmitry Medvedev established their residences in Rublevka. In more recent years, the area has become a refuge for ousted leaders, among them Ukraine’s Viktor Yanukovych and, as the Guardian previously reported, Syria’s Bashar al-Assad.
I did not expect to find many names there.

Our analysis had shown just how unevenly the burden of the war had fallen across Russian society. In some of the poorest regions, working-age men were up to 32 times more likely to die in the war than men of the same age in Moscow. I knew sons of the Russian elite who had left the country shortly after the invasion, keen to avoid being called up to fight.
My village, Zhukovka, returned no results.
I worked my way along the Rublyovo-Uspenskoye highway, the well-paved road connecting the wealthy settlements west of Moscow. Here and there, a lone death certificate appeared.
Then I typed in Gorki-10, a town a few miles further down the road, named after the famed writer Maxim Gorky, who spent his final years there.
One of the names on my screen was instantly familiar: Yuri Vladimirovich Kyrmyz, aged 31.
Place of death: Makiivka, Svatove district, in the Russian-occupied Luhansk region of Ukraine. Cause of death on 3 February 2025: an explosion during military operations.

Makiivka, a small village on the banks of the Zherebets River, had been the scene of months of bitter fighting as Russian forces sought to retake territory lost during Ukraine’s 2022 counteroffensive.
Two decades earlier, Yuri and I used to play football together as teenagers.

Though we were never particularly close, he was a reliable presence at our games, a quiet, unassuming defender who rarely had much to say. We had not spoken in years. Until that evening, I had no idea he had gone to fight in Ukraine, let alone that he had died there.
I also do not know what made him join Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

blocks.caption: Yuri Vladimirovich Kyrmyz died in the Russian-occupied Luhansk region of Ukraine. Photograph: VK

blocks.text: The Kremlin has worked hard to insulate Moscow and its suburbs from the war. In neighbouring Barvikha, at the Luxury Village shopping complex, visitors can still buy a Ferrari or a Chanel handbag, despite western sanctions. But for all its associations with wealth and power, Rublevka is also home to another Russia.

Parts of Gorki-10 consist of Soviet-era blocks of flats, built for families who serviced the rich or toiled at the local stud farm, which dates back to the 19th century. I remembered that Yuri’s family was not well-off. Before enlisting, Yuri worked as a car dealer.
The signing bonuses and salaries offered by the Russian military, in some cases amounting to several times the average annual wage, would have represented a life-changing sum of money.
He may also have believed in the war.

blocks.caption: The war appears to have given Andrei Solomatin a sense of public importance he had not enjoyed for years. Photograph: Telegram

blocks.text: Yuri was one of millions of Russians of our generation who grew up immersed in the memory of the Soviet victory over Nazi Germany. Victory Day, on 9 May, was one of the biggest occasions of the year, rivalled only by New Year’s Eve. Over the past two decades, Putin has appropriated that collective memory, telling a new generation of Russians that in Ukraine they are fighting the same “Nazi” enemy their grandfathers once faced.

Until I discovered Yuri’s name in the database, the only person I knew to have joined the invasion, other than the soldiers I had interviewed in the course of my reporting, was my former football coach Andrei Solomatin.
In his prime, Solomatin had played for CSKA and Lokomotiv Moscow, won 13 caps for Russia and appeared in all three of the country’s matches at the 2002 World Cup.

But his life unravelled after retirement. There were debts, problems with alcohol and a gradual slide into obscurity. By the time I met him, the former international footballer was eking out a modest living coaching our local Sunday league team.

Our team was an eclectic collection of nationalities, including Dutch (me), British and Nigerian players. I cannot recall Solomatin ever expressing hostility towards Ukraine. Politics, as far as I could tell, did not concern him.
The war changed that.

In autumn 2022, he began delivering aid to Española, a far-right military formation drawn from the ranks of Russian football ultras fighting in occupied Ukraine. By July 2023, he had joined the unit himself.

He was back on television, this time in military fatigues. In interviews, he spoke of his “complete trust” in Putin. The war appears to have given him a sense of public importance he had not enjoyed for years.

Yuri, like hundreds of thousands of other Russian soldiers who have died in Ukraine, left little public trace. Had hackers not obtained the records of Russia’s state statistics agency, I would probably never have learned of his death.
Although in some of the worst-affected parts of Russia nearly everyone knows someone who has died in the war, the full scale of the losses remains hidden from the Russian public.
Asked about the military deaths on Wednesday, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, dismissed the findings, insisting that only official data could be trusted.
Independent Russian journalists were quick to point out the irony, given that the figures came from the Russian state’s own statistics agency.

articles.title: Food for feed: The price paid beyond the plate
articles.summary: Much of the fishmeal and fish oil that support imported farmed seafood consumed in the Philippines comes from global supply chains linked to pollution, labor abuses, overfishing, and food insecurity…

blocks.text: In May 2025, a regional office of the Philippines’ fisheries agency in Visayas announced an initiative that would invite fishers to government meetings held to expand fish farming in the region.

Officials would introduce the fishers to ongoing fish breeding, processing, and distribution projects as part of a push to transform the local economy “from fish hunting to fish farming.” They emphasized that this transformation would ease stress on the ecosystem.
“Instead of constantly taking from the sea, let’s try to cultivate fish and give the ocean a chance to recover,” said community development officer Joel Lutao.

But critics worldwide have questioned whether the practice of catching and reducing whole, fresh fish to grow more seafood can ever be considered sustainable. The most popular types of farmed seafood — milkfish, tilapia, salmon, shrimp, and trout — are fed the kinds of wild fish that aquaculture claims to be saving, thereby accelerating ocean depletion, not slowing it.

Two-thirds of global aquaculture grows species that are fed fishmeal and fish oil. Before it reaches market, a farmed salmon, for instance, eats at some farms more than six times its weight in wild-caught fish.

The concerns about aquaculture extend far beyond the fate of the oceans. The feed that powers most of this industry comes with a huge variety of other hidden costs, according to a wide-reaching investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization based in Washington, DC.

These costs include the loss of artisanal fishing jobs, chronic chemical exposure, avoidable worker deaths, violent protests typically spurred by the horrid smell from fishmeal factories, and escalating geopolitical tensions as countries compete for scarce sources of protein.

What economists often call “externalities,” these social and environmental impacts exact a price primarily paid by the poorer countries where the feed ingredient is harvested and processed, far from where the resulting luxury seafood is eaten.

In The Gambia and Mauritania, the investigation documented how the industry drives food insecurity, as fish that once sustained local communities are increasingly being diverted into fishmeal factories for export.
In remote islands in Russia’s far east and in China’s Xinjiang region, the reporting detailed the use of forced labor on ships, at farms, and in factories.

In other countries, including India and Peru, this industry was tied to at least 80 incidents of civil unrest, some of them violent, usually in the form of labor strikes and community protests sparked by the water pollution or stench from factories cooking thousands of tons of decomposing fish, according to Bait to Plate, an online tool that tracks the fishing and seafood industries.

In Senegal, fishmeal has put local fishers out of work, so increasingly they are selling — or repurposing — their boats to flee to Europe, typically taking the roughly 930-mile sea journey to Spain’s Canary Islands, a route that claimed more than 3,000 lives in 2025.

“We’re fishermen, but there’s no fish left here, so we left,” said Cheikhou Omar, a 21-year-old fisher, in September 2024 as he sat on a beach in Senegal, rescued after the fishing boat he took trying to get to Spain capsized, killing two dozen.

The five-year investigation mapped roughly the entire global fishmeal industry, including more than 1,400 fishmeal factories across 64 countries, tracing supply chains from fishing vessels to processing plants, feed mills, fish farms, and seafood retailers. The reporting effort involved dozens of journalists from as many countries, visiting factories and farms and boarding fishmeal ships at sea.

The oceans bear an especially heavy and largely invisible burden of the fishmeal and fish oil industry. More than a fifth of wild-caught fish around the world is used for non-human consumption, especially as feed for fish, but also chickens and pigs.

The investigation assessed more than 2,400 ships tied to fishmeal production, operating in the waters of at least 30 countries. It found that most of these ships do not fully comply with the Global Charter for Fisheries Transparency, a guide created by leading ocean-focused civil society groups detailing accountability standards for industrial fishing fleets.

For example, less than 30% of the fleet had publicly available location information, and under 25% had a unique vessel identification number, or ship license plate. Such opacity makes the fleet difficult to police.

Scientific studies classified at least half of the species landed by the assessed fishmeal vessels as “overexploited” or worse. Most of the ships in this fleet are purse seiners or trawlers, which deploy vast nets to capture dense schools of fish. Both gear types are associated with high levels of waste, routinely hauling in large volumes of bycatch and non-target species.

At least 165 of the ships in the global fishmeal fleet were bottom trawlers, conducting a particularly destructive form of fishing that uses weighted nets that scrape the ocean floor, destroying virtually everything in their paths.
The problem of unsustainable fishing is compounded by heavy government subsidies that keep too many vessels operating, accelerating pressure on already stressed fisheries.

“Any accounting of the true impact of aquaculture has to start not with the farm, but with the feed,” said Daniel Pauly, project director of the Sea Around Us initiative at University of British Columbia. “And that kind of accounting offers a very different picture than the industry offers.”
As commodities, fishmeal and fish oil promise to grow in international importance.

Starting in 2022, more than half of the seafood eaten globally came from fish farms rather than wild catch. Aquaculture is a $313-billion industry and the fastest-growing segment of global food production. Most of these fish farms are powered by fishmeal and fish oil.

Fishmeal processing in the Philippines is concentrated in three cities. The first is the port city of Navotas, known as the country’s “fishing capital.” Located in Metro Manila on the island of Luzon, it has at least one fishmeal plant.

The second is Zamboanga, a city on the island of Mindanao regarded as the Philippines’ “sardine capital,” home to half a dozen fishmeal plants. The third is General Santos. The national “tuna capital,” it lies in Mindanao and hosts four fishmeal plants.

Many of these plants focus primarily on processing seafood for human consumption, but they also redirect inedible offcuts into fishmeal. This practice is widely cited as sustainable and socially beneficial, since it uses materials that would otherwise be thrown away.

Therefore, fishmeal production in the Philippines is less of a driver of food insecurity than it is in other countries that use whole edible fish. However, the Philippines suffers from severe food insecurity because of general overfishing and the export of most catch, be it small anchovies or larger species like tuna.

The far greater burden of food insecurity, social unrest, and air and water pollution is borne by the poorer countries that produce the fishmeal or fishmeal-fed seafood the Philippines imports. The country imported more seafood than it produced as of 2023.

Half of all seafood globally is farmed, and most of that is fed fishmeal. The fish farms in several of the countries that export the most seafood to the Philippines — including China, Vietnam, Papua New Guinea, Chile, and Japan — have ties to severe problems caused by fishmeal production, according to the investigation.
The investigation revealed a surprising diversity of hidden costs in the global feed industry.
In Senegal, fishmeal production accelerated overfishing, eroding traditional fishing grounds and contributing to thousands of young men attempting deadly and desperate voyages at sea to Europe.
In Russia, fishmeal workers were held captive in secluded company towns in remote parts of the country, or stuck on ships far from shore.

“People have nowhere to go, no money,” one worker said in a plea to Russian President Vladimir Putin, who participated in an episode of a call-in television show about the fishmeal plant. “Please, help us,” a second worker said.

In Chile, several hundred protesters burned tires and blocked coastal highways and railway tracks, demonstrating against the early closure of the fishing season, a move partly driven by overfishing tied to fishmeal.
The investigation also unveiled the hidden role of forced labor and land appropriation in China’s growing aquaculture industry. (To be continued) – Rappler.com
The reporting for this story was part of a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project.

articles.summary: A recap of news, sports, lifestyle, entertainment, and human interest images from the Philippines and around the globe

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — On November 24, the Supreme Court of the Philippines dismissed petitions questioning the arrest of former president Rodrigo Duterte, stating they were moot since he is in the custody of the International Criminal Court (ICC).

Duterte has been detained in The Hague, the Netherlands, since March 2025 after he was arrested due to crimes against humanity. His case stemmed from his drug war and the killings allegedly committed by the Davao Death Squad.
On November 30, the former president will be the first Asian head of state to face a trial due to crimes against humanity before the ICC.

Meanwhile, the Senate began plenary deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027 on November 23, with lawmakers proposing P204.634 billion in amendments that prioritize “basic needs,” including health care and education, while cutting billions of pesos in infrastructure projects.

articles.title: Eight killed in Peruvian military helicopter crash
articles.summary: The pilot was the sole survivor of the crash during a rescue mission in a remote area known for drug trafficking.

blocks.text: Eight military personnel have been killed in a helicopter crash in a remote area of Peru known for growing and trafficking drugs.

Authorities say the aircraft came down near the town of Sanabamba during a mission to evacuate an army patrol in the valley of the Apurimac, Ene, and Mantaro rivers, known by its Spanish acronym VRAEM.
Often referred to as 'Cocaine Valley', the area is Peru's largest coca-growing valley where gangs and the remnants of the former Shining Path rebel group operate.
The Peruvian ministry of defence said the pilot was the sole survivor of the crash, the cause of which is still unknown.
In its statement, the ministry said "search and rescue operations located the aircraft and the nine military personnel who were on board".
It named the pilot as Enzo Espinoza Roque and said he was evacuated to Lima to "receive specialised medical treatment".
The aircraft was reported missing on Thursday night after rescuing three army personnel.
No further information was shared about why the group needed to be rescued, but it was confirmed that they were among those who were killed in the crash.

Joint Command of the Peruvian Armed Forces posted a tribute online extending "deepest condolences to the family members, friends, and comrades-in-arms of the members of our VRAEM Special Command who lost their lives while carrying out a military mission. May God keep them in His glory".
In February, a MI-17 helicopter crashed in southern Peru in February killing all 15 on board.
Peru, along with Colombia, is one of the world's largest producers of coca leaves and cocaine, according to the United Nations.

articles.title: Turkish officials 'destroyed' pro-opposition TV channel, owner tells BBC
articles.summary: The headquarters of Halk TV were raided last month, the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed critical of the government.

blocks.text: Turkish authorities have "destroyed" one of the country's most-watched news channels, its London-based owner has told the BBC.
Speaking to the BBC's Newshour, Cafer Mahiroğlu said that nine people connected to Halk TV were arrested this week on charges including money laundering, bribery and spreading misleading information.

Mahiroğlu said that several of his family members were among those arrested when the pro-opposition channel was taken into government control last month, adding that the allegations against him and Halk TV are "completely wrong".
The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor' Office said that two former news anchors of the channel were among the most recent group of people detained.
In a statement, prosecutors accused the anchors of producing "false reports" in exchange for money.
Authorities have also issued an arrest warrant for the channel's news coordinator Kürşad Oğuz who is "abroad", the statement said, without specifying where.
Mahiroğlu told the BBC that he could be sent to prison if he tried to return to Turkey.
"[The government] wants to be in control of the whole media... I'm more worried about my country and my democracy than my channel," he said.

The headquarters of Halk TV was raided by Turkish authorities last month, halting the channel's live broadcasts, the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan and his administration.
The government subsequently appointed a new administrator to run the channel.

Erdoğan's government controls much of the country's media, which ranks among the worst globally for press freedom, external, though the government insists that it does not detain media workers for carrying out journalistic activities.
However, the president has scaled up a crackdown on dissent since his narrow victory in the 2023 presidential election.
Earlier this month, authorities took control of pro-opposition network Sozcu TV.
Erdoğan's main challenger, mayor of Istanbul Ekrem Imamoğlu, has been jailed on corruption charges and for violating election laws, which he and his party have fiercely denied.
Hundreds of Imamoğlu's supporters have faced similar accusations, while the government has also imprisoned other campaigners, lawyers and comedians.

articles.title: EXPLAINER | Duterte at ICC: The legal feud ahead of the trial
articles.summary: This GMA News Online Explainer series breaks down the legal developments in the nine months leading to the trial"s opening on November 30, the Prosecution"s allegations against the former president,…

blocks.text: THE HAGUE – Former president Rodrigo Duterte is set to stand trial before the International Criminal Court (ICC) for his crimes against humanity case. Now, with the Office of the Prosecutor, the Defense, and the Common Legal Representatives of the Victims (CLRV) having submitted their formal trial briefs, the ICC Trial Chamber III is ready to open proceedings in a trial projected to last for months, if not years.

This GMA News Online Explainer series breaks down the legal developments in the nine months leading to the trial’s opening on November 30, the Prosecution’s allegations against the former president, the Defense’s arguments for dismissal or domestic jurisdiction, and the hopes of the 539 victim families participating in the trial.
Where the proceedings are now

After Pre-Trial Chamber I rejected the Defense’s appeal on May 21, 2026, the case was transferred to Trial Chamber III, composed of Presiding Judge Joanna Korner, Judge Keebong Paek, and Judge Nicolas Guillou.
Even before Duterte’s trial began, the ICC courtroom saw intense arguments over evidence, procedure, and the former president’s fitness.

On June 19, 2026, Trial Chamber III issued its first Directions on the Conduct of Proceedings, which established rigid filing schedules for trial briefs, evidence rosters, witness sequences, and prior recorded testimony applications under Rule 68.

Prosecutors, Duterte’s defense, and victims’ legal representatives have been locked in legal disputes over the volume of evidence, protected witness testimony, and the procedural boundaries governing which victim families may participate in the proceedings.
Why did the Defense challenge Duterte's fitness to stand trial?

In a formal request filed on May 25, Duterte’s counsel, Peter Haynes, cited a previous medical expert who found that the former president had “a partial understanding of the accusations,” and requested a comprehensive medical re-examination. On June 12, Trial Chamber III appointed a panel of three independent experts—specializing in forensic psychiatry, geriatric and behavioral neurology, and neuropsychology.

The Defense further argued on September 14 that Duterte suffered from “significant memory impairment,” preventing him from retaining recent information or reliably recalling his Lead Counsel’s name or whether he had previously pleaded guilty.

However, both the Prosecution and the CLRVs noted that the expert panel unanimously found no evidence of cognitive decline since pre-trial assessments, attributing poor test results to test underperformance and inconsistent effort.

On September 28, Trial Chamber III ruled that Duterte is fit to stand trial. To ensure his fair participation, the Chamber instructed the Registry to make special courtroom accommodations, including over-ear noise-canceling headphones, flexible sitting schedules to accommodate time-zone differences for Philippine witnesses, options for remote video-link attendance from the ICC Detention Center, and continuous health monitoring by the Court’s Medical Officer.
Why is the Defense challenging the Prosecution’s charges and evidence volume?

On August 31, Duterte’s defense team filed a sweeping challenge to the form of the charges. Haynes argued that the Prosecution’s practice of relying on “non-exhaustive illustrative incidents” subjected Duterte to charges that he described as a “literal moving target,” violating Article 67(1)(a) fair trial rights to be informed promptly and in detail of the charges.

The defense challenges the sheer volume of electronic disclosure, including an August 5 notification from the Prosecution, in which it delivered 6,909 items containing incriminating, Rule 77 defense preparation, and exculpatory records between January and July 2026. Haynes complained that combing through thousands of electronic files placed an unmanageable burden on them and infringed on Duterte’s right to adequate time and facilities to prepare a defense under Article 67(1)(b).
How is the Prosecution streamlining its evidence and witness lineup?

In response to defense objections and judicial directions, the Prosecution submitted a restructured List of Evidence on October 12, organizing its repository into seven distinct categories, with Category 1 concerning material cited in its Trial Brief.

Crucially, prosecutors offered a procedural compromise: the OTP revealed it had already removed 253 items and offered to drop nearly 7,000 additional items from its formal evidence list if the Defense agrees to stipulated facts regarding the collection of a still-redacted category of evidence.

The Prosecution filed its trial presentation strategy in an Updated List of Witnesses on November 6, providing the number of key witnesses to testify via secure audio-video link (AVL). In a previous submission, the Prosecution informed the Chamber that it intended to call witnesses through Rule 68 applications. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Sara Duterte doubts fairness of father's ICC trial, says court wants to 'make a statement'
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte said she does not expect a fair trial for her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, before the International Criminal Court, claiming the tribunal wants to "make a…

blocks.text: November 28, 2026 | 10:53am

Vice President Sara Duterte says on Nov. 26, 2026 that she would accept whatever judgment the Senate impeachment court hands down in her trial, where she faces allegations of corruption and misuse of public funds.
The Philippine STAR / Michael Varcas

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte said she does not expect a fair trial for her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, before the International Criminal Court, claiming the tribunal wants to "make a statement" following criticism from major powers.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, November 27, the vice president cited the views of China, Russia and the United States, which she said consider the ICC a political organization.

"If you look at the opinion of other countries, particularly China, Russia, in our BFF (best friends forever), the United States, they would say that this is a political organization and doesn't serve any interests at all except theirs. So on that point, we don't expect a fair trial from the ICC, particularly because this is the only remaining case in the ICC already," she said.
Duterte said she believes the tribunal wants to prove that it is right following what she described as the "ganging up" of superpowers.
"So there is no one else there that they would like to make a statement, and that's the only—that's the case of Rodrigo Duterte," she said.

The United States announced sanctions against the ICC last month over its actions against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. US President Donald Trump has vowed to dismantle the tribunal "brick by brick."

Rodrigo Duterte, 81, has been detained in The Hague since his arrest in March 2025 on an ICC warrant over alleged crimes against humanity linked to killings during his administration's anti-drug campaign.
He is scheduled to enter a plea on Monday, November 30, over killings that allegedly took place between 2011 and 2019.
The vice president also renewed her call for her father to be allowed to attend his ICC proceedings remotely, saying it is unfair to require him to attend hearings every day because of his age.
"My feelings is that, I don't have the word right now. I think it's unfair that they are demanding that he attends the trial every day as long as there is a trial, because of his age," Duterte said.

"Apparently, he cannot sit 8 hours a day on a chair. And I don't think he can focus and give his time and attention—I mean, particularly his attention—to something for 8 hours. So, I think it's unfair to demand that of an 81-year-old man," she added.
The vice president also maintained that her father's ICC case and her own impeachment proceedings were politically motivated and intended to prevent her from joining the 2028 presidential race.
The House of Representatives impeached Sara Duterte in May. Her impeachment trial is pending before the Senate, where a conviction would permanently disqualify her from holding elected office.

Meanwhile, the Senate impeachment court was discussing Article II of the Articles of Impeachment, which includes allegations involving unexplained wealth and the business interests of Duterte's family.
The impeachment trial will resume on December 1.

articles.title: Australia’s east coast deluged by storms as roads flood and damaging winds forecast for NSW and Victoria
articles.summary:
Severe weather and flood watch warnings are in place as a storm band moves from central Queensland through NSW to Victoria and Tasmania

  • Get our

blocks.text: The final weekend of Australia’s wettest spring on record for an El Niño year is delivering a deluge of storms and heavy rain.
Severe weather and flood watch warnings are in place across the eastern states as a weather band moves from central Queensland through New South Wales to Victoria and Tasmania.
The Bureau of Meteorology’s Helen Reid said El Niño attracted great interest but was only one factor to consider when looking at a season and the continent in its entirety.

“El Niño is part of it, and we have had quite a lot of rainfall in the south-east but that’s … also a balance of what we didn’t have earlier in the winter season,” she said.
Tropical humidity has drifted across the continent and is being swept into the eastern states.
“We are looking at a very active system that’s going to be affecting southern Queensland, inland NSW, Victoria and also into Tasmania,” Reid said.
Damaging winds were forecast for the NSW alpine region and Victoria’s central and eastern districts, which were also expecting heavy rainfall.
The heaviest overnight falls in Victoria were 85.4mm at Amphitheatre Reservoir in the northern Pyrenees region and 72.8mm at Bet Bet Creek in the state’s west.
Victorian State Emergency Service volunteers reported a busy 24 hours, with more than 340 calls for help to 6am on Saturday.
Most calls related to fallen trees (105), building damage (96) and flooding impacts (97).
The state’s north-east and eastern ranges can expect six-hourly rainfall totals from 55mm to 70mm on Saturday morning.

A moderate flood warning is in place for Warrill Creek in Queensland, with initial flood warnings in Tasmania for the Meander and Mersey rivers and flood watches for most of the catchments in western, central and north-east Victoria.
Meanwhile, a heatwave in the Northern Territory is easing but intensifying from severe to extreme in Western Australia’s Kimberley and Pilbara regions.

“It’s only going to be a shortlived heatwave but it is going to be a couple of hot days through there,” Reid said.
“Picking out Kununurra as an example, they’re looking at 42 or 43C for the next few days during the daytime but only dropping down to about 27C overnight.”
An offshore trough off WA’s coast would create a low-intensity heatwave stretching to just north of Perth.
Meanwhile, firefighting crews are facing another difficult day as they continue battling raging bushfires on Tasmania’s remote Flinders Island.
As other parts of Tasmania brace for heavy rains and potential flooding, crews on Flinders Island are battling a blaze that had burned 15,000 hectares by Friday - more than 10 per cent of the island.
Forecast heavy rainfall has yet to reach Flinders Island but Tasmania Fire Service incident controller Steven Richardson said it could create further challenges rather than provide relief.

“At this stage, the weather may actually create further challenges for firefighters on the ground, reducing our ability to strengthen containment lines through backburning and creating wet, slippery conditions,” he said.
“While some warnings have been downgraded, our crews are expecting another long day on the ground focusing on containment and asset protection.”

articles.title: Taiwan election: DPP gains ground but loses Taipei race
articles.summary: Taiwan's ruling DPP has made gains in local elections, winning nine of 22 local governments. But it failed to retake Taipei, where incumbent KMT Mayor Chiang Wan-an defeated challenger Puma Shen.

image.caption: Taiwanese voters lined up at schools and temples across Taipei to cast their ballots in a tight race for mayorImage: Punit Paranjpe/AFP

blocks.text: Taiwan's ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) made gains in local elections on Saturday, winning nine of the island's 22 local governments, up from five in 2022.
The opposition Kuomintang (KMT) secured 12 local governments, two fewer than in the previous elections, while the Taiwan People's Party (TPP) won one city, according to local media reports.
The elections, in which voters chose mayors and county chiefs for four-year terms, are being seen as an indication of the political mood ahead of the island's 2028 presidential elections.
President Lai Ching-te campaigned for DPP candidates, while the KMT, which traditionally performs better in local polls and favours closer ties with China, sought to retain its local strongholds.
Closely watched Taipei mayor race goes to KMT

In the most closely watched contest, incumbent Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an of the KMT defeated DPP challenger Puma Shen, ending the ruling party's hopes of regaining control of the capital for the first time since 1998.
Shen conceded defeat in front of thousands of supporters, saying the voters' decision must be respected.
"Whoever wins, it is a victory for Taiwan's democracy," he told supporters.
Chiang thanked voters for backing his administration, saying they had recognised the city's work over the past four years.

China is paying close attention to the local polls, despite not currently featuring as a key campaign issue. Taiwan's government had warned its people to be vigilant against fake news on social media, citing a Chinese disinformation campaign.

Taiwan's 22 cities and counties are currently focused on issues such as transport, childcare and the environment. While these issues do not directly impact the China policy, Beijing has repeatedly weighed in.
China has denounced DPP candidate Puma Shen, who was sanctioned by Beijing and is wanted by Chinese police over alleged separatist activities.
He entered the mayoral race as an underdog but had managed to ride a political wave that drew huge crowds to his campaign rallies.
Nevertheless, the DPP announced Saturday evening that Shen had lost his bid for mayor, which was seen as a longshot as Taipei has not elected a DPP mayor in nearly 30 years.

blocks.caption: Shen's rallies had seen throngs of supporters in Taipei, with frenzied demand for his campaign ribbons, badges and other goodiesImage: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP

blocks.text: Earlier this month, Shen said Chinese police had never contacted him and that whoever wins, Taipei's election would be a victory for democracy in the face of pressure from Beijing.

Taipei turning to a progressive candidate in what has traditionally been a KMT stronghold would be seen as "quite shameful" in Beijing, Austin Wang, political science professor at the University of Nevada, told AFP news agency.
Why China is watching Taiwan's local elections so closely
China claims Taiwan as part of its territory under its "One China" principle and has recently increased pressure on Taiwan to accept its sovereignty claims, threatening force to seize the island.
Mayor Chiang campaigned against Shen, also pulling in thousands of supporters to his rallies. Chiang is seen as a potential future presidential candidate.
What impact could the vote have on presidential elections?

Analysts have cautioned that the local elections are not a reliable barometer of how people might vote for the presidential elections in 2028. Still, Saturday's results could influence the selection process for the KMT presidential candidate.

blocks.caption: Results of local elections are generally announced on the voting day itselfImage: Ann Wang/REUTERS

blocks.text: The DPP is likely to rally behind President Lai for a reelection.
The most likely KMT candidates are Taichung's outgoing Mayor Lu Shiow-yen and parliamentary speaker Han Kuo-yu.

KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun, who's pro-Beijing stance has even alienated her from many in the party, is also viewed as a potential challenger for the party's nomination. However, she could face pressure to step down if KMT performs poorly in the local elections.

articles.title: Judge reserves decision in bestselling author Steven Galloway's defamation lawsuit
articles.summary: Steven Galloway is suing a woman and three other defendants over alleged defamatory statements published on social media and elsewhere between 2015 and 2018 regarding claims of sexual assault.

image.caption: Steven Galloway is seen at his former office at the University of British Columbia on March 31, 2014. A judge has reserved a decision on the bestselling author's defamation lawsuit after a trial that lasted over a month. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Steven Galloway is suing a woman and three other defendants over alleged defamatory statements published on social media and elsewhere between 2015 and 2018 regarding claims of sexual assault.
Galloway has sued multiple people after he was accused of sexual assault, with trial taking over a month
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 27, 2026 9:18 PM EST | Last Updated: 40 minutes ago

The B.C. Supreme Court trial has concluded in author Steven Galloway's defamation lawsuit against the woman who accused him of rape, and other defendants, with the judge reserving her decision for a later date.

Justice Neena Sharma told the courtroom that judgments take time, especially when she is hearing other, separate matters, and while she aims to release her written decision within six months, she can't promise she will meet that timeline.

The conclusion of the trial in Vancouver came moments after Sharma dismissed a last-minute application by the lawyer for Galloway's accuser to put the trial over to next year in order to deal with a contempt application involving the woman.

The trial has heard the woman, who cannot be named under a publication ban and did not testify or appear at the trial, violated a court order compelling her to sit for a discovery examination, setting off the contempt application.

The woman's lawyer, Arden Beddoes, had sought to reopen her case shortly before the trial's scheduled conclusion, saying he understood the application was to be dealt with during the trial and he intended to bring evidence related to her risk of suicide in response to it.
The court has heard Galloway is seeking millions of dollars in damages from his accuser and other defendants. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

The request to extend the trial until an expert report by a psychiatrist was finished drew a sharp response from Sharma, who questioned Beddoes about why he hadn't raised the issue before or during closing his arguments.
"That would have been the point to say, 'I'm not closing my case, I still have evidence that you need,'" the judge said during the hearing Friday.
Sharma said there was "a way to look at this as the defence changing its position on a fundamental issue at the close of submissions."
Beddoes said he didn't agree that it was a fair characterization.

items: Steven Galloway defamation trial begins in B.C. Supreme Court
Defendant in Steven Galloway case 'honestly believed' accuser's allegations: lawyer

blocks.text: Galloway denies his accuser's allegations of rape and sexual assault and he is suing the woman only identified as A.B. and three other defendants over alleged defamatory statements published on social media and elsewhere between 2015 and 2018.

Galloway's lawyer, Daniel Burnett, told Sharma he recalled making it clear at the start of the trial they would seek a negative inference to be drawn from A.B.'s absence and file a contempt application related to the discovery examination.
Several settlements
Earlier Friday, Burnett said the court had expressed "reservations" about whether the contempt application should be heard as part of the trial and the issue was left unresolved.
"So, from that point forward, nobody had any business making assumptions about what the court would decide on that point," Burnett said.
Beddoes said it was his client, not Galloway, who would suffer prejudice if she could not bring evidence about her "suicidality" during the trial.
Bestselling author Steven Galloway's defamation trial in 4th week
Sharma said A.B.'s non-attendance at trial had always been a "huge issue" in the years-long proceedings after Galloway first filed his lawsuit in 2018.
The judge said she hadn't received first-hand evidence of any kind from A.B. since an affidavit filed in 2021, though her suicide risk was "not a new issue" in the case.
A retired judge hired by the University of B.C., where Galloway was chair of creative writing, found the rape and assault claims against him unsubstantiated.

Sexual assault claims 'flat out never happened,' ex-UBC professor tells defamation trial

blocks.text: But Galloway, author of the bestselling novel The Cellist of Sarajevo, was fired from his post. He has testified his career was destroyed.

The trial has heard Galloway is seeking millions of dollars in damages from A.B. and the other defendants, along with an "explicit" finding by the court that the rape and assault allegations are false, should he win his lawsuit.
Several people originally named as defendants in the lawsuit settled with Galloway and issued public apologies before the trial began.

articles.title: Nigeria's 'ultimate hard man' who become an online meme
articles.summary: Before becoming a household name in the Nigerian film industry, Edochie built a career in broadcasting.

blocks.text: For generations of Nigerians, Pete Edochie was more than a celebrated actor.
He was Okonkwo – the fierce, proud and troubled warrior whose portrayal in Things Fall Apart made him a household name and earned him a place in the hearts of millions.
Even in death, many Nigerians still refer to him by the character's name, a testament to the enduring impact of a role that defined his career.
Edochie died on 25 November, aged 79, in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.

In 1987, Edochie starred in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel. His portrayal of Okonkwo would change his life, establishing him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors and bringing him international recognition.
The series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.
Joy Nnamdi, a fan of both the novel and its television adaptation, believes Edochie was the perfect choice for the lead role.
She said nobody else could have brought the character to life as convincingly.
"His character Okonkwo gave a face to the highly celebrated novel," she told the BBC in Nigeria's biggest city, Lagos.
The role also cemented his reputation as a hard man, a screen persona he would maintain through much of his career.
"It was very rare to see him laugh in movies. He was the ultimate tough man," Nnamdi added.
With his deep, authoritative voice, imposing presence and effortless command of African proverbs, Edochie had a way of dominating a scene without raising his voice.
Whether playing a village elder, a wealthy businessman or a feared traditional ruler, he became an enduring embodiment of patriarchal authority on screen.
Edochie went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has grown into one of the world's largest.
From Kenya to South Africa, MultiChoice's Africa Magic channels helped take his films into millions of African homes as Nollywood became a cultural phenomenon across the continent.
Although many of his films were rooted in his Igbo culture, their themes of family loyalty, inheritance disputes, spiritual beliefs and the abuse of power resonated with audiences far beyond Nigeria.
Before becoming a household name in the film industry, however, Edochie had built a successful career in broadcasting.
Born on 7 March 1947 in Zaria, northern Nigeria, he attended primary and secondary school in Kaduna before studying journalism and television at the School of Journalism and Television in the UK.
He joined the Eastern Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation in 1967, the year Nigeria's civil war broke out.
He joined the pro-separatist Voice of Biafra, and recently described the war years as the greatest personal challenge he ever faced.
"During the war, the experience that we had as Biafrans, you know, survival was difficult. Hunger was driving us into eating all sorts of nonsense," he recalled.

He rose through the ranks to hold senior management positions but then switched to acting. Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals and Billionaire's Club.
His career also bridged the transition from home-video productions to global streaming platforms.
The 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart, which became Netflix's first original Nigerian film, introduced his work to a wider international audience.
He also worked in Ghana, where he starred alongside some of the country's biggest film stars in the 2017 comedy John and John.
His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).
He also received several other accolades, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.
In recent years, Edochie found an unexpected new audience online.
His distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films became popular social media memes, introducing his work to a younger generation of Africans.
For many who had never watched Things Fall Apart or his early Nollywood films, his stern expressions became a humorous way of conveying disbelief, disapproval or exasperation at everyday situations.
But his reputation as a formidable screen presence was no joke to those who grew up watching him.
Sani Muazu recalls that parents in the northern Nigerian city of Kano would sometimes invoke Edochie's name to keep misbehaving children in check.
"They would tell you: 'Okonkwo will come and visit you if you don't stop' and we would begin acting right," he said.

"To be honest, we grew up scared of him. Even though he was on the screen and not physically present, some of his roles added to our fears because he played some popular occultic roles, and villain roles suited him."
Tributes poured in from fans and fellow actors following news of his death, with many describing him as a giant who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.
Popular actress Genevieve Nnaji paid her tribute in a post on X.

"I will let the assurance of the fact that you are a chosen one; and therefore, have returned to the most high God override my grief and heartbreak. May the heart of a true lion forever rest in peace. We love you," she wrote.
Patience Ozokwor, popularly known as Mama G, who appeared alongside Edochie in several productions, remembered him as a brilliant actor and a source of wisdom.
"He has been a father to stories that are told, like an elder sitting down telling you how things were done in those days," she told BBC News Pidgin.
"I called him any time, any day. He'll tell you what to do and what not to do."
Film director Babangida Bangis told the BBC that Edochie's death was a loss not just for Nigeria or Africa, but for the global film industry.
"Just days ago, during a seminar for filmmakers across the country, his name popped up as an example of brilliance on the screen, longevity and professionalism," he said.
"I think his loss is one for the world, not just Nigeria or Africa. We all grew up watching and loving him."
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu also mourned the veteran actor, describing his death as a major loss to the country's film industry and cultural heritage.
The president, like many admirers, singled out Edochie's portrayal of Okonkwo, saying the performance and his subsequent roles had established him as one of Nigeria's most accomplished actors.
But beyond the fame and formidable character he portrayed on screen, his family remembers a man whose greatest legacy was the importance he placed on honesty and speaking the truth.
Leo Edochie, his son, told the BBC that his father was a strong-willed man.
"Of all his legacies, I think the whole world would agree that these two were the most important: telling the truth and remaining honest," he said.
He described his father as a man who lived an exemplary life, offering a model that young people could learn from and aspire to follow.
"I don't really have a choice, but the truth is that I have to carry on that legacy for our family," he added.
Edochie's influence also extended to his family, with two of his six children, Yul and Linc Edochie, following him into the Nigerian film industry.
Yet, for an actor so closely associated with stern expressions and intimidating characters, some of his most endearing moments came when he let his guard down.
In 2021, he made a brief appearance in music star Phyno's video for the song Highway, surprising fans with a display of dance moves that showed a lighter, more playful side of the septuagenarian.
It was a refreshing reminder that the man behind the formidable screen persona could also laugh, dance and enjoy himself.

articles.title: Actual malice must be proven in cyber libel cases vs gov't officials — Supreme Court
articles.summary: Press freedom groups have long raised concerns about the use of cyber libel against Filipino journalists, especially during the presidency of Rodrigo Duterte.

blocks.text: November 28, 2026 | 9:08am
The logo of the Supreme Court at the Supreme Court Building in Manila.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui
MANILA, Philippines — To convict someone of committing cyber libel against a government officer, the prosecution must prove they acted with “actual malice,” the Supreme Court ruled.
In a statement on Friday, November 27, the Supreme Court said that “actual malice” occurs when a person making a statement despite knowing it is false or having serious doubts about its truth.
The high court clarified that prosecutors must prove this element in cyber libel cases involving public officers, warning that such cases may have a chilling effect on the public.
The clarification follows Jade Karla Tan’s acquittal of cyber libel through a decision penned by Associate Justice Jhosep Y. Lopez.
Tan was previously convicted over Facebook posts she made after plans to open a fast-food branch in their town fell through.
In the posts, she accused a mayor of corruption and alleged that a high-ranking local official demanded bribes in exchange for building and business permits.

Witnesses testified that the posts referred to Catanauan Mayor Ramon Orfanel because Tan mentioned someone “who was sitting on the highest position” and the color orange, which Orfanel used in his campaign.
The SC ruled that no actual malice was proven, saying that the lower courts only relied on Tan’s grudge and her failure to verify the claims before posting them.
In a separate concurring opinion, Senior Associate Judge Marvic Leonen agreed with the acquittal.
“There can be no enlightened citizenry if citizens live with the fear of prosecution whenever they gain the courage to call out government wrongs,” Leonen said.
Under the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012, cyber libel is committed when a defamatory statement is posted online with malice and the person referred to can be identified.
Press freedom groups have long raised concerns about the use of cyber libel against Filipino journalists, especially during the presidency of Rodrigo Duterte.

In October 2026, his son Rep. Paolo Duterte (1st District, Davao City) filed libel and cyber libel complaints against National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag, dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. and several GMA Network journalists.
