articles.title: Spain's Sanchez makes final appeal to voters before election
articles.summary: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez told people to turn out in large numbers so the country does not go "backwards." Polls suggest an end to his eight-year leftist leadership of Spain.

image.caption: Pedro Sanchez made his final pitch to voters on FridayImage: Isabel Infantes/REUTERS

blocks.text: Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Friday hit the campaign trail one last time before Spaniards head to the polls on Sunday, telling people to "vote, vote, vote" to make sure the country doesn't go "backwards."
Opinion polls point to a change in government, with the conservative People's Party (PP) slated to come out on top, bringing an end to Sanchez's eight years of leftist leadership.
Spain's general election this Sunday is also crucial because it kicks off a round of elections on the continentand because it is yet another test of the region's shift to the right.
The PP would potentially have to rely on support from the far-right anti-immigration Vox party to form the next government in Spain.
There's also a chance that the election ends in a hung parliament, with neither the right-wing coalition nor the left bloc securing a majority.

blocks.caption: Pedro Sanchez's immigration-friendly policies made him an outlier in Europe where populist parties have surged to powerImage: Isabel Infantes/REUTERS

blocks.text: Sanchez has so far campaigned on a platform of having boosted the Spanish economy when its European Union partners were struggling.
He has pointed to his policies of having increased the minimum wage and having lifted pensions in line with inflation.

But people are frustrated that the cost of living has soared and that they're not able to enjoy the fruits of economic growth, with many unable to leave their parents' house because of very high rental prices.
Spain’s housing crisis becomes main election issue
Sanchez doubles down on attempt to appeal to leftist voters
Sanchez said during his final rally in Madrid that the "elections are about moving Spain forward, not moving it backwards."

He doubled down on an attempt to appeal to left-leaning voters, telling them that a right coalition government, with far-right members in parliament, would reverse the years of social progress and gut public services.
Oscar-winning Spanish film director Pedro Almodovar was also at the rally this evening.
Sanchez wore a red T-shirt that said "the power of the people," telling people that a "progressive majority is within our reach."
Sanchez has also become the standard-bearer for Europeans frustrated with the Trump administration.
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo dismisses Sanchez's campaign of 'fear'
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo, who has said that he wants to maintain good relations with US President Donald Trump, dismissed Sanchez's campaign of "fear."
Feijoo won the most seats during elections in 2023, but he was not able to form a government.
"And when a government has nothing to offer but fear, it means it has nothing else left to offer," he told supporters at his campaign finale in the southern city of Seville.

blocks.caption: Alberto Nunez Feijoo's pitch to voters has largely focused on improving government management and the competence of public officials. Image: Matteo Secci/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," said Feijoo, who built his career running central public bodies and the northwestern Galicia region.
He has advocated for tough immigration policies and stronger border management.
Santiago Abascal, the leader of the Vox party, favors a much tougher approach, with his party having advocated for mass deportations.
Addressing a closing rally at a bullring in the eastern city of Valencia, Abascal told supporters not to "vote out of fear. Vote with courage."
"What we are up against is a criminal mafia led by a ruthless boss, a liar," he said, referring to the corruption scandals that have surrounded Sanchez and his government.

articles.title: The Indian 'Tamasha queen' whose fans paid for a show that never happened
articles.summary: A new Bollywood flim spotlights the remarkable life of dancer and singer Vithabhai Narayangaonkar.

blocks.text: Few things could keep Vithabai Narayangaonkar, one of the greatest stars of Maharashtra's folk theatre, away from the stage.
Not even, it would seem, the birth of her child.
In the 1960s, the singer, dancer and troupe leader was performing in Shikhar Shingnapur, a village in the western Indian state, when she went into labour.
"She quietly stepped behind the stage into a makeshift tent while the rest of us continued performing," her daughter, veteran folk artist Mangala Bansode, told BBC Marathi.
Outside, the restless audience kept shouting: "Where is Vitha?"
When Vithabai returned to the stage, she was cradling her newborn son, the seventh of her eight children.
"The audience was stunned, but they quietly left, saying, 'We will watch your performance later'," Bansode recalled.

Outspoken and quick-witted, Vithabai held audiences across Maharashtra in thrall for decades, earning the title of Tamasha Samradnyi – the empress of Tamasha, the state's traditional travelling folk theatre.
Now, more than two decades after her death, her life has inspired a Bollywood musical, Eetha, starring Shraddha Kapoor, and due for release on 4 December.
Directed by Laxman Utekar, Eetha is based on Yogiraj Bagul's Marathi book chronicling Vithabai's life.

Rooted in devotional poetry, Tamasha evolved into a lively mix of music, dance, comedy and drama. At its heart is Lavani, a song and dance tradition in which verses ranging from the bawdy to the politically incisive are performed to the beat of the dholki, a percussion instrument.
Eetha evokes the world of Tamasha in its heyday. Kapoor, who had never performed Lavani before, learnt to dance while wearing musical anklets weighing 4kg each.
"The lives of Tamasha artists have been very tough, so in their dance you see pain as well as joy," Kapoor recalled at a promotional event.
Many Tamasha performers, including Vithabai, came from oppressed castes, facing discrimination even as their artistry drew large crowds.

How much of that history Eetha will capture remains debated. Utekar says it is not a biopic, but his decision to rename the protagonist Vithabai Bhau Gavkar instead of Vithabai Bhau Mang Narayangaonkar has drawn criticism.

For critics, much of Vithabai's history was contained in her name – Mang identified her with a historically oppressed Dalit community, while Narayangaonkar spoke of her family's roots in Narayangaon village. Both featured in the name of the troupe she inherited from her father – Bhau-Bapu Mang Narayangaonkar Tamasha Mandal.

Vithabai spoke openly about caste and the indignities Tamasha artists faced, themes that also surfaced in her songs. In a 1960s Lavani documented by historian Shailaja Paik, she rebuked men for lewd gestures, reminding them she danced to earn a living, not to please them.
It was a livelihood she had inherited from generations of performers in her family.
Like her son, Vithabai was born during a Tamasha performance, in 1935. Her mother, Shanta, had continued touring with her husband Bhau's troupe throughout her pregnancy.

Vithabai joined a theatre group at eight and her father's troupe at 13, soon becoming its star. After her father and co-leader Bapu died in quick succession, she took over the troupe with her husband and cousin.
Her career flourished during Tamasha's golden age, when productions grew more elaborate, drawing on mythology, history and contemporary life, says folk arts scholar Sukhada Khandge.
Khandge, who watched Vithabai perform as a child, recalls her sparkling eyes and commanding presence. She was as expressive with her face as she was with her feet.
Her fame carried her beyond Maharashtra.

During India's war with China in 1962, Vithabai performed for soldiers in the North-East Frontier Agency, now largely Arunachal Pradesh, braving freezing conditions just three months after giving birth, Bansode says.
At a conference in 1996, she recalled meeting soldiers from the historically oppressed Mahar and Mang communities at the frontier.

"Our Mahar-Mang soldiers were expected to fight and lay down their lives defending the nation, but the very same people would not even allow our bridegroom to pass through the village entrance," she said.

Despite offers from leading filmmakers, including Raj Kapoor, and roles in Marathi cinema, Vithabai refused to leave theatre. Film fame, she felt, would benefit her alone, while her troupe supported some 50 families, Bansode says.
There was a tenderness, too, in her relationship with audiences.
In his book on Vithabai's life, which inspired Eetha, Yogiraj Bagul recounts a performance in Mumbai during Diwali in 1971.

Despite the threat of rain, spectators insisted on buying tickets, saying the money would be their Bhau Beej gift to Vithabai if the show was cancelled – a festival celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters.
When the rain came, people left chanting: "Bhau Beej, Bhau Beej."
No one asked for their money back.

But Vithabai's fortunes failed to match her fame. Her husband, Maruti Sawant, mismanaged the troupe's finances and took loans in her name, family members say. By the time she left him in 1982, she was heavily indebted.
Bagul also writes about a 1986 column in a Marathi daily that revealed how the empress of Tamasha was now travelling on public buses and staying in cheap accommodation.
Despite public support, Vithabai was forced to disband her troupe in 1990 – the same year she received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, one of India's highest performing arts honours.
Vithabai successfully campaigned for government pensions for Tamasha artists. But many of the hardships she knew persist today, says Marathi writer Pradnya Daya Pawar.

Troupes spend nearly eight months a year on the road, with performers struggling to feed their children and educate them, she says. Despite government aid, many remain indebted to private moneylenders.
Vithabai's financial struggles persisted until her death in January 2002. Her family could pay only 4,000 of the 5,900 rupees owed to the Pune hospital where she died, the Times of India reported.
Fellow artists and admirers chipped in to bring her body home to Narayangaon.
Maharashtra has since instituted a lifetime achievement award in her name.
Eetha could now introduce Vithabai to a generation that never saw her perform, though the changes to her name have left some uneasy.
Marathi writer Pragya Daya Pawar argues that omitting the reference to Vithabai's caste risks obscuring the difficulties she confronted.
"It erases the social location, struggle and resistance that shaped her remarkable journey, reducing an extraordinary artist's story to a purely individual achievement," she says.
But Bansode, who spent years performing alongside her mother, says there is much to celebrate.
"The name doesn't matter to me. I am simply proud that a film is being made about my mother," she says.

articles.title: Victorian election 2026 live: voters head to the polls as Coalition seeks to topple Labor – latest news
articles.summary: Follow live updates today and results tonight as Labor’s Ben Carroll and Liberal leader Jess Wilson seek victory in Victoria’s state election

blocks.text: Key events

items: 51m agoWelcome

blocks.text: Jess Wilson and Ben Carroll ‘confident’ as they cast votes

My colleague Benita Kolovos has informed me that the premier, Ben Carroll, voted at his old primary school St Christophers in Airport West, while the Liberal leader, Jess Wilson, voted at Our Lady of Good Counsel primary school in Deepdene.
Wilson told a reporter at the polling booth she was “confident of the victories statewide today” and downplayed what it would mean for her to become the first elected female premier in Victoria.
She said:
double quotation markIt’s not about me. If I’m given that honour, we’re absolutely ready and I’m ready. But this is about Victorians and fixing this state.
Carroll told reporters he was “fighting every day” for the state. He said:

double quotation markI am confident because I’m getting that message. I’ve got it all day yesterday. People do feel like they’ve been sold down the river by the Liberal party, after 50% of Victorians voted, to come out with a radical privatisation agenda around kinder, renewables and water. People do feel very angry about that.

blocks.caption: Ben Carroll and his wife, Fiona Rothville, and their daughter, Madeline, at St Christopher's primary school in Airport West. Photograph: Con Chronis/AAP

blocks.text: Who are the leaders?

Going into the election, the Labor government is led by the premier, Ben Carroll. Carroll, who has only led Labor since late July, became leader after a spill against Jacinta Allan. Allan herself only became leader after the resignation of Daniel Andrews, who led Labor to the “Dan-slide” of 2022.

Victorian Labor has never won an election after changing leaders and this time they have done it twice. But Carroll has made an effort to distance himself from his predecessors saying, “I will do things differently”.

blocks.caption: The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, outside the Olivia Newton-John Cancer Research Institute in Heidleberg, in Melbourne, on Tuesday. Photograph: James Ross/AAP

blocks.text: Jess Wilson is the Liberal leader, hoping to become the next premier. She became leader after a period of instability in the Victorian Liberal party that saw three leaders since the last election.
If she wins, she will be the youngest person to lead Victoria and the first woman to be elected premier. (Both Joan Kirner and Jacinta Allan became premier after their leaders resigned).

blocks.caption: Jess Wilson during a visit to an early voting centre at Heidelberg Scots Uniting Church in Melbourne on Tuesday. Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAP

blocks.text: There’s also the minor parties.
The Victorian Greens are led by Ellen Sandell. In 2014, she became the first Greens MP to be elected to Victoria’s lower house after campaigning against local toll roads.

Sandell hopes to take a page from progressive leaders around the world such as the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani. At the News24 leaders’ debate, Sandell outperformed Ben Carroll, according to an audience poll.

blocks.caption: The Victorian Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, in Melbourne. Photograph: Con Chronis/AAP

blocks.text: Leading the insurgent One Nation is Warren Pickering. He is running in the marginal Labor seat of Pakenham in Melbourne’s outer east. The former Australian army combat engineer was also a unsuccessful One Nation Senate candidate.
At the News24 leaders’ debate, Pickering was outperformed by Sandell but audiences still preferred him over Carroll.

blocks.caption: The One Nation Victoria leader, Warren Pickering. Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAP

blocks.text: What the polls say
The Coalition is poised to win 55 of 88 lower-house seats according to a YouGov poll of more than 4300 voters, commissioned by the Herald Sun and News24 and published on election eve.
One Nation would gain 12 seats and the Greens would add five more MPs to their pack of three, according to the analysis conducted between 6 and 23 November.
A Newspoll reported by The Australian late on Thursday had the Coalition extending to a 15-point lead over Labor on a two-party preferred basis.
The Coalition’s lead of 57.5% to Labor’s 42.5% compares with the Coalition’s 55-45 lead in October before the election campaign began.
If the polls are correct the Victorian Greens will have their most successful campaign on record, gaining between 13% and 17% of primary votes.
The party leader, Ellen Sandell, received the second-highest approval rating among undecided voters during the campaign’s only four-way leaders debate on 17 November.
– Australian Associated Press
Welcome
Good morning, and welcome to the Victorian election live blog.
I’m Josh Taylor and I will be taking you through until later this afternoon.

Going into today, polls suggest the Coalition will comfortably win majority government, while Labor faces an electoral wipeout after 12 years in government, with suggestions the premier, Ben Carroll, could lose his own seat.
More than 2.2 million people had already voted as of Friday, according to the Victorian Electoral Commission, meaning nearly half of those eligible have already cast their vote.
Just as well, too, given the weather in Victoria today. Those democracy sausage sandwiches will be a little wet today with all the rain.

There is a flood warning for parts of west, central and north-east Victoria, with possible minor flooding from Saturday morning for rivers including the Yarra. Rain is likely to continue throughout the day, easing into the evening with up to 30mm of rain expected in Melbourne.
Now let’s get into it.

articles.summary: In a news release posted on its Facebook page, the upper chamber announced it finished marathon deliberations on next year"s budget “after days of rigorous plenary debate.”

blocks.text: Published November 28, 2026 8:29am
The Senate on Saturday wrapped up its deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027.
In a news release posted on its Facebook page, the upper chamber announced it had finished marathon deliberations on next year’s budget “after days of rigorous plenary debate.”
During its deliberations, the Senate said it advanced the proposed budgets of major government institutions, namely:

items: Congress of the Philippines - P27.89 billion
Judiciary - P84.132 billion
Department of National Defense - P326.9 billion
Department of Health - P378.629 billion
Department of Public Works and Highways - P587.9 billion
Department of Agriculture - P175 billion
Commission on Higher Education (CHED) - P38.821 billion
Department of Migrant Workers - P11.894 billion

blocks.text: The Senate added its deliberations also covered peace, social, and regional development offices, including the Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity (OPAPRU) at P9.304 billion; National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) at P1.738 billion; Marawi Compensation Board (MCB) at P1.247 billion; National Amnesty Commission (NAC) at P266.6 million; Commission on Filipinos Overseas (CFO) at P187.8 million; and Metropolitan Baguio City, La Trinidad, Itogon, Sablan, Tuba, and Tublay Development Authority (MBLISTTDA) at P45.4 million.

The upper chamber said it took up the proposed allocations of other executive offices, including the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) at P8.514 billion; National Intelligence Coordinating Agency (NICA) at P3.086 billion; National Security Council (NSC) at P1.122 billion; Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) at P335 million; Film Development Council of the Philippines (FDCP) at P311 million; Philippine Racing Commission (Philracom) at P202.8 million; Movie and Television Review and Classification Board (MTRCB) at P69.742 million; Optical Media Board (OMB) at P53.462 million; and other agencies. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
articles.summary: While many people find a diagnosis for ADHD or autism affirming, a government-funded clinic in Sweden is re-assessing people who feel it does not reflect them.

blocks.text: Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRIS
Johanna, 24, began questioning her ADHD diagnosis when she discovered it could act as a barrier to becoming a police officer
ByKate Bowie
Global Health
Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.
Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.
But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.
This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.
At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.
But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.
Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police.
"I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.
If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police.

The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis.

The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate.

And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable – and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions.
Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Psychologist Sebastian Lundström runs the clinic, which operates one day a month

blocks.text: Psychologist Sebastian Lundström runs the clinic, which operates one day a month
Barred from jobs
Like Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier.

This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally.

Since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (£1,100) privately.
When Freya was referred to the clinic, she says she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free.
Johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers.

But as she grew into adulthood, she says she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate.
Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes.

Johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer.
What is an ADHD or autism reassessment?

Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test.

The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present.
"This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian Lundström, the clinic's lead psychologist.
The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the new assessment.

Lundström says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older.
But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not currently showing symptoms is a contested approach.
"We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," says Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families.
"Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds.

Symptoms could reappear later in life, he says. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support."
Lundström says he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support.
During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnoses but the psychologist said, "we still feel that you meet the criteria".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis as she feels she was misdiagnosed

blocks.text: Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis as she feels she was misdiagnosed
'I was stuck'
Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma.
"I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it."
It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, Lundström explains.
"It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month.

Before opening the clinic, Lundström conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group.
"It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds.

During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to Lundström, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment.
The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry.
"It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way."
In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women.

During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ.
Freya says she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment.

But the doctors are adamant that they do not just give attendees the outcome they want. They conduct other checks such as assessing body language and communication skills, speaking to younger patients' parents, and checking medical files for ongoing treatment.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people, says it is important to remember autism and ADHD are lifelong conditions

blocks.text: Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people, says it is important to remember autism and ADHD are lifelong conditions
Fears about stigma
The opening of the clinic has drawn criticism from those who fear it sends the wrong message about autism and ADHD.

"The clinic presents neurodiversity and autistic people as a bad thing, like we are a problem that needs to be fixed - we are not," says Jenny Hedin, from charity Organiserade Autister Västernorrland, an advocacy organisation run by and for autistic adults.

Hedin, who is autistic and has ADHD, warns that people who can successfully "mask" or mimic neurotypical behaviour might feel under pressure to lose their diagnosis in order to be better accepted by society.
"That is especially a problem with women and girls, because girls are usually great at masking," she adds.
Others say the focus should be on changing the rules that make it difficult for people with ADHD or autism to pursue certain careers.
Eric Donell, the chairman of Riksförbundet Attention, a national Swedish charity, lobbies to remove employment restrictions affecting neurodivergent people, which he says are unfair.

He stresses that for many people, getting a diagnosis is extremely important. "Instead of asking people to get rid of their diagnosis, sometimes we should just ask whether the rules themselves are justified," he says.
Reassessments risk becoming "a way of adapting the individual to society instead of adapting society to human differences," he adds.
'Magic spell'
People from the UK, Denmark, Norway and Germany have also been in touch for reassessment, says Lundström, but they have been turned away, as the clinic only serves locals.
Georgina, 35, from the UK, contacted the clinic because she wants to have the autism diagnosis she received at 25 "removed".
"It felt like a magic spell, that I'd get this label and the world would be more understanding," she says.
Instead, she says, her colleagues belittled her.

Georgina has since been offered an NHS reassessment. The process is the same as the original assessment she went through, and can result in patients receiving more diagnoses, fewer diagnoses or no change.
The Swedish reassessment clinic says they generally would not apply new or additional diagnoses to people - something Georgina was attracted to.

"The situation where you can go in and then come out with other labels... that's really off-putting," she says. For now, she has decided not to undergo an NHS reassessment. Instead, she is trying to find out how often a diagnosis is reconsidered, before deciding whether to go ahead.
Back in Sweden, a few hours after Freya entered the clinic, she re-emerges from a consultation room. The doctors here have found that, right now, she does not meet the criteria for an ADHD diagnosis.
She says it is "confirmation" that she was right to question her diagnosis.
"Now, finally, I have the same opportunity as everyone else."

articles.title: Purse found of woman, 24, swept from California beach three weeks ago
articles.summary:
Se Nah Park was overwhelmed by a wave at the notorious Panther Beach

The purse of a 24-year-old who was swept into the ocean at a notorious

blocks.text: The purse of a 24-year-old who was swept into the ocean at a notorious California beach three weeks ago was found on Wednesday, as the west coast saw record high king tides.
The Santa Cruz county sheriff’s office confirmed that Se Nah Park’s purse was found by a beachgoer at 4 Mile Beach, south of Panther Beach, where she was swept away into the ocean on 8 November.
According to a GoFundMe started by Park’s friends, Park and five others had gathered around a bonfire beyond the keyhole at Panther Beach that night.
Four members of the group, including Park, attempted to make their way back through the keyhole when a powerful wave struck, sweeping Park into the ocean.
The three individuals managed to get back up the cliffslide, but tragically, Park did not.
Three weeks later, Park’s body has not been located yet, but the discovery of her purse may lead her community closer towards locating her body. .
The coast guard suspended the active search efforts to find Park on 9 November.

“Given the extensive search effort of the surrounding area and environmental conditions, we have suspended active search efforts pending further developments,” Lt Max Holloway, Sector San Francisco search and rescue mission coordinator, said at the time.

“We worked closely with our partner agencies and exhausted all available resources in our attempt to locate Ms Park. Our deepest condolences are with her family and loved ones,” the statement concluded.
In the weeks since, Park’s family and friends have not given up on their search efforts.
Her family and friends continue to “hold on to the hope that Senah can be found and brought home to rest”, her friends shared in a message on GoFundMe.

articles.title: OpenAI countersues Apple for allegedly stealing trade secrets
articles.summary:
Lawsuit also alleging pressure on hardware suppliers comes after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching employees

OpenAI sued

blocks.text: OpenAI sued Apple on Friday, accusing the company of ⁠stealing its trade secrets ​and discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices.
The suit, filed in northern California federal court, comes after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching its employees to gain access to its technology.

OpenAI filed the counterclaims ⁠in California federal court on Friday, saying that Apple’s employment practices were designed to “trap” employees and prevent them from working on competitors’ technology.
OpenAI is developing AI-enabled personal electronic devices that threaten to “outcompete Apple on what ⁠Apple views as its own turf”, the company said in its Friday court filing.

OpenAI said in the filing that Apple ​gained confidential information by rehiring a former employee who worked ‌at OpenAI for six months. In ‌that time, the employee gained access to specific information on a new device as well as OpenAI’s roadmap for future hardware ‌products.
“Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place,” OpenAI said.
Apple denied using the rehired employee to access OpenAI’s confidential information and denied trying to suppress competition in AI device manufacturing.
“OpenAI’s counterclaims are a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple’s lawsuit,” Apple said in a Friday statement.
Tensions between the two tech companies have escalated as the intensifying race to develop AI products fuels competition for ‌talent and proprietary technology.
Apple sued OpenAI and the former Apple employees Tang Tan and Chang Liu in July, alleging misappropriation of its trade secrets to benefit the ChatGPT owner’s foray into consumer hardware.

Tan, ​a 24-year Apple employee who was a vice-president of product design for iPhone and Apple Watch, was part of the group that launched the AI device startup io Products before it was acquired by OpenAI in 2025.

OpenAI and the employees have denied those allegations and said that Apple’s lawsuit depended on its unauthorized monitoring of Liu’s personal messages after he stopped working for Apple. OpenAI and ⁠attorneys for Tan and Liu did not immediately respond to a request for comment on ​Friday’s court filing.

In Friday’s filing, OpenAI criticized ​Apple for encouraging employees to do work on ​their personal Apple devices and accounts, then preventing those employees from an orderly separation of work and ​personal accounts when they leave ‌for new jobs.

OpenAI said ​that Apple continues to access ​former employees’ personal devices and accounts after they leave the company, enabling Apple to “monitor and ensnare departing employees” when they leave for competitors.
OpenAI said that 400 employees have left Apple for OpenAI so far, and Apple wants to intimidate other employees from leaving to find other tech companies.

articles.title: US disables ship in Gulf of Oman under Iran blockade
articles.summary: The United States said it was continuing "to strictly enforce the blockade" of Iran's ports. Meanwhile, Kuwait summoned Iran's ambassador over a strike that killed two Italian technicians.

image.caption: US Central Command (CENTCOM) said Washington's forces fired on a ship that had left Bandar Abbas and entered the Gulf of OmanImage: US Central Command/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: The United States military on Friday announced it had fired at a ship in the Gulf of Oman that it said was violating Washington's blockade of Iranian ports.
A US aircraft fired "precision munitions" in the stern of the Palau-flagged Pacific Archer, US Central Command (CENTCOM), said, adding that it "continues to strictly enforce the [US] blockade."
CENTCOM oversees US forces in the Middle East.
The statement said that "the ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled" and stressed that "the civilian crew was unharmed."
It said that the ship had left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas.
The US blockade has disabled six ships and redirected 158 others.
Washington launched its blockade of Iranian ports in mid-July following the collapse of an agreement with Tehran.
The war broke out in February after the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran, which prompted Tehran to impose its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.
Kuwait summons Iran ambassador over strike on military site
Meanwhile, Kuwait summoned Iran's ambassador after a Thursday drone strike killed two Italian technicians at a Kuwaiti military site.
A Kuwaiti citizen and a Pakistani citizen were also injured and hospitalized in the attack.
Iran has denied responsibility for the strike.
Iran denies role in drone strike that killed 2 Italians in Kuwait
Kuwait's Foreign Ministry said Deputy Foreign Minister Hamad Al-Mashaan condemned the "continued Iranian attacks" and said Kuwait reserved its right to self-defense.
The two technicians worked for Rheinmetall Italia, a subsidiary of the German defense firm Rheinmetall.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the strike, calling on "all parties to exercise restraint."

Guterres is "deeply concerned by the continued escalation in the region," according to his spokesman, Stephane Dujarric. "Renewed hostilities would have devastating consequences for the region and beyond."

articles.title: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
articles.summary: China's immense clout now also has the flex of soft power. Critics and dissidents say their voices are being drowned out.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
China's economic might is drowning out our voices, say activists and dissidents
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.
"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."

It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.

But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.
It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .
But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades

blocks.text: Image source, Dolkun Isa
Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades

Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls, Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.

China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power, drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.
Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.

Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.
The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Sheznhen, a rich, buzzing city on the soth-eastern coast, has emerged as one of China's star attractions for tech and tourism

blocks.text: Sheznhen, a rich, buzzing city on the soth-eastern coast, has emerged as one of China's star attractions for tech and tourism
China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.
"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities."

China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.
This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.

In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded.

His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.
That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.
"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping have held three summits so far this year

blocks.text: Donald Trump and Xi Jinping have held three summits so far this year
Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".
The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? "We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas."
Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.
"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.
These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.
In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Consul-General Wei Xiaodong (in the red scarf) pictured sending people off in January

blocks.text: Image source, Chinese Consulate General in Istanbul's WeChat account
Consul-General Wei Xiaodong (in the red scarf) pictured sending people off in January

"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.

Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.
The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.
"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.
Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.

Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China.
"She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim.
"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Xinjiang has been sold as an exotic destination, bringing in huge numbers of tourists

blocks.text: Xinjiang has been sold as an exotic destination, bringing in huge numbers of tourists
When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity.

The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial".
"It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says.
"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable."
These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say.
Abduweli Ayup, a prominent Uyghur linguist based in Norway, has observed former activists going off the grid after returning from these trips.

"Some have deleted their social media accounts and cut off contact with us," he says. "Others appear to be suspicious of us or concerned that what we were doing would compromise theirs or their families' safety."
The fact that only a few get selected to visit the homeland "creates confusion within the diaspora," says Tibetan activist Karma Rinchen.
"They get sidelined when they return... Very sadly, our suspicions that some of them are feeding information back to the Chinese authorities have turned out to be true."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Karma Rinchen's parents were among thousands who fled Tibet alongside the Dalai Lama in 1959

blocks.text: Image source, Karma Rinchen
Karma Rinchen's parents were among thousands who fled Tibet alongside the Dalai Lama in 1959

Rinchen serves as information secretary in the Tibetan government-in-exile in the northern Indian town of Dharamshala. His parents were among thousands who followed their spiritual leader Dalai Lama into exile after China annexed Tibet.

Over the decades, waves of others have fled Chinese rule seeking greater freedom or asylum from Beijing's crackdowns - dissidents and student activists in the wake of the Tiannanmen Square massacre; lawyers, journalists, purged officials and critics in the years after, and, more recently, Hong Kong saw a steady exodus build as the pro-democracy movement was crushed.
Many have kept on fighting. But now, they say, Beijing's might is chipping away at their struggle, making it ever harder to stand up to the Chinese Communist Party.

"Many among us have been separated from our families for generations and are eager to set foot on Tibet soil," Rinchen says. "This is exactly the kind of desperation the Communist Party seeks to target."
But he adds this only means communities have to "work harder to make sure their voices are heard".

blocks.caption: Image caption, A memorial for Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen who set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
A memorial for Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen who set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York

"For Tibetans, this is not something we can simply walk away from. Our struggle is about our identity, our culture, our religion and the basic rights of our people. We have been doing this work for many decades, and we have learned to remain patient and persistent," Rinchen adds.
For many, that persistence continues to be tested on a personal level.
Uyghur musician Mirkamel Tourghoun has lived as a refugee in Paris since 2008, spending most of his time writing music and making films about Uyghur culture.
The 42-year-old has chosen the painful path of cutting off contact with his family who remain in Urumqi.
In January, he received a call from someone claiming to be an official from the city.
"What if we get rid of all this [political] pressure, and allow you to return and see your parents? Do you have such plans?" the caller asked.
"What's happened in the past is in the past. You should turn a new page. The pen is in your own hand."
The official claimed his father was gravely ill and that time was running out to see him. "It's emotional blackmail," Mirkamel says.
He declined the official's invitation: "Tell my family to forget they ever had a child like me. There is no other solution."
* Name changed on request to protect interviewee's identity

articles.title: The future of the notwithstanding clause is now up to political leaders
articles.summary: The task of governing the use of the notwithstanding clause has been left to the players in the political arena. If invoking the clause is to become politically difficult again, it will be up to…

image.caption: The Supreme Court ruled on Friday that Quebec's secularism law, which pre-emptively used the notwithstanding clause to temporarily override certain Charter rights, was largely valid. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Two weeks after he pieced together the "kitchen accord," Jean Chrétien stood in the House of Commons as justice minister to present a new constitutional resolution, including a Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
In his remarks on that momentous occasion, Chrétien made a specific effort to defend the presence in the Charter of an "override" clause.

"The effect of this provision is, first, that it will be politically very difficult for a government to introduce without very good reason a measure which applies notwithstanding the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in the Constitution," he said on the afternoon of Nov. 20, 1981.

items: Supreme Court of Canada rules Quebec's secularism law is constitutionally valid
Advocate ready to continue fight as Sask. school pronoun policy heads to Supreme Court
Supreme Court to rule on minority rights debate

blocks.text: Chrétien quoted a prominent lawyer — Alan Borovoy, the general counsel for the Canadian Civil Liberties Association — who said the notwithstanding clause would be a "red flag for opposition parties and the press."
"This will make it politically difficult for a government to override the Charter," Chrétien quoted Borovoy as saying. "Political difficulty is a reasonable safeguard for the Charter."

Forty-five years and one week later, amid growing concern that the clause is now being invoked too easily and too casually by governments and legislatures to pass laws that would otherwise be found to violate the rights of Canadians, the Supreme Court of Canada delivered a landmark ruling on the political compromise of 1981.

The court upheld the Quebec legislature's use of the clause in the case of Bill 21 and it did not find that there should be new limits on how the clause can be used. A majority of justices did find that the invocation of the clause does not prevent a court from publicly declaring that the rights of Canadians are being violated — a measure that may, in future, make it somewhat harder for governments to do so.

But the larger task of governing the use of the notwithstanding clause has been left to the players in the political arena. If the notwithstanding clause is to become politically difficult again, it will be up to political actors.
'The courts have a crucial role to play'

The question of whether courts might provide "declaratory relief" — a judicial declaration on whether rights have been unreasonably infringed, but without invalidating the law in question — even after the notwithstanding clause has been invoked had split the governments that filed arguments with the Supreme Court.

The federal government as well as the governments of Manitoba and British Columbia thought it permissible and potentially useful. Ontario, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Quebec were opposed (Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon reiterated his province's opposition to declaratory relief on Friday).
The seven justices of the Supreme Court were also split, but with the majority in favour.

"The five-year expiry period set out in [the notwithstanding clause], which corresponds to the maximum duration of the House of Commons or a legislative assembly under s. 4 of the Charter, is clearly intended to place in the hands of the electorate the choice of whether to renew the override provision," Justice Nicholas Kasirer wrote in Friday's ruling.
"Furthermore, the court's opinion is useful for the public, particularly where a vulnerable minority is affected by an overriding statute."
'A full attack on Charter rights': Critics warn of fallout from Bill 21 ruling

Justices Andromache Karakatsanis and Michelle O'Bonsawin concurred that, "courts have a crucial role to play in dialogue between the legislatures and electorate by informing both of the scope of a Charter right and whether and to what extent it is infringed by a statute that invokes the notwithstanding clause."

That courts can offer comment even after the notwithstanding clause has been invoked also goes some way toward answering concerns about recent "pre-emptive" uses of the clause — when governments invoke the clause even before a court has had a chance to pass judgment on the law.

"The court confirmed that Canadians have the right to know when their Charter rights have been unjustifiably infringed when the notwithstanding clause has been invoked," Sean Fraser, the federal justice minister, said in a statement on Friday. "This is an important part of ensuring transparency, accountability and a healthy democracy."
That may be of limited solace to those whose rights are in question. But it points back to the political arena.
The price of liberty?

Even if one disagrees with all previous uses of the clause there might still be a case for what Chrétien called a "safety valve" (one of those who pushed for the clause was Allan Blakeney, the NDP premier of Saskatchewan). And even critics of the clause might need to wrestle with arguments that there could be significant downsides to doing away with it — that, in the absence of a notwithstanding clause, courts might only become more politicized, with political leaders more incentivized to appoint judges who will decide a certain way (as it is in the United States).

A future court may some day decide that a particular use of the notwithstanding clause has gone too far (in Friday's ruling, three justices seemed to allow that there could be some theoretical outer limits). For now, the options for outright overriding the override may be limited to either the difficult (constitutional negotiations to amend the Charter) or the dangerous (reviving the federal Parliament's power to disallow provincial laws).
If the court had ruled on Friday that there were significant legal limits on the use of clause, the result could have been a constitutional crisis.
Carney says his government won't use notwithstanding clause following Supreme Court ruling

At the federal level — where the notwithstanding clause has never been invoked — Sen. Peter Harder has proposed a bill that would at least establish new rules and requirements around any use of the clause by Parliament. Under Harder's bill, for instance, the support of two-thirds of MPs would be required to invoke the clause.
It would, in other words, make it somewhat more difficult to invoke the clause.

Eugene Forsey, the late senator and constitutional scholar, once colourfully described the notwithstanding clause as a "dagger pointed at the heart of our fundamental freedoms." One might agree with that sentiment and yet still agree with Roy McMurtry, the attorney general of Ontario in 1981, who said that "political accountability is the best safeguard against any improper use of the 'override clause.'"

If it has become too easy to invoke the notwithstanding clause in recent years, it is still likely not for the court to rewrite the Charter — to change the result of a compromise brokered by political actors. Rather, it suggests that political accountability has been lacking.
"For those who remain concerned about the override clause, let me remind them that it has been said that the price of liberty is eternal vigilance," Chrétien told the House in November 1981.
It is actually unclear who, if anyone, ever actually said that. But the sentiment might still be worthy.

"Pressure groups must remain vigilant," Chrétien said, commending the "vigilance" of women who were then pushing for Section 28 of the Charter, on gender rights, to be excluded from the notwithstanding clause. (On Friday, the Court found Section 28 did not invalidate Bill 21.)
Vigilance may not be the most satisfying answer. But it might be the best or only one available.

articles.title: Prosecutors seek 25-year prison term for 'poison seller' Kenneth Law
articles.summary: The Canadian man, who pleaded guilty to 14 counts of aiding and abetting suicide earlier this year, will be sentenced at a later date.

blocks.text: Canadian prosecutors are seeking a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries.
Kenneth Law pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.
The 61-year-old will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.
During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.
If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.
As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".
"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.
She also said Law's motives were financial.

"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.
Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for many of their battles with mental illness.
He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims.

"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."
Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.
The sentencing hearing on Friday followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.
Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.
Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.
If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

articles.title: Lululemon founder makes 'egregious' remarks about women at Calgary leadership forum
articles.summary: CBC News has confirmed with two attendees that Chip Wilson's comments included that women aren't having as many children as men want, that birth control is crucial to women's professional development…

image.caption: Lululemon founder Chip Wilson is shown in Vancouver in September 2022. Wilson is under fire for comments he made at a women's leadership forum in Calgary on Monday. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New

CBC News has confirmed with two attendees that Chip Wilson's comments included that women aren't having as many children as men want, that birth control is crucial to women's professional development and that the top female brands are run by men because men know what looks good on women's bodies.
Chip Wilson's comments include that men know what looks good on women's bodies
It was meant to be an intimate chat about entrepreneurship with the founder of Lululemon.

Instead, Chip Wilson is under fire for his "egregious" comments about women's bodies and reproductive choices, which reportedly included his assertions that men are importing brides from Thailand to have their children.

"It sounds like you’re painting a future reminiscent of The Handmaid’s Tale," Nuvyn Peters, the CEO of non-profit Axis Connects, told Wilson during the fireside chat on Monday at the Axis Connects Leadership Forum in Calgary, referring to Margaret Atwood's 1985 dystopian novel.

More than 700 business leaders attended the women's forum, where some of the speakers included former Alberta premier Jason Kenney, Olympic ice dancing gold medallist Tessa Virtue, musician Jann Arden and Wilson — the billionnaire founder of Lululemon Athletica who stepped down as company CEO in 2013.
Wilson's talk does not appear to be posted anywhere online. But CBC News has confirmed with two attendees at the forum that his comments, first reported by the Globe and Mail, are correct.
A screengrab of an Instagram post by Axis Connects from Oct. 1 advertises Lululemon founder Chip Wilson as a speaker at its Nov. 23 leadership forum in Calgary. (@axisconnects/Instagram)

They include that women aren't having as many children as men want, that birth control is crucial to women's professional development and that the top female brands are run by men because men know what looks good on women's bodies.

Wilson, 71, who was born in Los Angeles and has dual American-Canadian citizenship, also said that men are resorting to importing brides from other countries like Thailand, according to the attendees who spoke with CBC News.
Calgary career coach Madeleine Natale was at Monday's event and described Wilson's comments as "egregious."

"Coming on the heels of the empowering talk by Jann Arden, it felt like the wind was knocked right out of my sails," Natale said. "In this day and age, attention is one of the most precious gifts we can give. It didn't take me long to realize that my attention was not a gift I wanted to give during that talk."
'Concern and disappointment'

Wilson's event at the women-focused leadership forum was advertised online as an "intimate fireside chat" and an "honest conversation about how a serial entrepreneur thinks, builds, struggles and keeps moving forward."

CBC News reached out to Wilson but has not yet heard back. But a spokesperson for him told the Globe and Mail earlier this week, "This is an effort to discount Chip Wilson’s record of mentoring women who have become executives and entrepreneurs in their own right to drive revenue with a clickbait headline."

items: Lululemon founder Chip Wilson says pants 'don't work' for some bodies

blocks.text: It's not Wilson's first controversy. He stepped down as Lululemon CEO in 2013 during the fallout from his comments that seemed to blame people's bodies for an issue the company was having with its pants being too sheer. That year, the company had recalled nearly one-fifth of its pants because of the problem.
"Quite frankly, some women's bodies just actually don't work for it," Wilson said in a Bloomberg TV interview. "It's really about the rubbing through the thighs, how much pressure is there."
A Lululemon store is shown in Toronto in November 2025. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

Wilson, who remains one of Lululemon's top shareholders, also came under fire in 2024 for comments blasting the company's inclusion and diversity efforts, in which he objected to the company's use of models with a range of body types.
Axis Connects, a non-profit that works to advance women in business leadership roles, said Wilson's comments on Monday don't align with its values.

"We recognize that several comments made by Chip Wilson at the leadership forum were offensive and inconsistent with the values and mission of Axis Connects," the organization said in a statement to CBC News.
"We understand why those remarks caused concern and disappointment among members of our community."

items: Lululemon founder faces backlash for blasting company's diversity, inclusion efforts

blocks.text: Natale, the career coach, said she's "very disappointed" by what she heard Wilson say on Monday, but she also wants the conversation to move on from one person's voice.
"I am choosing not to give these words any more of my energy than that," she said.

She lamented that Wilson's comments have received so much attention, "when so many other women's voices from the conference should be amplified." Arden, for instance, spoke about adapting to change and "held everyone's rapt attention," Natale said.
"This is a moment in time where we can all think a little more deeply about the challenges women continue to face in leadership."
Lululemon founder steps down
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.
