articles.title: Palace, several senators reject proposed coffee tax
articles.summary: Malacañang and several senators on Friday expressed opposition to a proposal to impose taxes on coffee products.
articles.byline: GISELLE OMBAY, TINA PANGANIBAN-PEREZ, GMA News

blocks.text: Malacañang and several senators on Friday expressed opposition to a proposal to impose taxes on coffee products.
In a statement, Presidential Legislative Liaison Office Secretary Joey Salceda said the government opposes taxing coffee itself.

"If more Filipinos are drinking coffee instead of alcohol, that is a good thing. It means that sin taxes on alcohol are working as designed. Simply put, you can drive after drinking coffee. You should not drive after drinking alcohol. The distinction is that simple," Salceda said.

During the Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed P378.629-billion budget of the Department of Health (DOH) and its attached agencies and corporations for 2027, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian also opposed the proposal, noting that coffee is widely consumed in the Philippines.
He said that even workers who render overtime rely on coffee to stay awake.

"Personally, I don't think taxing coffee is a good idea. Well, first of all, coffee drinker po ang Pilipinas. Ang dami ngang Starbucks dito, ang daming mga coffee shops. Naging pastime natin 'yan," he said.
(Personally, I don't think taxing coffee is a good idea. First of all, the Philippines has many coffee drinkers. There are so many Starbucks and coffee shops. Drinking coffee has become our pastime.)
"We should also be sensitive to the products that our farmers, fishermen, and also our ordinary kababayans drink if they want to go overtime," he added.
Gatchalian also welcomed the commitment of House members not to pursue any proposal to tax coffee products.
The proposal to tax coffee in the Philippines was earlier raised by Olivia Limpe-Aw, president of the Distilled Spirits Association of the Philippines.
Senator Pia Cayetano, meanwhile, welcomed the statement of House ways and means committee chairperson Miro Quimbo that any proposal to impose taxes on coffee products was "dead for good."
"So hindi na 'yan makakarating sa 'tin kasi I'm one with you na 'yung product nga na 'yun, tinutulungan nga natin 'yung farmers," Cayetano said.
(So that will no longer reach the Senate because I share your view that the product actually helps our farmers.)
"On that note, buhay pa rin ang kape sa Pilipinas (the coffee industry in the Philippines is still alive). No tax, no tax on coffee!" she added.
Senator Joel Villanueva also weighed in on the proposal.
"'Pag 'yan ang pinag-usapan, Mr. President, maghahalo ang tinalupan sa binalatan (If that matter is discussed, Mr. President, all hell will break loose)," Villanueva said.
Tax on 3-in-1 coffee?
Meanwhile, Quimbo said 3-in-1 coffee could be subjected to taxation in the next few years if manufacturers fail to reduce the sugar content of their products.
Unlike regular coffee, 3-in-1 coffee contains sugar and other caloric ingredients, making it a potential candidate for inclusion in the sweetened beverage tax, he explained.
Quimbo said 3-in-1 coffee was exempted from the sweetened beverage tax when it was first implemented several years ago because it was widely consumed by ordinary Filipinos.
However, he noted that manufacturers have since increased the sugar content of their products.
Some members of the House of Representatives have proposed imposing a tax on 3-in-1 coffee, Quimbo said.
However, he said his committee was not inclined to support the proposal, citing the product's widespread consumption among lower-income Filipinos.
Still, Quimbo stressed the need to consider the health effects of excessive sugar consumption and encourage manufacturers to reduce the sugar content of their products.
He said manufacturers could be given a three-year transition period to reformulate their products and lower their sugar content.
Otherwise, 3-in-1 coffee products exceeding a measurable sugar threshold could be subjected to taxation after the transition period, he added.
Salceda said proposals to extend the sweetened beverage tax to sweetened coffee, including 3-in-1 mixes, should be evaluated on their own merits and not based on declining alcohol tax revenues.
"Sin taxes are punitive by design. They are meant to discourage socially undesirable behavior, not to compensate for declining revenues from other sin taxes," he said. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Sara Duterte to Claire Castro: Are you admitting Marcos ordered 'kidnapping' of FPRRD?
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday questioned the supposed contrasting statements of Palace Press Officer Usec. Claire Castro with those of President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos regarding the…

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 11:29pm

Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday questioned the supposed contrasting statements of Palace Press Officer Usec. Claire Castro with those of President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos regarding the arrest and transfer of former President Rodrigo Duterte to The Hague.

Duterte said this in a press conference, reacting to the earlier statement of Castro that surrendering Rodrigo Duterte to the custody of the International Criminal Court (ICC) was allowed under Republic Act 9851.
The Palace official also said the matter had nothing to do with sovereignty as the Philippines was a voluntary member of the ICC before it withdrew from the Rome Statute in 2019.

The Vice President, in response, pointed out that Castro’s statement was seemingly contrary to the previous remark of Marcos that his administration would not cooperate with the inquiry of the ICC into the case of his predecessor.

“Nagtataka ako bakit ganyan ang sagot niya. Quite the opposite sa sagot ni President Marcos noong tinatanong natin siya noon ‘di ba about ICC cooperation. And then he answered that ‘we shall not cooperate in any way, shape, or form with the ICC,’” Sara Duterte said.

(I wonder why she gave such an answer. It’s quite the opposite of the statement of President Marcos when we asked him about ICC cooperation. He said that ‘we shall not cooperate in any way, shape, or form with the ICC.’)
She also cited an official correspondence from the Office of the President, where Marcos supposedly said that the ICC is an affront to Philippine sovereignty.
“I think may split personality na ata ang mga tao diyan sa Office of the…President,” she said.
(I think the people at the Office of the…President might have developed a split personality.)
“This is an example of our government right now. Sinasalamin nila ‘yung P20 ang kilo ng bigas (they’re reflecting the P20-per-kilo rice promise),” she added.
Duterte further asked if it was Marcos who was lying in the official correspondence or if it was Castro with her recent statement.

“At inaamin na ba ngayon, kasi nagde-deny sila noon ‘di ba na the government had anything to do with the kidnapping, it was an Interpol red notice. So ngayon ba, inaamin na niya, ni Claire Castro, na si President Marcos talaga ang nag-utos sa pag-kidnap kay President Duterte?”

(And are they admitting it now, since they previously denied that the government had anything to do with the kidnapping, claiming it was an Interpol red notice? Is Claire Castro admitting now that it was actually President Marcos who ordered the kidnapping of President Duterte?)
The Vice President also took a jab at people who take illegal drugs.
“Epekto kasi minsan ‘yan talaga ng droga, sa totoo lang. Hindi ako nagbibiro. I am not joking. ‘Yung mga nagdo-droga, minsan talaga sabog na ’yung pag-iisip nila,” she said.
(To be honest, that is sometimes an effect of drugs. I’m not joking. Sometimes the minds of people who use drugs are completely scrambled.) —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: CRTC orders Bell, Rogers, Telus to stop charging prohibited wireless fees by Dec. 27
articles.summary: Canada’s telecommunications regulator says Bell, Rogers and Telus have charged consumers fees that are prohibited under the Telecommunications Act, and has ordered them to stop by Dec. 27.

image.caption: Canada’s telecommunications regulator says Bell, Rogers and Telus have charged consumers fees that are prohibited under the Telecommunications Act, and has ordered them to stop by Dec. 27. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Business·Breaking
Canada’s telecommunications regulator says Bell, Rogers and Telus have charged consumers fees that are prohibited under the Telecommunications Act, and has ordered them to stop by Dec. 27.
Decision follows introduction of new hardware-related charges earlier this year
That includes fees for providing and setting up cellphones when signing up for a service plan, the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) said in its decision on Friday.

In June, the CRTC banned internet and mobile providers from charging fees to activate, change, or cancel a service plan. Following that ban, major carriers introduced SIM- and other hardware-related charges that the CRTC flagged as potential disguised activation fees.

"We identified a number of fees charged by certain of the largest telephone companies that appeared to be prohibited. We notified them that the fees may be out of compliance," Sean Carter, the CRTC’s acting vice president of consumer analytics and strategy, told reporters at a virtual briefing on Friday.
"Since these companies chose to continue those fees, and they argued that they were not prohibited, we immediately took action to decide the issue."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. In 2025, he was a Columbia University energy journalism fellow.

articles.title: John Simpson: Ukraine is bowed but still unbroken as freezing weather sets in
articles.summary: Ukraine settles in for another devastating winter as the questions persists: how will it all end?

blocks.text: ByJohn Simpson
World affairs editorReporting fromKyiv

blocks.caption: John Simpson

blocks.text: Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?
Surviving blackouts

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kyiv is entering its fourth winter following Russia's full-scale invasion

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Kyiv is entering its fourth winter following Russia's full-scale invasion

To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.
Raving through the war

I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.

We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.

Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% — way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zelensky's ratings have dipped considerably

blocks.text: Zelensky's ratings have dipped considerably

What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.

Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method — sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.

Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia — "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a café here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.

It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.

There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.
How does it all end?

The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.

So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.

But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.

Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.

And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Tens of thousands of soldiers have died since the outbreak of war

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Tens of thousands of soldiers have died since the outbreak of war

Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.

Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.

At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.

The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.

articles.title: Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
articles.summary: Stormy weather in New York City prompted organisers to push back the Macy's parade by two days - leaving some musicians stuck.

blocks.text: Touring musicians from across the US who descended on New York City to perform at the Macy's Thanksgiving parade have turned to fundraising to cover their costs, after getting stuck when the event was rearranged due to a storm.
A band from Texas told the BBC's US partner, CBS News, it had raised some $350,000 (£267,000) to pay for an extended stay for its 500 members. It saluted the kindness of its supporters.
A group of student musicians from Hawaii, meanwhile, voiced their relief after friends and family rallied around to cover their additional hotel, coach and meal costs.
The parade, a famous annual event, is now scheduled to take place on Saturday.
Earlier this week, organisers said they would it push it back by two days, in part due to the concerns around flying giant inflatables in strong winds.
The balloons were temporarily deflated for a few days - and so too were the spirits of those who had journeyed to the city to watch the action.
The move represented the first time the event had been postponed, although it was suspended altogether during World War Two.

Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, some of them from high schools, to provide music for the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions of people in person and on TV.

Meanwhile, the Hawaii group, the the Nā Koa Aliʻi Hawaiʻi All-State Marching Band, said it would still be able to participate in the parade, as a result of the efforts of families, friends, and other supporters who raised more than $500,000.
Speaking to the BBC earlier on Thursday, the group's director Rickey H Badua described the time pressures. "We are racing to get this done," he explained.
The band is made up of hundreds of musicians from dozens of schools across the state. It had travelled almost 5,000 miles (8,000km) to get to New York.
"Getting the news that we got the parade postponed was not easy, and emotional, for our students," Badua said.

But the musicians sprang into action quickly, he said. "We come from a very far place," Badua said, adding that "to get so close to the finish line and not show up for it, we couldn't give up that easily".
The response from friends and family had been "incredible", he said.
Badua was hopeful his group would get the same experience he had when he first performed in the parade in 2003, as student drum major.
"The energy is palpable, people are just excited to see a band that is great."
Another musical act, from Illinois, told the BBC on Thursday it was trying to raise $175,000 to cover another night in a hotel, additional food, and bus costs back to the city of Champaign.
"Things are going well due to the very generous support of so many amazing human beings," said Prof Barry Houser, director of the University of Illinois Marching Illini.
While awaiting the parade, musicians and punters alike have sheltered from the heavy wind and rain that were brought by a storm to eastern areas of the US.
Hundreds of thousands of homes lost power, and coastal areas were flooded. The National Weather Service (NWS) expects conditions to improve gradually on Friday.
Additional reporting by Jessica Murphy

articles.title: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
articles.summary: The law faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their funadamental rights.

blocks.text: Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.
The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their funadamental rights.

Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.
The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely-watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.
On Friday, the Supreme Court ruled that Quebec's use of the "notwithstanding clause" is valid, except for a section of Bill 21 that bars elected officials from wearing a face covering.
The court found that this provision of the law violates a section of the Canadian Charter protecting the democratic rights of all citizens, which is not covered by the notwithstanding clause.
Barring elected officials in Quebec's legislature from wearing a face covering would infringe on an individual's right to run for public office, the court found.

The court's majority also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the rights Charter even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.

articles.title: Airline Norse Atlantic files for bankruptcy, succumbing to aviation fuel costs
articles.summary: The low-cost airline was only founded a few years ago and had been struggling to turn a profit. The spike in aviation fuel prices caused by the war in Iran has now driven Norway's Norse Atlantic into…

image.caption: Norse Atlantic Airways was a relative newcomer in the industry, founded in 2021 and airborne since 2022 [FILE: July 17, 2025]Image: dts-Agentur/picture alliance

blocks.text: Norwegian low-cost airline Norse Atlantic's operating unit has declared bankruptcy, the carrier said on Friday.
The airline had warned on Wednesday that its financial situation was "critical," and suspended all flights the following day, saying it was urgently seeking emergency funding to fend off bankruptcy.

Like many commercial airlines, Norse Atlantic is highly exposed to the vastly increased jet fuel prices of 2026, attributable in very large part to the war in Iran and resultant tension throughout the wider Middle East.
What did Norse Atlantic say about the bankruptcy filing?

Norse had said slightly earlier on Friday that its lessors had terminated their leasing contracts for all 12 aircraft in the carrier's fleet, demanding that the planes be handed back. Initially the company said it planned to contest this claim, which would have rendered it effectively unable to operate.
But the announcement of plans to file for bankruptcy followed fairly soon after.

"The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution," Norse CEO Eivind Roald said in a statement.

Other companies in the group like the stock market-listed Norse Atlantic ASA parent company and the Norse Atlantic UK subsidiary are not part of the filing and are still attempting to stay in business, the company said.

"The board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations," Roald said.
The company said on Thursday that it planned to file for bankruptcy unless financing could be arranged and had warned: "There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found."

Founded just five years ago and based in Arendal in Norway, Norse Atlantic had a fleet of 12 planes and serviced a total of 14 destinations. It had recorded a net loss of $61.9 million (€56.5 million) in 2025, even before the additional economic strains caused by the war in Iran.
Why has the war in Iran put such strain on the aviation industry?

Small and lower-cost airlines are struggling in particular, but the aviation industry in general is facing severe problems amid the strains on global fuel deliveries caused by the conflict in the Gulf.
In early 2026, as the US launched attacks on Iran — soon leading to reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — aviation fuel rapidly spiked, more than doubling in price at its peak.

It rose higher even than in the immediate aftermath of Russia's full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Although it dipped in mid-summer amid hopes of a resolution to the conflict, it rose once again as these faded and a stalemate developed.

This has posed the worst crisis for the industry since the COVID pandemic drastically reduced the volume of air traffic in 2020 and beyond, a much larger issue that many carriers were still struggling to recover from.

articles.title: Jess Wilson’s plan for Melbourne sewage plants risks water and wetlands without bringing debt down, experts say
articles.summary: Academic says Victorian Liberal proposal to lease treatment plants and generate profit with no compromise of services ‘a total furphy’

blocks.text: Experts have warned the Victorian Liberals’ plan to lease Melbourne’s sewage treatment plants is a “smoke and mirrors” way to pay off debt that risks compromising the state’s water resources and crucial wetlands for nearly a century.

On Thursday – two days out from the election – the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, announced plans for a 90-year lease of the Eastern and Western treatment plants, which process the vast majority of the city’s sewage and are run by Melbourne Water.
The lease is estimated to be worth $9.2bn, with Wilson saying there would be “no change” to water bills or the Essential Services Commission’s regulation of prices across the sector.
Experts are concerned the move could lead to worse services for Victorians, and compromise vital wetlands in Melbourne’s west.

Dr Erin O’Donnell, a water law expert at the University of Melbourne Law School, said given the prices would still be regulated, it would be difficult for private companies to extract value from the services, and the money gained from the lease would amount to only about 5% of the debt held by the state.
“I wouldn’t even classify it as a sugar hit – it’s smoke and mirrors,” O’Donnell said.
“This will not make a significant dent in the debt that Victoria holds, and we are compromising the future of our water resources 90 years into the future.”

O’Donnell said Victoria already required corporations to pay significant dividends to the state government, with strict controls over pricing. It means there is no profit to be realised for private owners while also delivering the same quality of services, she said.

“Victoria has some of the lowest water charges of anywhere in Australia and the idea that there is unrealised profit that could be safely stripped out without compromising those services is a total furphy – I can’t say it any clearer.”

O’Donnell and Prof Stuart Khan, a water quality expert and head of the school of civil engineering at the University of Sydney, both pointed to the UK privatisation of water services in the 1980s under Margaret Thatcher as an example of how it can all go wrong.

The privatisation has been described as an “unmitigated disaster”, with hopes the Burnham Labour government will renationalise the utilities following years of declining services, and rivers polluted by private operators.
Khan said the UK’s services were privatised without guardrails around pricing or minimum standards of services.

“Practically every single river in England now has sewage contamination in it,” he said. “That’s the sort of situation that we need to make sure that we avoid because obviously private players are only going to be there if there’s a profit to be made.”
Victoria’s Labor state minister for the environment, Jaclyn Symes, pointed to the UK system and said it resulted in bills going up by 40% and “left wildlife swimming in a toilet”.
Khan said the NSW government’s privatisation of Sydney desalination plant could be a model that would work.

“It’s price regulated. It has requirements around managing water quality and they put drinking water straight into Sydney’s distribution system,” he said, adding it also has requirements from NSW Health and the state’s environmental protection agency.

Biodiversity Council member and waterbird and wetland expert Prof Richard Kingsford warned the privatisation could have disastrous consequences for Melbourne’s environment, including the wetland in the Western treatment plant at Werribee.

In 1983, the site was listed under the Ramsar convention as an internationally significant wetland, and more than 300 species of bird – including many threatened species such as the orange bellied-parrot – have been recorded there.
“It’s absolutely one of the more important wetland systems,” Kingsford said.
“I think it’s becoming increasingly important because we’ve had more wetlands drying up, less flooding and, particularly in dry times, it provides dependable habitat.”
Kingsford said privatisation “would likely drive different ways of management that might actually not have any consideration for the environmental value of the system”.
O’Donnell said it was “extraordinarily disingenous” for the Liberal party to announce the policy less than two days before the election when many Victorians had already voted.
“I think there is a real concern there, in terms of the openness around their policies [and] this will have significant implications for things like a swimmable Birrarung [Yarra River],” she said.
A Victorian Liberal party spokesperson said the criticism was “another desperate scare campaign by Labor.”
“We are not selling Melbourne Water. It was Labor that had a plan to privatise Melbourne Water. What we are proposing is a lease. When you lease something you still own it.
“The proceeds will be used to reduce Victoria’s debt and interest bill.”
The proposal has already been thrown into doubt after One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, vowed to block it should the party hold the balance of power after the election.
The Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, also promised to “fight Jess Wilson’s privatisation agenda tooth and nail should her Coalition form government”.

blocks.text: November 27, 2026
Germans in favor of continued European military support for Ukraine — survey
European military backing for Ukraine in its fight against the ongoing Russian invasion continues to enjoy widespread support in Germany, according to the results of a new survey published on Friday.

The representative "Politbarometer" poll published by public broadcaster ZDF found that 37% of Germans consider the current level of European support for Ukraine to be just right, while another 31% think it should be increased. Fewer than 30% were in favor of a reduction in military support.

The survey also found that almost two thirds of Germans (64%) think Russia poses a large (39%) or very large (25%) threat to Germany, while the rest consider the threat posed by Moscow to be not so big (23%) or non-existent (11%).

When broken down politically, the survey found that supporters of almost all parties consider the danger posed by Russia to be big or very big. Only far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) voters bucked the trend with 75% believing that Moscow poses either no threat at all or only a minor one.

The ZDF survey results differ slightly from those published by the Körber foundation on Tuesday, which suggested for the first time that German military backing for Ukraine no longer enjoyed majority support among the population.
The ZDF survey, however, asked respondents about "European" support for Ukraine rather than about Germany specifically.
Why Germany's military ambitions face a battle at home

articles.title: Informer TV owner Vucicevic arrested: Has the reckoning with Serbia's pro-Vucic media machine begun?
articles.summary: The arrest of media owner Dragan J. Vucicevic raises questions about whether Serbia is holding the people behind the country's pro-Vucic media accountable — or whether this is another political power…

image.caption: Dragan J. Vucicevic, owner and editor-in-chief of Informer TV, was arrested on November 25 and remanded in custody for 30 days. He is pictured here earlier this monthImage: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Beat them! Break their ribs," shouted the man in the studio during a live TV broadcast.

The man in question was Dragan J. Vucicevic, editor-in-chief of the channel Informer TV, and he was urging police officers to use force against demonstrators during a major student protest in June 2025.

On November 25, Vucicevic was arrested by police on suspicion of causing panic and disorder and obstructing justice. According to the authorities, his appearances "created an atmosphere of public lynching," and he labeled 97 citizens as enemies of the state.
The authorities cite instances where he described protesters as "scum," "hyenas" and "vultures," and spread claims that the students were preparing a "bloodbath" and a "civil war."
Ready to break free: How Serbia's media are changing

The prosecution says that between 2023 and 2026, Vucicevic systematically used Informer TV to conduct a campaign that incited hatred and targeted activists, independent journalists and political opponents of the previous government.
Who is Dragan J. Vucicevic?
Vucicevic's arrest comes at a time of profound political change in Serbia.

Following the Student List's victory in the parliamentary election in late October and the end of the Serbian Progressive Party's (SNS) 14-year rule, questions have arisen about the accountability of people who were part of the previous political and institutional system.

Critics have described Vucicevic as the mouthpiece of former President Aleksandar Vucic — a man who said publicly what the president was thinking but could not say himself because of the office he held.

"He [Vucicevic] is someone who stopped being a journalist a long time ago, and I think he crossed the line of being merely a propagandist some time ago. He was, in fact, a weapon in the hands of Aleksandar Vucic and his party," said Ivana Stevanovic of the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, a Belgrade-based organization named after a Serbian journalist who was killed in 1999 that provides media support and fights for press freedom.

Stevanovic told DW that Vucicevic used his media platforms to "target and endanger people, spread falsehoods that threatened their safety," all as part of a campaign against political opponents, journalists and media outlets who were critical of the government's record.

blocks.caption: Protesters in April 2025 called for media freedom and adherence to ethical standards outside the offices of the tabloid newspaper Informer. The sign on the left reads 'Colorful (fake) revolution? Colorful lie.' The sign on the right: 'Bottom, bottom of the bottom, des-Informer' Image: SPASA DAKIC…

blocks.text: "This man showed a female student's intimate photographs live on air. He stalked people. He had his notorious 'Viewer Intelligence Service,' which secretly followed people and filmed them in their everyday lives, then turned that material into disgusting reports," she said.

"We had calls for violence, threats and insults against prosecutors who were doing their jobs and judges who were issuing lawful rulings, expressed in indescribable language. We had wiretapping, recordings of conversations in restaurants presented as conspiracies to overthrow the state. Media outlets and journalists were accused of plotting to assassinate the president, while their reporting was portrayed as treason and selling out Kosovo," she told DW, adding that "the entire television channel is one big criminal offence."
Court cases and compensation
The Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media (REM) has already issued several warnings and temporarily halted the broadcasting of certain programs on Informer TV.
Journalists' and media associations, civil society organizations and representatives of academia have launched an initiative to have the channel's broadcasting license revoked.
According to the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, more than 1,000 court cases concerning the protection of reputation and honor have been brought against Informer in recent years.

"Of the cases concluded over the past three years, courts upheld the claims in 92% of them," said Stevanovic. "Compensation was awarded to people whose rights had been violated. Informer even paid damages to the same individuals several times for the same lies, which it kept publishing about them. None of these financial penalties made them stop."

blocks.caption: Members of the Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media (REM) met on November 4 to discuss an initiative to revoke TV Informer's broadcasting licenseImage: Milan Ilic/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: On one occasion, Dragan J. Vucicevic himself asked REM to impose a financial penalty on him rather than ban part of his program.
Money, it seems, was not a problem for Insajder Tim, the company behind all Informer media platforms (a daily tabloid newspaper, a television channel and an online portal).
Where did the money come from?

According to an investigation by Raskrikavanje, a fact-checking website that monitors the output of Serbian media, Insajder Tim, received around €273,000 ($299,000) in public funds in 2024 alone through public procurement contracts, advertising and media project funding.
Representatives of the Student List have claimed that the state-owned telecommunications company Telekom Srbija paid Informer between €500,000 and €700,000 a month.

Telekom Srbija, which also owns a cable network distributing television channels to millions of users in Serbia, cited business confidentiality when asked about the details of its cooperation with Informer.
SNS lawmakers protest
Vucicevic and his lawyers reject the accusations.
The defense argues that the proceedings amount to punishing someone for words they have spoken and raise questions about the boundary between freedom of expression and criminal liability.

Former President Aleksandar Vucic said Vucicevic had been arrested solely because of his journalistic work. SNS lawmakers walked out of a parliamentary session following news of the arrest and gathered outside the police station where the Informer editor was being held.

blocks.caption: On the day after the October 25 parliamentary election, protestors confronted Dragan J. Vucicevic (center) in the offices of InformerImage: @veljars/TikTok/REUTERS

blocks.text: Stevanovic maintains that by arresting Vucicevic, Serbia is fulfilling its international obligations, including those arising from the European Convention on Human Rights and international conventions protecting civil and political rights.
"What constitutes a call for violence and a threat to democracy, security and health must be sanctioned and removed from the public sphere," she said.
A reckoning or an internal power struggle?
Vucicevic has been remanded in custody for 30 days.
The offence of causing panic and disorder through the media carries a prison sentence of between six months and five years.

Stevanovic points out, however, that the outcome of the case is not certain because the executive branch, the police and the Ministry of the Interior formally remain under the control of the outgoing government until such time as the Student List forms a new cabinet.

"What is happening now could be an internal power struggle within their own ranks, or an attempt by some prosecutors to clean up their records and ingratiate themselves with the new authorities, assuming what their wishes and intentions regarding Informer might be," she said. "Or it could be a serious manipulation, a staged arrest designed to portray Serbia abroad as a country carrying out revolutionary terror, which, of course, is not true."

articles.title: BSW set to play major role in German politics once more
articles.summary: Sahra Wagenknecht's BSW party is set to disrupt German politics yet again. Espousing a mix of left-wing economic policy and populist far-right anti-migration rhetoric, it now stands to play kingmaker…

image.caption: BSW founder Sahra Wagenknecht has long been a disruptive force in German politicsImage: Jens Kalaene/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: This fledgling party has experienced many highs and lows in quick succession. Launched in January 2024, it was named the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) to capitalize on the high profile and momentum of its founder, a former communist who had just exited the socialist Left party.

Since October 2026, the acronym BSW has instead stood for theAlliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason. In the past 34 months the newcomer party celebrated election successes at the European Parliament level and in German state elections. In the eastern states of Brandenburg and Thuringia, the party even took part in governing coalitions; however, both of these collapsed relatively quickly.

Even more painful for the BSW was its defeat in the German general election in February 2025. The party failed to gain the 5% share of votes required to enter parliament, by less than 10,000 votes. With that, it was denied the country's most important political stage and took the matter to court, demanding a complete recount.
Far left? Far right? What is Germany's BSW?
'Germany has the election scrutiny process of a banana republic'
But Germany's Constitutional Court dismissed the BSW's election challenge as inadmissible, pointing to a lack of evidence.
"Simply insinuating the possibility of voting errors or expressing an unproven assumption does not meet the requirements for claiming an electoral mistake," the court explained.
The court's decision was published about a week before the party's federal conference is due to be held in Dresden, the capital of the eastern state of Saxony.

"Germany's election scrutiny process resembles that of a 'banana republic'," was the angry reaction of former party leader Sahra Wagenknecht, who stepped back from frontline leadership of her eponymous party in December 2025. Since then, she has led its commission on fundamental values.
One of her successors at the top of the BSW is European Parliament lawmaker Fabio De Masi. In his view, the decision of the Constitutional Court was a "black day for democracy in Germany."
Fellow co-leader Amira Mohamed Ali did not want to accept the rejected recount.
"It remains unclear whether the Bundestag is correctly composed and whether the approximately 2.5 million BSW voters have unjustly been deprived of their parliamentary representation," she said.

The disappointment at the failure to enter the Bundestag runs deep. The party has not recovered from this setback. It again failed to win representation in 4 out of 5 state parliaments in elections this year, albeit narrowly.

In Baden-Württemberg and Rhineland-Palatinate, as well as in the city-state of Hamburg in 2025, the BSW received less than 2%. This clearly shows that it is politically irrelevant in the western German states.
Will the BSW help the AfD to power in Saxony-Anhalt?
They find themselves in the spotlight, however, because of the role they are set to play in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the BSW got 5.3% of the vote in September.

Despite being the smallest party in that state parliament, they are set to play a pivotal role. They are the only political party that has indicated a readiness to help the election winner, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), into power.

The AfD, which is classified as right-wing extremist in Saxony-Anhalt by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, won the election with almost 44% of the vote. Although his party does not hold an absolute majority in parliament, lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund wants to be voted Germany's first-ever AfD state premier in December.

The BSW has not indicated any intention to vote for Siegmund, but if he falls short of winning the absolute majority of 42 votes in the first two rounds of voting, a third round will be held in which a simple majority will suffice to win. The BSW has announced plans to abstain from that vote. Siegmund would then only need to pick up one more "yes" vote or abstention.

During the secret ballot for the state parliament speaker, AfD candidate Tobias Rausch received 9 votes more than his party has lawmakers. It is not known exactly who they came from. Alongside the AfD and BSW, there are 4 other parties in the state parliament: the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), environmentalist Greens, socialist Left Party and center-left Social Democrats (SPD).
What next after far-right AfD win in regional election?
Sahra Wagenknecht rejects a firewall against the AfD
The situation in Saxony-Anhalt will be at the center of the party's upcoming conference in Dresden, because the BSW's increasing closeness with the far-right party is highly controversial.
Several BSW members, including board member Christian Leye, criticized this path in a column published in the weekly Die Zeit.
Leye recalled their party's founding consensus: "The clear political demarcation from the AfD."
He quoted party founder Wagenknecht, who at that time had said: "Of course we will not collude with the AfD."

"We are starting a party so that all the people who are considering or have voted for the AfD out of anger or disappointment — but not because they are right-wing — have a credible political home," Wagenknecht had continued.

But Wagenknecht has also long argued that the so-called "firewall" policy of mainstream parties refusing to work with the AfD has failed. This is why she is rejecting the idea of entering a mathematically possible governing coalition with the other parties in Saxony-Anhalt.

"We are basically agreed that we neither want to go into coalition with the AfD, nor tolerate them, just as much as we do not want to participate in a firewall coalition," she told German news agency dpa.
How the BSW plans to make its way through this dilemma at its party conference is unclear. Fabio De Masi, who replaced Wagenknecht as co-chair in December 2025, seems well aware of this.
He told German media network RND that dealing with the AfD continued to be like "riding on the edge of a razor blade."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Russia sports ban: Ukraine's Heraskevych hails EU pushback
articles.summary: As European countries challenge Russia's sporting return, Ukrainian Olympian Vladyslav Heraskevych believes the IOC is facing a "very big crisis."

image.caption: Vladyslav Heraskevych has described an EU move to stop Russians from competing in the bloc as 'better late than never'Image: Robert Michael/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukrainian skeleton racer Vladyslav Heraskevych has welcomed a move by the European Union to take a tougher stance on Russian athletes competing in the 27-member bloc.

Heraskevych is one of the most outspoken critics of Russia's reintegration into international sport. He made headlines at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan-Cortina when he was disqualified for his helmet honoring Ukrainian athletes killed in the war with Russia.

On Monday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed banning Russian athletes from competing under their own flag at sports competitions within the European Union and urged member states to consider denying visas in such cases.
"Sports events cannot be a forum for propaganda activities," she said.
In an interview with DW, Heraskevych described the EU move as coming "better late than never."
"We waited a long time for this backlash," he said at the International Bobsleigh and Skeleton Federation World Cup in Altenberg, Germany, his first competition since the Winter Olympics.
"I'm really happy to see that people start to care about sports and they understand the value of sports as a huge platform," he added.
Europe pushes back

In July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) paved the way for Russia's full return to international sport by ending its recommendation that Russian athletes be allowed to compete as neutrals, without their flag, colors or anthems. The IOC also said Russian teams should be allowed to return to international competition.

blocks.caption: Vladyslav Heraskevych was disqualified from competing in Milano Cortina over his helmet depicting Ukrainian athletes killed in Russia's invasionImage: Franck Fife/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Several major Olympic sports, such as swimming and gymnastics, have already fully reinstated Russia, despite the country's ongoing attacks on Ukraine.
"It makes no sense to me," Heraskevych said.
However, in recent weeks there has been a growing European pushback against the easing of Russia's sporting isolation.

Among the catalysts was a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) to overturn a ban on Russia in international ice hockey. That prompted seven European countries to say they would refuse to play against Russia, while Germany, at one point, said withdrawing as host of next year's men's world championship was an option.
Putin wades into dispute
The dispute over the CAS ruling drew a response from the Kremlin.
"It is a flagrant violation of the Olympic Charter [the IOC's rulebook] and leads toward the destruction of Olympism as a whole," Russian President Vladimir Putin said in China last week.
"Sport, like art, should bring people together."
Meanwhile, a group of Nordic and Baltic countries want the EU to go even further, pushing for an immediate EU-wide visa ban on all Russian athletes.

"The matter is too urgent to wait until [new visa rules] enter into force," the leaders of Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Sweden wrote in a November 23 letter to von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.
"From my perspective, the IOC is in a very big crisis," Heraskevych said, referencing the European pushback.
Blanket bans could have a huge effect on qualifying events in Europe for the 2028 Los Angeles Summer Olympics.
Can sport be separated from politics?

Under its president, Kirsty Coventry, the IOC has sought to bring Russia, an Olympic powerhouse, back in from the cold. Coventry has argued that athletes shouldn't be punished for the actions of their governments, and the IOC has strengthened its political neutrality rules in the Olympic Charter.
However, Heraskevych takes exception to the idea that sport should be kept out of politics.
"We are not living in a bubble," he said.

"Already more than 800 people who were part of the sport family in Ukraine were killed. Ukrainian hockey stadiums, Ukrainian swimming pools, anything related to sports have also been attacked. So we cannot separate sport and politics in Ukraine. The same way Russian sport is involved in politics."

Critics have accused Coventry of cozying up to Russia. In September, it emerged that she had written a letter to Mikhail Degtyarev, Russia's sports minister and president of the Russian Olympic Committee, wishing him luck ahead of an international sports forum.
Degtyarev has been sanctioned by the EU. The IOC has declined to comment on the letter but not denied its existence.
Heraskevych said he was not "angry" with any particular Russian athlete, and even floated the idea of a team of Russian refugees.
"I am not against peaceful athletes competing," he said.
"They should be part of competition only if they are part of a refugee team. So, if they have refugee status in another country, and if they condemn the war that Russia started in Ukraine."

articles.title: Sentencing hearing to continue for poison seller Kenneth Law
articles.summary: A sentencing hearing is set to continue Friday for an Ontario man who sold potentially deadly substances online to people who then used those products to take their own lives.

image.caption: A sentencing hearing is set for Friday for an Ontario man, who pleaded guilty earlier this year to 14 counts of aiding suicide in the deaths of 14 people in the province. (Pam Davies/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto
A sentencing hearing is set to continue Friday for an Ontario man who sold potentially deadly substances online to people who then used those products to take their own lives.
Law is suspected of being tied to at least 147 deaths around the world: CBC News investigation

Lawyers for the Crown and the defence are expected to present what they believe would be an appropriate sentence for Kenneth Law, who pleaded guilty earlier this year to 14 counts of aiding suicide in the deaths of 14 people in Ontario.
The former chef has been linked to dozens of deaths worldwide, including 79 in the United Kingdom that are being considered as part of the sentencing process.
Scores of grieving family members and friends told the court about the lasting impact of Law's crimes over two days in September as his sentencing hearing got underway.
Some delivered the message in person, others did so by video and others in written statements read by prosecutors.
Kenneth Law case: Families reveal the devastating toll in 'The Poison Seller'
Law's plea deal in May came soon after he was set to stand trial on the aiding suicide charges and another 14 counts of first-degree murder related to the same victims.
Prosecutors are expected to withdraw the murder charges after Law is sentenced. Individuals found guilty of aiding suicide can face up to 14 years in prison.
An agreed statement of fact presented after his plea said Law ran several websites that were used to sell sodium nitrite and other products that can be used for self-harm.

items: Poison seller Kenneth Law pleads guilty to abetting Ontario suicides, won't be prosecuted for deaths in U.K.
Shopify paid Kenneth Law $149K for deadly poison sales to at-risk buyers, court records show

blocks.text: He shipped products to people in more than 40 countries, knowing his customers were likely to use them for suicide, the document said.

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: Rodrigo Duterte on trial at the ICC
articles.summary: Bookmark this page for the latest developments in former president Rodrigo Duterte’s landmark trial at the International Criminal Court

blocks.text: The historic trial of former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte at the International Criminal Court (ICC) begins on Monday, November 30, as he faces charges of crimes against humanity.

The charges against Duterte stem from killings linked to his so-called war on drugs during his time as mayor of Davao City and his presidency. He is the first former Asian leader to be tried at the court in The Hague, going on trial more than a year since his pivotal arrest in March 2025.

On this page, we bring you the latest news, analyses, videos, and photos of Duterte’s trial at the ICC. For more updates and to share your own views, you can also join the Justice and Crime chat room in Rappler’s Muni app.
LATEST UPDATES
31 minutes ago
People we lost under Duterte
In his six years in office, Rodrigo Duterte’s rhetoric and policies made violence the norm in the country.
When Duterte stepped down in 2022, Rappler took a look at the lives lost during his administration.
