articles.title: How East Germany boosted Vietnam's coffee industry
articles.summary: When East Germany could no longer afford to import coffee, it introduced a substitute blend containing rye and chicory in 1977. A public outcry ensued. The solution to the problem lay 9,000…

image.caption: GDR Politburo members enjoying coffee during a visit to a construction siteImage: Volker Hohlfeld/IMAGO

blocks.text: Coffee lovers, brace yourselves: Imagine taking your first sip, expecting the rich aroma of roasted coffee beans, only to discover that your cup contains a concoction made from ingredients you can barely identify.
That's exactly what millions of outraged East Germans experienced in 1977. But what led to this?
Foreign currency deficit versus soaring prices

A poor harvest in Brazil saw global coffee prices skyrocketing, creating a major problem for East Germany. Unlike West Germany's Deutsche Mark, the East German Mark was a domestic currency with no value abroad.

Even under normal circumstances, the country constantly struggled to obtain the hard currency it needed to pay for imports. In 1974 and 1975, East Germany spent around 150 million Valutamarks — the term used in East Germany for the West German Deutsche Mark — on imported coffee. The following year, it had to pay almost five times as much.

blocks.caption: Historian Stefan Wolle still vividly recalls the coffee crisis of the mid-1970s Image: DDR Museum

blocks.text: However, this rate of inflation could not be passed on to consumers because, "In the GDR, there was the dogma of stable prices — set by the state through law," explains historian Stefan Wolle, a consultant at the DDR Museum in Berlin. "Prices were set by the Politburo, not by businesses. And they weren't allowed to change. What sounds wonderfully socially minded at first glance had serious negative economic consequences, because production costs were far higher than retail prices."

The government needed a solution. On August 1, 1977, it introduced "Kaffee Mix" as a substitute for popular coffee brands back then such as Kosta, Rondo and Mocca Fix. The fine print on the packaging promised "a blend of select green coffee beans and carefully balanced coffee substitutes."

In plain English, that meant 51% of the blend consisted of imported coffee beans. The rest was a mixture of rye and barley, along with chicory and either spelt or sugar beet. It tasted disgusting, Wolle recalls.
Even the coffee machines appeared to reject the concoction. The mixture expanded and clogged the filters in cafeterias and restaurants. Some machines were even said to have exploded.

blocks.caption: During the 1977 coffee crisis, the SED Politburo came up with a solution that few people liked: the 'Kaffee Mix'Image: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'Pure rat poison'

Public discontent boiled over during this "coffee crisis." People responded by boycotting the product and with biting sarcasm. "The difference between a neutron bomb and coffee mix: There isn't one — the cup stays intact, but the person is destroyed.." A sharper dig? "It's pure rat poison."

More than 14,000 complaint letters poured into government offices. On September 1, the Ministry for State Security, better known as the Stasi, reported to the leadership of the ruling Socialist Unity Party of Germany or SED, that Kaffee Mix was being "rejected by broad sections of the population." (Editor's note: The SED was the only ruling party in East Germany then).

To understand the intensity of the backlash, it's important to recognize coffee's special place in East German society. "Coffee was, in a way, the social glue that held together East Germany's particular brand of conviviality and camaraderie," says Wolle. During the 1960s and 1970s, people would gather for coffee after lunch, often accompanied by homemade cakes or treats from the bakery. "It was a sacred hour in every workplace and office. It was a huge mistake for the SED leadership to slaughter this sacred cow, so to speak."

blocks.caption: In the GDR, both women and men worked full-time. During breaks, coffee was the order of the dayImage: Peer Grimm/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Care packages from relatives in the West

According to Wolle, real coffee was still occasionally available in the larger cities. But in smaller towns and rural areas, people often had no choice but to make do with Kaffee Mix. East Germans who had relatives or friends in West Germany and regularly received packages from them could count themselves lucky. "Our relatives and friends in the West knew what was in short supply in East Germany, so they would usually include a big bag of good West German coffee," Wolle recalls.

It is estimated that around 25% of all coffee consumed in East Germany came from the West. During the height of the coffee crisis, that share was briefly even higher. "Of course, the SED leadership had mixed feelings about people receiving so many packages from the West," Wolle says. "Police officers and full-time party officials weren't allowed to have contacts in the West. But ordinary citizens didn't care." Especially after the blend stirred up such negative reactions.

blocks.caption: Coffee was also a symbol of prosperityImage: Klaus Rose/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: Trading weapons for coffee

East Germany's leaders responded by looking to their socialist allies in Africa for help. They negotiated special agreements with Angola and Ethiopia. "Instead of paying in hard currency, they paid with military equipment — weapons and trucks," Wolle explains. "Weapons that were used in Ethiopia's civil war."

But the East German leadership sought a long-term solution, and eventually established a partnership with another socialist ally: Vietnam. "Coffee had already been grown there under French colonial rule," says Wolle. "People knew that coffee grew well there and that the quality was good."

blocks.caption: Vietnam is now the world's second-largest coffee producerImage: Bernd Bieder/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: Coffee from Vietnam: Too late for East Germany

Starting in the 1980s, East Germany invested heavily in developing the infrastructure needed for large-scale coffee cultivation in Vietnam, Wolle explains. It supplied machinery and equipment, built transportation routes, and provided housing for plantation workers. "There was just one catch: Coffee plants take several years before they can be harvested."

By the time the plants were finally ready to produce coffee, the Berlin Wall had fallen and East Germany was a thing of the past. "But the Vietnamese benefited enormously," says Wolle. "They converted the plantations into private enterprises fairly quickly." Today, Vietnam is one of the world's largest coffee exporters. "What's surprising is that most people don't even know that."

There’s no mention of it on the packages — and if there is, it’s in microscopic print. "The Vietnamese don’t make a big deal out of their role because they themselves probably still believe that coffee has to come from Brazil — or at least from Latin America — to be any good," says Wolle.
Passionate coffee drinkers may not care where the hot beverage comes from — as long as it doesn't taste like spelt and sugar beets, as the much-maligned East German Kaffee Mix once did.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Indian workers fill Germany's labor gaps, but face hurdles and risks
articles.summary: The number of Indians working in Germany has grown rapidly in recent years. But many continue to face challenges in the labor market. Some also fall victim to recruitment scams, leaving them…

image.caption: Germany, facing a shrinking and rapidly aging population, is seeking skilled professionals in a number of sectors Image: Gunter Hübner/dpa/picture-alliance

blocks.text: Pratyay Saikia was studying food technology in 2022 when he saw an advertisement from Magic Billion, a recruitment agency that places skilled and semi-skilled Indian professionals in verified jobs abroad.
The 25-year-old from the northern Indian state of Haryana reached out to explore employment opportunities.
Four years later, he is working as a butcher at Metzgerei Lederer in southern Germany, having completed a three-year apprenticeship at the butcher shop.

"I came to Baden-Württemberg with 180 other Indians who came here to do an Ausbildung [apprenticeship] program. Me and seven others did our Ausbildung at Lederer [butcher shop], while others went into the construction sector. I now have a full-time job here," Saikia told DW.
He is not alone as the number of Indian workers subject to social security contributions in Germany has grown sevenfold over the past decade, to over 140,000 professionals.
Many of them work in the IT and health care sectors.
India meets German engineering
Pressing need for workers, but hesitant to hire

But Germany, facing a shrinking and rapidly aging population, doesn't just need software specialists and nurses. It is also seeking skilled professionals such as electricians, mechatronics technicians, solar panel installers and truck drivers.

A 2024 study by Bertelsmann Foundation concluded that Germany needs 288,000 foreign skilled workers per year until 2040 to fill the shortage left by retiring workers. Another report from the consulting firm FMC Group noted that over 369,000 skilled job positions went unfilled in 2025.

Despite the pressing need for skilled workers, many firms, particularly the renowned Mittelstand (small and medium-sized enterprises), remain hesitant to recruit from places like India, say observers.

"Hiring an electrician from India is a relatively new concept for German companies, so they are hesitant," said Daniel Raja, managing director of NM NextMittelstand GmbH, a Düsseldorf-based recruitment firm focused on connecting German firms with skilled workers from India.
The Mittelstand companies are often overlooked by young talent abroad, while many of these firms are not actively recruiting international skilled workers, Raja said.
This disconnect, coupled with the often high German language requirements, means that many skilled positions remain unfilled, he explained.
Germany looks to India to address skilled labor shortage
Language a key hurdle
Saikia, the butcher, had studied German to the B1 level, considered intermediate proficiency, but soon realized it was not enough for everyday communication at work.

"Initially, I found the theory classes of my Ausbildung quite difficult. But my co-workers helped me. After one year, my German improved, and I realized integration happened automatically as my language level improved," he said.
David Kipp, researcher in the Global Issues Research Group at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), said he's "skeptical" about lowering language requirements.

"Language skills are an important selection criterion so people actually know where they are going. Sending people with very little language knowledge makes exploitation easier because they have less direct contact with German institutions," he told DW.
Language, however, isn't the only hurdle.
Raja said workers' councils also often resist hiring from abroad.

"Company decisions in the Mittelstand involve the team and the shop floor," he pointed out. "In some cases, the workers' council resists hiring from India because they mistakenly believe 'cheap Indian labor' will take their jobs or undercut their wages."
Raja said he often uses unconventional outreach methods, including hosting TikTok Live sessions, to engage directly with industrial employers and workers and dispel concerns and misconceptions.
Delivered! — The courier driver business
Exploiting the EU mobility loophole?
German companies have traditionally relied on workers from Central and Eastern European (CEE) nations such as Poland, Romania and Slovenia to fill labor market gaps.
But studies show CEE workers are increasingly reluctant to relocate to Germany, as faster economic growth and stronger career prospects improve opportunities in their home countries.
The situation has prompted recruitment agencies in these countries to look beyond the EU for workers.

These third-country nationals (TCNs) obtain residence permits in CEE states and are then posted to German job sites under the Vander Elst visa. The mechanism allows non-EU citizens legally employed in one EU member state to be temporarily sent to work in another.

"European Labour Authority's (ELA) 2025 study on the posting of third-country nationals found that the number of posted TCNs is increasing. The main sectors concerned are construction and transport," said Pia Fallstrom, ELA spokesperson.
The exact number of TCNs posted across the EU is difficult to gauge, as data exchange between sending and receiving countries by nationality and sector is limited.
"Finding out how blue-collar workers get here really requires fieldwork," said Kipp, noting that Indian recruiters are aware of this mobility loophole and take advantage of these opportunities.
While there are regulations to protect workers posted to Germany from another EU state, ELA said the practice has often led to wage-dumping.

"ELA's work has identified issues such as difficulties accessing information on applicable rules, complex subcontracting arrangements, letterbox companies, bogus self-employment and other cases of non-compliance," noted Fallstrom.
"Posted third-country nationals can be particularly vulnerable because they may also depend on their employer for their work and residence permits."
Cost of a dream: Indian students in Germany
Raja said he had seen cases of workers falling victim to recruitment scams and being exploited as a result.

"I know of a family that took out a loan so that their child could enroll in an institute which promised a job in Germany," said Raja. "When the candidate realized it's a scam, they ended up in Bahrain doing a tough manual labor job just to pay off the loan."
What to do to prevent exploitative hiring practices?
Saikia, the butcher, stressed the importance of workers verifying that a recruitment agency is legitimate.
In his case, he said the agency's detailed website and its CEO's willingness to speak with him during the early stages of the recruitment process gave him confidence that it was not a scam.

Kipp, the SWP expert, argued that preventing exploitative hiring practices requires streamlining migration procedures, expanding pre-departure cultural training and becoming more effective at identifying trusted entities and combating social media scams.
"India is the most important country for experimenting with how work migration functions. If we don't pay attention, we'll just send people into the low-wage sector and into disappointment," he said.

articles.title: Momentous decision awaits after judges’ call for Netanyahu charges to be dropped
articles.summary:
Dropping of corruption charges against Israeli PM after unusual intervention could set damaging precedent

The Israeli judges presiding over Benjamin Netanyahu’s corruption trial have called…

blocks.text: The Israeli judges presiding over Benjamin Netanyahu’s corruption trial have called on prosecutors to end proceedings, a highly unusual intervention that leaves the attorney general facing a momentous political decision.

The prime minister has been charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three complex and overlapping criminal cases that hinge on his relationship with telecoms magnates and other wealthy businessmen. Ending the trial without a ruling could set damaging precedents for media independence and how politicians are held to account.

“There were evidentiary difficulties in the case, but the position the judges laid out effectively means abandoning the media to the whims of politicians and publishers, and setting an impossible bar for conviction in corruption cases,” said Yael Freidson, the legal correspondent for Haaretz, who has covered the trial since it began in 2020.

The judges urged prosecutors to drop one case because “the chances of a conviction are low”, seek a plea deal in a second, and reconsider the third set of charges. Even if prosecutors were to prove the allegations of fraud and breach of trust in that case, it was not clear that Netanyahu’s alleged behaviour amounted to criminal conduct, they said.

The attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, who was summoned to court to hear the judges’ statement in person, must now decide whether to accept their recommendations and end a trial that has dominated and shaped Israeli politics for the best part of a decade.

The decision is not straightforward, even though the current bench has in effect indicated a not guilty verdict is a foregone conclusion. If the trial continues, their ruling could still be appealed to a higher court, where fresh judges could take a different stance.

“[The former prime minister] Ehud Olmert was acquitted on all charges by the district court and was subsequently convicted by the supreme court on a minor charge,” Ben Caspit wrote in Maariv. “It ain’t over till it’s over.”

“[Baharav-Miara] could opt to reach a lenient plea bargain agreement with the defendant and put it all to rest, but that would be an admission of the entire justice system’s failure and would further fuel the conspiracy theories that Netanyahu and his disciples have been pumping ever since he was indicted.”
Settling or dropping all charges would immediately and permanently absolve Netanyahu, ending the threat of jail time and dispelling the legal shadow hanging over his political future.
A bill making its way through the opposition-controlled parliament would in effect bar him from serving as prime minister until the trial was concluded.

Netanyahu, who has pleaded not guilty to all charges, claims he is the victim of a political witch-hunt and welcomed the judges’ recommendation as a vindication. “The truth has finally come to light,” he said.

Baharav-Miara has withstood pressure from the judges in the case twice before. In 2023 and in 2025 they urged prosecutors to drop bribery charges, the most serious ones that Netanyahu faces, although they stopped short of suggesting the whole trial should be wrapped up.

Perhaps the single point of agreement between Netanyahu’s supporters and his critics in relation to the trial is concern that it has been allowed to drag on for too long. Testimony from Netanyahu had extended over a year and a half, across 98 hearings, the longest by a single witness in Israeli judicial history, Freidson said. The transcripts from all the hearings run to more than 60,000 pages.

Oren Persico has sat in every hearing since the case began in 2020, covering it for the investigative magazine The Seventh Eye. Over that period he watched the judges slowly lose control of their courtroom, he said.

“It started with giving the defence a lot of rope to do what they wanted. Netanyahu’s lawyer lashed out at the prosecution and humiliated them, almost every day, and attacked the judges, which should be an absolute red line in court,” he said. “I think the judges are afraid and tired; they just want to get it all over with.”

The sense of a bench cracking under pressure was exacerbated by the recommendation to reconsider charges in one of the cases against Netanyahu. These were laid out by prosecutors seven years ago, and have not changed since, prompting joking questions about whether the judges had even read the indictment, and serious ones about their political judgment.

When Netanyahu was indicted, he decided to fight the charges both inside and outside the courtroom, declaring war on the prosecution, the media, the police and key democratic and judicial institutions, Persico said.

“To keep himself out of jail, he tried to form an authoritarian state here in Israel, which tore apart society. I understand the interest in putting an end to that,” Persico said. “But ending the trial would send a terrible message to criminals and politicians and media bosses: that if you fight strongly enough you can get away with anything.”

articles.title: Supreme Court set to deliver ruling on Quebec's secularism law

image.caption: People watch the Supreme Court of Canada live broadcast in the lobby during hearings in March. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: What’s at stake as the Supreme Court rules on Quebec’s secularism law

The Supreme Court of Canada will make its decision on Quebec’s Bill 21 and could rule on the government’s pre-emptive use of the notwithstanding clause. The bill, enacted in 2019, bars some public workers in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols on the job. Friday’s ruling could also set new rules for how provinces across Canada can use the notwithstanding clause.

items: November 27Arguments for and against the bill — and what's at stake todayWhy all Canadians’ rights are at stake in the Supreme Court challenge of Quebec’s Bill 21Quebec’s Bill 21 bans religious symbols for some civil servants. Now, the legal battle has shifted from the ban itself to whether the province overstepped by invoking the notwithstanding clause in the text of the law, to bypass Charter rights.I covered the Supreme Court hearings of the Bill 21 case last spring for CBC Montreal, and I'll be covering the decision today. Let's talk a bit about what's at stake.First, there's the simple question of whether the ban on wearing religious symbols at work for some Quebec civil servants will be maintained or struck down. The overwhelming majority of people affected by Bill 21 and subsequent secularism laws are Muslim women who wear hijabs. Some teachers in Quebec have lost their jobs because of the ban, others have seen their careers stalled, and people studying to be teachers have abandoned that career path.But this case goes beyond the religious symbols ban. It's become much more about how the Quebec government used the constitutional notwithstanding clause to shield the ban from legal challenges.

How Bill 21 reached the Supreme CourtHolly CabreraPeople watch the Supreme Court of Canada live broadcast in the lobby during hearings in March. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)Today's ruling marks the latest chapter of a seven-year legal battle. In June 2019, the province's majority Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) government passed Bill 21, An Act Respecting the Laicity of the State, and pre-emptively invoked the notwithstanding clause — which is contained in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms — to shield it from court challenges. The English Montreal School Board contested the law in Quebec Superior Court that October.In April 2021, Justice Marc-André Blanchard largely upheld the legislation, save for two exceptions: one for English-language school boards and another allowing National Assembly members to wear face coverings while sitting. The Quebec Court of Appeal overturned the exemption for English-language school boards in 2024, and the Supreme Court of Canada agreed to hear appeals in January 2025, setting the stage for today's decision.

Supreme Court to rule on Quebec's secularism lawHolly CabreraThe Supreme Court of Canada as seen from Parliament Hill in Ottawa. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)Canada's top court is getting ready to rule on Quebec's Bill 21, after spending months deliberating the province's secularism law.The case was heard over four days in March, making it one of the longest hearings in the history of the Supreme Court of Canada. A record 51 interveners took part in the proceedings, including six attorneys general. Bill 21 prevents employees in positions of authority in Quebec, such as teachers and police officers, from wearing religious symbols while on the job, and also requires civil servants to keep their faces uncovered when providing services. We'll bring you the decision as soon as the embargo lifts at 9:45 a.m. ET, along with the ensuing reaction and analysis.

articles.title: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
articles.summary: More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia has not.

blocks.text: South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.
The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.
Campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.
More than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

items: In India, growing clamour to criminalise rape within marriage
Marital rape: Delhi high court gives split verdict
India government says criminalising marital rape 'excessively harsh'

blocks.text: Pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.
Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan.

A new penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal says. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.
Unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it.
"The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.
"But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal."
The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.
In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.
Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.
There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.
But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh".

items: India refuses to criminalise marital rape. This new series shines a light on it
India anger as judge frees man accused of raping wife who then died

blocks.text: Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.
"Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very important in our countries," Silwal says.
"They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men."
Also a change in law, she says, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.
Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year.
In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

articles.title: Mad about mara: the DIY dance movement helping young Nigerians escape the daily grind
articles.summary:
What started as one artist’s response to being cut out of a music video has exploded, becoming a driving force in Nigeria’s cultural landscape

As a student in the central Nigerian city of…

blocks.text: As a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth.

In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed vocals from a hypeman sent it viral. He was invited to the music video shoot in Lagos and thought his big break had finally come, but when the video was released, he was absent.
“I was in a restaurant and everybody was anticipating seeing me, but my face did not show once,” the 27-year old, known as DJ Khalipha, said. “I felt disgraced. I stopped posting the song.”

blocks.caption: Lawal Habeeb Kola, aka DJ Khalipha. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: Khalipha retreated to his dorm and revisited the DIY “cruise beats” genre of dance music that he had previously worked in. Taking its name from the pidgin expression “catch cruise”, meaning to joke around, cruise beats is a lo-fi, frenetic genre that incorporates amusing voice samples from Nollywood and memes.

Khalipha raised the already fast 115-120 beats per minute of cruise beats to 140-150bpm, added melancholic undertones and named the new style mara, meaning to lose one’s senses. The popularity of the sound soared, eventually crossing over from the Lagos underground and becoming incorporated into the sound of mainstream musicians.

As the genre exploded, Khalipha lost creative control. “It became a trend that every producer and DJ was hopping on,” said Feranmi Abiola, 24, who directed the 2025 documentary Mara Mania. “They were making sounds and whether it was mara sound or not, they would just title it mara fever, mara this, mara that.”

Like its predecessors, mara’s spread was driven by choreography. One dancer, Obi “Odogwu Mara” Madubogwu, named himself after the sound and dropped dance routines on social media weekly, gaining street credibility. His death in unclear circumstances at the age of 26 galvanised interest in mara, especially among young Nigerians for whom posting and responding to dance challenges in his style became a form of escape from poor job prospects in Nigeria’s sluggish economy.

blocks.caption: Mara producer Azzi On The Beat, left, and his manager, Kadima. Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The Guardian

blocks.text: “We’ve seen area boys [street urchins] switching to become dancers,” said the producer Azzi On The Beat, an early adopter of mara who has stayed true to the sound. “The music is spiritual.”

The hectic but harmonious sound has become a fixture at raves, which in Nigeria take the form of street-style block-gatherings populated by young people tired of the markup on alcohol at nightclubs and “bottle culture” – the buying of expensive bottles of champagne and spirts in VIP sections, often as a means of flaunting wealth.
Top musicians have been enlisting the sound in search of new hits, but mara’s originators remain relatively unknown, their work often restricted to the thriving underground “TrenchTok” scene.
Khalipha said bookers assumed that mara DJs would have an air of chaos and violence, due to the raw sound of the music and its association with street culture.

Abiola agreed. “[Mara DJs] are not harmful, but they face stereotypes because of their background, how they look and how they dress,” she said. “In my documentary, I wanted people to see these people for who they were … young people innovating and contributing to the cultural identity of this generation. Regardless of where they are from, they deserve to be taken seriously.”
after newsletter promotion

Without institutional backing, the DJs have been learning how to navigate the music industry on the go. When the samples they were using were flagged for copyright issues, they created their own instrumentals from scratch using plugins.

Many artists are self-funded, investing money earned as social media influencers or from royalties into shooting videos and promotion. Female dancers talk of sexual harassment and financial exploitation in the industry.
“The financial challenges are more apparent for the dancers, because people don’t really take dancers seriously,” said Abiola.

Pointing to a square littered with weeds and rubbish, where goats roamed next to a woman sieving black-eyed peas on a tray, Azzi’s 27-year-old manager, Sangokunle Anuoluwapo – known as Kadima – said: “We do most of our videos here.”

Despite the challenges, the people involved in mara harbour dreams of global traction. Support from the French embassy helped Azzi perform at festivals in Uganda and parts of Europe. A few industry friends on the rise or those who Kadima at one point managed also help intermittently with funding or promoting projects for free.
“I understand what we want for this culture so we keep pushing really hard,” said Kadima. “It’s family work, so we try to split revenues among everybody.”

Azzi was given a leg up from the Footprints of David Art Academy, a children’s dance theatre troupe that held performances behind his mother’s shop. He honed his dancing skills, learned how to drum, and met Kadima there. “We were taught how to fight through tough times,” Azzi said.

The art director Seun Awobajo launched the academy in 2005 with the aim of channelling the energy of disadvantaged children into creative endeavours. “[I had] the notion that no child is useless, they are only used less,” he said.

Awobajo is proud of his former wards and the mara scene more generally. “Being proud is an understatement,” he said. “But I think I feel more fulfilled seeing what they’ve become because these are children who the upper class of the society have written off.”

articles.title: New Zealand election: final results show ruling coalition needs minor party to govern
articles.summary:
Incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon loses majority and needs support of Opportunity party to remain in power, or country faces another election

The final results of New Zealand’s…

blocks.text: The final results of New Zealand’s general election show the incumbent rightwing coalition will need the support of a centrist newcomer party to form a government, and to avoid sending the country back to the polls.

Preliminary results on 7 November handed the National party and its two coalition partners, the populist New Zealand First and libertarian Act parties, a slim two-seat majority, making the election too close to call until final votes were tallied.

On Friday, the electoral commission released the results from nearly 485,000 “special votes” – those cast from overseas or outside a voter’s electorate. National dropped two seats to 40, Labour stayed on 36 seats, the Greens picked up one seat to 17, Act had 13, New Zealand First 12, Opportunity seven and Te Pati Māori five.
The National-led bloc currently has 65 seats. In the 130-seat parliament, 66 seats are needed for a majority.

The revised results mean the National-led coalition has the only realistic path to power – if it can negotiate a deal with Opportunity. If it cannot, New Zealand will probably need to hold another election.

Three electorate seats changed hands after the special votes. Labour won Wairarapa off National with just 81 votes, and took Hamilton East from National with 173 votes. The Greens won Wellington Bays from Labour with 1,610 votes.

If National applies for a recount and wins back just one of those seats, it could return to power with a slim majority and without needing Opportunity. Applications for a recount must be made by 3 December, and results could take another five days.

Special votes in previous elections have favoured the left, and typically have cost the right one or two seats. Until Friday, a question mark hung over whether National would be able to govern comfortably alongside its coalition partners, or whether it would be forced to cut a deal with the Opportunity party – a newcomer centrist party that incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon had previously ruled out working with.
After the election, Luxon softened his stance on his initial rule-out, saying he intended to find common ground with the Opportunity party.
On Friday afternoon, Luxon said National will now begin formal negotiations with New Zealand First, Act and Opportunity, but he cautioned discussions would be “challenging” and could take some time.
“Getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly,” Luxon said. “Kiwis won’t thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart, or for sending them back to the polls.”

Lara Greaves, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, said the prospect of New Zealand heading back to the polls was unprecedented, because negotiations between the four parties will be so complex.
“It’s not a 0% chance, it’s the highest chance we’ve ever had of it being another election,” she said.
Opportunity, led by Auckland businesswoman Qiulae Wong, has long said it will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of seats.

After the final results were announced, Wong confirmed she would speak with Luxon and that her party’s bottom-lines – which include climate and environment policies and capping political donations – were non-negotiable.
The party would focus on bringing New Zealanders a stable government, Wong told media, and she did not rule out heading back to the polls.

“Clearly stability is important. But setting that more hopeful and aspirational vision, where we can come together as much as possible as New Zealanders and move forward, I think is the priority,” she said.
Having Opportunity in parliament was a “pivotal moment” for the country, Wong said.
“I have every expectation that we will get in there and we will deliver, regardless of what shape the government takes.”

Previously, Wong has said its vision for a low-emissions future, and an inclusive New Zealand, will drive its final decision. Its five bottom-line issues include action on New Zealand’s supermarket duopoly, capping political donations, a 10-year cross-party plan for health, ending bottom trawling in the fishing industry and strengthening New Zealand’s climate commitments.

Negotiations with Opportunity could hit a snag with National’s coalition partner New Zealand First. On Friday, Wong confirmed she would not strike a deal if New Zealand First’s leader, the veteran politician Winston Peters, serves as foreign affairs minister – a position he has held on three occasions.
“We think that his behaviour over successive governments is not the kind of behavior that we expect of someone in that position,” she said.

blocks.caption: New Zealand prime minister Christopher Luxon pictured in February with the foreign minister, Winston Peters, and deputy prime minister David Seymour, who is leader of Act. Photograph: Ben Strang/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: In other points of tension, New Zealand First and Act have diametrically opposed climate policies, and Act are also unlikely to back Opportunity’s drive for political donation reforms.

Greaves said the Opportunity party will have to make difficult decisions over what it is prepared to gain, or lose. “For minor parties, it’s really hard to go into coalition, or be seen as being too close to a major party or propping up a government, and then turn around later and sell their brand ... as separate from that [major] party.”
Labour leader Chris Hipkins said he was proud the party had gained the highest share of the party vote, but was disappointed it could not deliver a change of government.
It is the second election Hipkins has lost, raising questions over his political future. Hipkins said a decision over his leadership would be made after a government had been formed.

New Zealand could be facing weeks of negotiations in what could become its first ever four-party coalition. In 2023, negotiations took five weeks. With Christmas just four weeks away, New Zealand may need to wait until 2027 to know the shape of its next government.

articles.title: Threat from China looms large over Taiwan’s local elections
articles.summary:
Taiwanese officials raise alarm over interference by China in elections that will shape fortunes of ruling party

Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local…
articles.byline: Amy Hawkins and Yu-chen Li in Taipei

blocks.text: Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local elections that will shape the fortunes of the ruling Democratic Progressive party (DPP) as it navigates an increasingly precarious set of relationships on the global stage.

Saturday’s vote will choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across 22 districts. Unlike the presidential elections, in which foreign policy is often a key issue, the local elections, held every four years, are largely focused on bread-and-butter issues such as housing affordability and wealth distribution.

Nevertheless, China looms large over the vote, which takes place against the background of intense military pressure from Beijing. China claims Taiwan as part of its territory despite never having ruled the self-governing island. Taiwanese officials have raised the alarm over thousands of incidents of suspected misinformation or election interference, and certain candidates have been subjected to harassment from the Chinese authorities. There have also been reports of hundreds of China-linked AI-generated videos spreading disinformation about Taiwanese politicians disliked by Beijing.

Beijing calls the allegations of election interference “completely fabricated”. Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for China’s Taiwan affairs office, said the allegations “stir up anti-China sentiment to win votes”.

Wei-Ting Yen, a political scientist at Academia Sinica, Taiwan’s national research academy, said: “Even though local elections are not about China, the outcome of local elections will have huge implications for cross-strait relations.”

Most races are a tight competition between a candidate from the ruling DPP and the main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT). The KMT promotes closer ties with Beijing, and its chair, Cheng Li-wun, travelled to China this year to meet Xi Jinping, China’s leader. Xi has vowed to unify China with Taiwan, and has not ruled out using military action to achieve that aim.

blocks.caption: Cheng Li-wun travelled to China to meet Xi Jinping. Photograph: CTI/Reuters

blocks.text: Yen said if the KMT loses some of its traditional strongholds, Beijing “may need to reconsider what is the most effective strategy for influencing Taiwanese people”.

One of the most contentious votes is the race for Taipei mayor, an office that has been held by the KMT for three decades. The DPP has selected as its challenger Puma Shen, a national legislator whom Beijing declared a “diehard separatist” in 2024. It is the first time a candidate under sanctions by Beijing has run to be mayor of Taiwan’s capital city. In the neighbouring New Tapei City race, the DPP’s Su Chiao-hui is also proving to be a ferocious challenger to the incumbent KMT.
Shen said in a recent interview that even if he didn’t win, the capital’s mayoral race was “a slap to China” because it proved that “democracy works here in Taiwan”.

Huang Bo-kai, a 23-year-old law student, said his top concern was cross-strait relations and how US-China relations were evolving. “The world’s three major powers are increasingly willing to flex their muscles: the US attacking Iran, Russia attacking Ukraine. I think Taiwan could very well be the next target [of China],” he told the Guardian.

Taiwan’s president, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te, is detested by Beijing and has taken a bolshier stance on cross-strait relations than his predecessor, Tsai Ing-wen, who was admired for her ability to drum up support in Washington while walking a delicate tightrope to avoid angering China.

blocks.caption: Taiwan’s president, Lai Ching-te, is detested by Beijing. Photograph: Ann Wang/Reuters

blocks.text: Lai has pushed for greater spending on weapons to deter military aggression from China. The government has proposed a record 18% increase in defence spending for next year, including for drones and missiles, taking it above 1tn Taiwan dollars (£23bn) for the first time.

But many Taiwanese voters would rather that money was spent on more immediate economic issues. Lev Nachman, a political scientist at National Taiwan University, said the national leaders of the DPP and KMT had been notably absent from the mayoral races, reflecting the extent to which campaigns were focused on local issues.

Going into the campaigns for the 2028 presidential elections, Lai would “try to take advantage of the momentum that [Shen] and Su have built for the DPP,” Nachman said, noting that support for those candidates would not necessarily translate into support for Lai.
Tony Yeh, a Taipei man in his 70s, said: “To put it simply, the authorities should do more to boost the economy and buy fewer weapons.”

Taiwan’s economy has boomed this year, largely thanks to the pivotal role that its semiconductor industry plays in the global artificial intelligence rally. The economy grew by more than 14% in the first nine months of the year, the fastest rate in 50 years. But nearly 70% of workers earned less than the average monthly wage of 49,152 Taiwan dollars (£1,137) in the same period.
Yeh said: “Most traditional industries are having a really tough time.”

William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “The issues that really are going to determine their votes are livelihood issues including the stagnant wage, the astronomically high housing price, the affordability issue, and how the government can better make sure Taiwan’s incredible economic boom fuelled by the global AI growth is going to be distributed more evenly.”
Other voters have more niche concerns. Walking her dog in a park, Kuo Wei-tong, a nail salon worker, said policies affecting pets were among her top concerns.
“People are having fewer children and getting more cats and dogs,” she said. “I think that’s something worth giving serious consideration to as well.”

articles.title: US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough, Zelensky tells BBC
articles.summary: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is "strange" Trump has described Vladimir Putin as a friend.
articles.byline: Sarah Rainsford, Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent

blocks.text: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks.

In an interview with the BBC at his office in central Kyiv, Ukraine's president also said it was "very strange" that Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend".
"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, suggesting it was like hugging Adolf Hitler during WWII.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.
Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it wasn't clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.
The Kremlin appears to be resisting.
In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Amercians were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
So whose decision was that?
"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."
Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.
On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.
Zelensky defended the strikes, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".
He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without coordinating with its partners.
He declined to be more specific.
But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.
Recent strikes on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.
Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.
They've also plunged much of the city into darkness.
"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.
"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

articles.title: Zelensky questions 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview

blocks.text: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced his frustration with the United States and questioned Donald Trump's relationship with Vladimir Putin in an interview with the BBC.

"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky told the BBC's Sarah Rainsford at his office in central Kyiv.
